Researchers at the LHC have carried out precise measurements of the B^0_s meson's lifetime and the B^0_s->Mu+Mu- decay rate, also determining the CP-violating phase phi_s in the process. These calculations were performed by LHCb utilizing 3 fb^-1 of proton-proton collision data at 7 and 8 TeV centers. First, the B^0_s lifetime was found to be 1.502 ps by analyzing the B^0_s->J/psi Nu_Nu decay and then confirming the outcome with the B^0_s->Mu+Mu- decay rate, yielding a result that aligns with, yet doesn't surpass, the Standard Model's prediction by 0.7 sigma. Furthermore, determining the CP-violating phase phi_s was achieved by reconstructing the B^0_s->Mu+Mu- decay chain in different energy ranges, establishing a value of 0.375 radians with an uncertainty of 0.019 radians. When combined with previous outcomes, this result contributed to a more precise estimate of the difference between the maximum and minimum values of the CP-violating phase in the process, ultimately narrowing the range to 0.018 radians. Given that these measurements are highly sensitive to phenomena beyond the Standard Model, their accuracy is expected to significantly impact future constraints on several types of new physics. Specifically, the outcomes will place more stringent limits on several contributions involving flavor-changing gluons and their counterparts, as well as new contributions to CP-violating processes in the electroweak sector and certain supersymmetric scenarios, with new phases of MSSGR and NMSSM also amenable to such constraints. Nevertheless, the outcomes will remain relevant even in the absence of new physics, with the B^0_s->Mu+Mu- decay rate and the CP-violating phase phi_s being crucial inputs for a global fit of flavor and CP-violating processes at the LHC and in future experiments. Consequently, it is anticipated that heightened precision in such calculations, attainable through LHCb's 6 fb^-1 of data at 14 TeV centers, will greatly contribute to a more nuanced comprehension of the B^0_s meson and its implications for the Standard Model and its adversaries. This paper explores the convergence of optimized control policies in a stochastic control setting, where the underlying problem is partially resolved using a finite-dimensional grid while the rest is defined through a continuous stochastic differential equation. The challenge of approximating a rough stochastic differential equation component is addressed by introducing an additional variable in the finite-dimensional part, effectively refining the grid based on the current estimate of the solution. By doing so, we establish an abstract result highlighting the convergence of an optimized control policy as the grid is successively refined. This general strategy is applied to a specific setting involving a stochastic Navier-Stokes equation, and we demonstrate the convergence of an optimized control policy by refining the grid successively. The key innovation in our approach is the introduction of an auxiliary variable in the finite-dimensional part, allowing us to establish a continuous relationship that ensures the convergence of an optimized control policy. This relationship enables the use of a more efficient algorithm, one that successively refines the grid more effectively. As a result, we can achieve a comparable level of accuracy with a significantly smaller number of grid refinements. To demonstrate this, we provide a numerical example involving the stochastic Navier-Stokes equation on a two-dimensional torus. In this example, we show that our algorithm succeeds in achieving a similar level of accuracy with approximately one-tenth the number of refinements required by the standard approach. This represents a significant improvement in computational efficiency.

Our research extends the analysis of cosmic ray anisotropy observed by Akeno Giant Air Shower Detector (Agede3) to energies exceeding 4 EeV. Between 1995 and 2018, we found a dipolar component in quadruple moments of hourly counts for local solar time systems and found that its amplitude increases from 15.2 to 41.5 percent relative to the average flux over the same energy range. However, the direction of the dipole component remains nearly constant at right ascension 268.5 degrees and declination 42.2 degrees. We also identified quadruple moment variations of approximately 0.7 degrees in both right ascension and declination within the dipolar component, oscillating in sync with the 27.3 day solar period and showing opposite latitudinal dependencies for energies above and below 7 EeV. The dependence of the dipole's amplitude and phase at the GLE-79 event's energy of around 102 EeV is distinct from that at lower energies. The observed phenomena are interpreted as the combination of primary cosmic ray modulation by the interstellar medium and the effects of solar particle events on cosmic ray spectra and composition, with the threshold between these two components occurring at approximately 50 EeV. The study provides detailed data available from April 1995 to April 2022, offering a broader time span and more precise results than earlier analyses, and is in line with recent findings that cosmic ray anisotropy exhibit features related to solar particle events above 20 EeV. The research includes methods for eliminating the effects of solar flare events and deep dips on cosmic ray data and offers findings related to the dependence of the dipole's amplitude and phase on energy, but also finds additional complexity in the structure of quadruple moments that requires more in-depth analysis. The study sets the stage for deeper investigations into the connection between cosmic ray anisotropy and solar particle events, specifically by identifying small-scale components that may be related to GLEs and investigating the relationship between the dipole's phase and the rigidities of solar particle events. Our research examined the relationship between the centrality of collisions and the variation of the nuclear modification factor (NMUF) in heavy ion physics. We discovered that NMUF exhibits concentration in more central collisions, with a corresponding increase in a statistical model that accounts for events with mixed charged particles. Furthermore, our findings suggest that NMUF variations are influenced by the interplay between different collision centralities, with implications for experimental measurements of particle production in heavy ion collisions. We also developed event-mixing techniques that allow for the measurement of true variations of NMUF, even when selecting events based on their own properties rather than those of other events. These techniques may be particularly useful for analyzing experimental data in more central collisions, where events with different charges are rare and essentially unmeasurable within a single event. We demonstrated the applicability of these techniques to mock experimental data, with parameters relevant to current and future heavy ion experiments. The methods we introduced are relevant not only to NMUF but also to other observables that show similar behavior in heavy ion collisions. In addition, we identified potential opportunities for new research inspired by the event-mixing approach. In this case, the position operators can be represented in a straightforward manner using harmonic oscillators in separate directions, and a phase-space analog of the creation and annihilation operators is revealed. This structure also shows that certain classical symbols, which are known as star products, can be directly related to polynomial expressions involving the commuting momentum components. Furthermore, we have established that polynomial functions behave in a quadratic manner under these symbols, a property that extends beyond quantum mechanics to polynomial algebras in general. In addition, we have shown that our description of noncommutative quantum mechanics is equivalent to a set of decoupled harmonic oscillators by utilizing the properties of differential operators in the momentum space, and we have proven that the energy spectrum consists of a superposition of individual oscillator spectra. Finally, we have explored the context of Wigner functions and found that they maintain their classical behavior in the presence of noncommutative effects. Wigner functions now serve as a tool for understanding the phase-space structure of quantum systems that exhibit planar noncommutativity. Lastly, we have reviewed the fundamental principles of classical mechanics, Poisson brackets, and Weyl-Wigner theories to establish their relationships with noncommutative quantum mechanics. The success of immunotherapy in cancer treatment relies on a thorough understanding of the lymphocytic population within tumors. Advances in imaging and computational modeling have improved the analysis of tumor microenvironments, particularly when dealing with complex, three-dimensional structures. However, the existing methods fall short in accounting for the tumors' spatial distribution and infiltrating lymphocytes cells due to limited data resolution. To address this issue, a novel computational framework is introduced, which utilizes high-resolution data to accurately quantify the tumors' paracancerous lymphocytic infiltration using spatial statistics. This approach reconstructs the complex tumor environment by accounting for lymphocytic populations in the surrounding tissues and provides valuable insights into the lymphocytes' spatial distribution within tumors. The performance of this method is demonstrated on synthetic models and actual cancer tissue samples, showing its potential to guide immunotherapy treatments. Furthermore, the introduced framework is made publicly available as an open-source tool, facilitating the adoption of computational pathology in clinical applications. This is achieved through the open-source software called OpenLymph, which can be accessed via the following link: https://doi.org/10.5281/nao.chgUKf8vVxJQVgA. By making this method publicly available, it is hoped that it will be utilized by both the scientific community and the medical sector to enhance the effectiveness of immunotherapy in cancer treatment. Additionally, OpenLymph can be utilized in other computational pathology applications where the intricate structure of tumors is being analyzed. This is accomplished by utilizing the VTK/JNIB library, which enables the integration of the algorithms developed by various researchers into the proposed framework. The open-source nature of OpenLymph also facilitates the modification of its algorithms, which is crucial for addressing the challenges posed by diverse types of cancer, such as lung, brain, and breast cancer. To further advance the adoption of computational pathology, proposals for future research are presented, along with suggestions for improving OpenLymph, such as incorporating machine learning algorithms to account for the diversity of cancer types. By making the code publicly available and proposing future research directions, the aim is to encourage the adoption of OpenLymph as the go-to solution for quantifying the spatial distribution of lymphocytes within tumors and to stimulate additional research on computational pathology. To mitigate burst errors in high-speed optical communication systems, a method is proposed that combines Equalizer and Maximum Likelihood Sequence Estimation techniques. Initially, a discrete fourier transform equalizer is used to reduce the impact of linear distortions, followed by an mlse decoder that addresses the effects of burst errors. By incorporating this approach into the design of optical transceivers, systems with improved tolerance to burst errors and reduced equalizer tap counts can be achieved, resulting in more compact equalizer circuits with lower computational demands. Furthermore, this proposed method exhibits superior performance and efficiency compared to conventional mlse decoding and adaptive equalizer techniques. Experimental verification of the proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simultaneous transmissions of two 112 Gb/s optical channels over 50 km of optical fiber. Results show that the proposed method yields a significant improvement in performance, supporting data rates up to 128 Gb/s after 50 km of transmission. Additionally, the technique's ability to adapt to varying data rates and modulation formats is also illustrated. Lastly, potential applications and future directions for further research and development are also outlined. Time-series forecasting using temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) has gained significant interest recently. TCNs are particularly sought after for their ability to learn patterns in time-series data. However, TCNs tend to increase model size to enhance prediction accuracy, leading to elevated inference latency. In this paper, we introduce an innovative automatic dilation optimizer (ADO) to automate the dilation factor optimization in TCNs. ADO increases model efficiency by optimizing dilation factors, resulting in a significant reduction in model size with lower inference latency. We propose a novel dilation factor learning technique using a path-based strategy and a gradient-based optimizer. The proposed ADO is a versatile framework that can be applied to various dilation-based TCN architectures, enhancing the model's performance both efficiently and effectively. Experimental results demonstrate that ADO leads to a substantial model size reduction (up to 90%) and lower inference latency (up to 50%) without compromising accuracy across multiple datasets and metrics. Furthermore, we analyze the influence of different dilation factors and architectures, highlighting the advantages of our proposed ADO. The code for this paper is available at: https://github.com/hjdw2/ADO. Keywords: time-series forecasting, temporal convolutional networks, automatic dilation optimizer.

We establish the fundamental theorem for finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras, 
specifically that any such algebra is nilpotent and solvable, with a step-by-step 
analysis based on its Jacobson radical properties. Furthermore, we explore the 
relationship between finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras and their counterpart, 
finite-dimensional Jordan algebras, revealing that the latter can be viewed as 
a variation of the former with an added multiplication module. Alongside, we 
prove that for a finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra to be commutative, it must 
admit nilpotency of step 2, thereby establishing the connection between its 
commutativity and nilpotency. Alongside these findings, we also identify and 
characterize the simple finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras. Finally, we offer 
some specific examples of gradual Zinbiel algebras. 

Keywords: Zinbiel algebra, Jordan algebra, commutativity, solvability, nilpotency, 
simple algebra, example of a gradual algebra.

This paper examines the relationship between the quark-gluon plasma's macroscopic properties and the fluctuations in energy and entropy observed in heavy-ion collisions. Initially, we calculate entropy and energy fluctuations for the 1+1d Bjorken model, followed by conversions to more relevant physical quantities that can be measured in heavy-ion experiments, such as net-proton and charged-particle distributions. Next, we model the effects of initial conditions and collective expansion on these quantities using pseudo-peak parameters. Finally, we analyze how these quantities behave under varying conditions of initial conditions and temperature, and compare our findings to existing data from the LHC. Our study demonstrates that the models' entropy and energy fluctuations exhibit distinct pseudo-peak patterns as a function of temperature, and that initial conditions significantly influence the net-proton distribution, while the charged-particle distribution remains relatively insensitive. Furthermore, we observe that the collective expansion has a substantial impact on the development of pseudo-peak patterns, and that the net-proton distribution's behavior is more sensitive to this effect than the charged-particle distribution. Additionally, we investigate the sensitivity of these quantities to second-order coherence effects, specifically Machado-Pescialozzi splitting, and find that while they have a minor influence, this influence grows with increasing temperature. Finally, we propose that experimental investigations of net-proton and charged-particle distributions in various centrality classes will provide valuable insights into the quark-gluon plasma's macroscopic properties and the underlying dynamics governing the collisions. Our proposed algorithm, ALBA, is designed to calculate first-order correspondents in LE and LE-inductive logic with additional axioms, specifically focused on the subset of inductive definitions comprised of positive induction and negative mutual induction. ALBA's development is in the context of the HEPS architecture, an automated theorem-proving system that uses multiple reasoning modules connected by a mediator, specifically tailored to handle the concept of corresponding formulas. The algorithm addresses the challenge of determining corresponding formulas by breaking down the problem into a series of sub-problems and establishing a meaningful connection between them. Building on ALBA, we extend its application to compute dLE (dynamic LE) correspondents and demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through practical implementations. The ALBA algorithm serves as an innovative solution to an important problem identified during the development of the HEPS architecture, and its successful execution paves the way for further exploration of the underlying ideas in ALBA. Additionally, the algorithm's extension to dLE corresponds raises interesting theoretical questions about the relationship between LE and dLE and their corresponding calculi. Recently, a four-valued logic approach was introduced by Eichinger and Frischmann for consistent query answering in databases. Their approach has been further developed to accommodate additional features of existential data by incorporating a form of existential commitment similar to that proposed by Hiroyuki Seki. In this paper, we build upon this existing work and enhance the four-valued logic framework to incorporate the existential commitment and data by establishing a correspondence with the first-order logic over an extended language. Additionally, we demonstrate that the advanced features of existential data can be represented within the original three-valued logic approach, thereby indicating the redundancy of the four-valued logic framework when dealing with existential data. Nevertheless, the paper also presents an instance of database knowledge base which necessitates the use of the advanced four-valued logic with existential commitment, prompting an open question on whether such an extended framework is ever necessitated for consistent query answering. Moreover, we present a method for translating the four-valued logic with existential commitment into first-order logic with duality, followed by an examination of the consequent computational complexity. Lastly, we examine the relationship between consistent query answering and the four-valued logic approach, encompassing an investigation of the role of existential commitment within first-order logic with duality. An analysis of the syntax of the first-order logic with duality is conducted to identify the fundamental concepts which give rise to the four-valued logic approach, thereby enabling the demonstration of translation methods from the four-valued logic with existential commitment to both the first-order logic with duality and its simplified counterpart. Consequently, our findings entail a distinction between the necessary features of the four-valued logic approach and the mechanisms governing consistent query answering, prompting an exploration of the possibilities for consistent query answering via four-valued logic across various data sources. In this context, our study introduces the concept of combined databases comprising fragments of both data and ontology, thereby introducing the notion of combined query answering that considers the interconnections between data and ontology. Furthermore, an examination is conducted of whether the four-valued logic approach can be applied to an isolated fragment of such a combined database, necessitating further investigation of the relationships between different fragments. Ultimately, our study proposes the adoption of a unified approach to query answering, one which takes into account the diverse features and their corresponding logics. The TV-PARX model utilizes a parameter learning approach to capture complex dynamics within time series, including nonlinear trends and sudden changes, thanks to the inclusion of covariates that enhance the model's flexibility. A specific application of the TV-PARX model is the Time-Varying Poisson Probit AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PPARX) model, which is an adaptation of the TV-PARX model for modeling binary time series. We evaluate the performance of the TV-PARX and TV-PPARX models through simulations, followed by an empirical analysis utilizing two real-world datasets, a poverty rate dataset and a stock price dataset, with the former employing TV-PPARX and the latter employing TV-PARX. The results demonstrate the capability of the TV-PARX model to process complex datasets, accommodating various dynamic scenarios, and we provide a comprehensive implementation guide for the model's algorithm in an R package available at https://github.com/ChenWenKaiT/WMTVPARX. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields, a novel framework that uses a specialized neural network to represent complex task data and learn from just a few demonstrations. By defining a structured representation for task information, we've developed several useful properties that enable the easy combination of demonstrated behaviors with physical simulations. This allows our framework to learn manipulation tasks quickly, even with limited data, and we demonstrate this by training a Neural Descriptor Field to fold a blanket using a folding tool, based on just two input states provided by a human teacher. We've included video recordings of our results on this project, which can be viewed at the provided URL. Further details and source code are available at the specified website.

A unusual red giant star has been identified in the metal-rich open cluster Tononzintla 2. This specific red giant, located at 7.2 kiloparsecs from Earth, exhibits an extraordinary metal content 1.5 times greater than typical findings in rich globular clusters and a considerable spread in elemental abundance similar to that seen in medium-metallicity globular clusters. The abundance of s-process elements in this star is significantly higher than average and is characterized by a peak in the neutron capture process at iron, a pattern also observed in two other high-metallicity red giants found in the bulge of the Milky Way. The abundance distribution in this star is distinct from field RR Lyraes and is more in line with that found in medium-metallicity globular clusters like Omega Centauri, the highest metal content globular cluster in the Milky Way's halo. The abundance of s-process elements in this star merits further study to determine if it may be a member of the class known as Anum-1, characterized by a significant spread in metal content and varying abundance of elements with a pattern of nucleosynthesis that peaks at iron. If this star is determined to be an Anum-1 member, it would mark the second known Anum-1 member in the galaxy and the first found in an open cluster. Additionally, if the abundance of anti-matter in this star is found to be similar to that seen in the hydrogen anti-cloud found in the center of the Milky Way, it could provide evidence for the presence of massive dark matter particles with the opposite charge of matter in the galaxy. To determine the abundance of anti-matter, a spectral analysis of this star is needed using the MSND telescope at the Gran Telescopio Canarias in La Palma, Spain. If the abundance of anti-matter in this star is found to be significantly greater than average, it could mean that the galaxy contains massive dark matter particles with the opposite charge of matter. This research examines the structure of the dependency graph within the Formal Archive by Analyzing and Evaluating Proofs (FAEP) and compares it to equivalent analyses in the SMTLib benchmark suite and a general scale-free network model. A distinct correlation between the degree of individual nodes and their position in the network is observed, which justifies a proposal for an updated citation policy aimed at reducing reference redundancy in future FAEP proofs. Computational simulations validate the effectiveness of this approach in achieving significant reductions in citation count with minimal impact on proof length. The proposed policy is anticipated to promote clearer and more concise proofs by providing a formal incentive for proof clarity. The FAEP archive is anticipated to benefit from this policy, which is now part of the HAHA theorem prover. The proposed policy is subject to evaluation using the HAHA prover and the SMT solvers Zenon and Lean, with results showing a notable decrease in citation count for certain problems while maintaining comparable proof length. The proposed policy is seen as a crucial step towards assessing the clarity of formal proofs and facilitating learning from expert mathematicians within the HAHA ecosystem. The methodology employed is also applicable to other formal verification tools. The analysis of citation degree in FAEP reveals a distinct correlation with the scale-free model, characterized by a unique 'rich get richer' phenomenon, which is being addressed by the proposed policy. In complex real-world scenarios, a single image can facilitate the pose estimation of multiple objects for an autonomous agent. To tackle this, we propose a novel approach called Projection Grouping, where we leverage projections from multiple images to inform each other and jointly estimate pose and scene structure. Specifically, this involves three key components: first, we use a coarse-to-fine strategy with implicit functions to determine scene geometry from individual images; next, we apply a multi-view consistency check to eliminate inaccurate projections and prune the tree hierarchy; finally, we use a iterative optimization process to synthesize and combine relevant projections and estimate pose. Through our approach, we demonstrate significant improvements over baseline methods on pose estimation in challenging real-world scenarios. Additionally, our method surpasses current state-of-the-art levels in pose estimation and benchmark performance in the KITTI dataset. Moreover, our approach proves effective in handling scenes with occlusions, by successfully estimating the pose of hidden objects in indoor scenes using the Scene Understanding dataset. Our code and models are available for download at https://github.com/lingoer/pg-baro. With this method, we achieved the top score on the KITTI dataset at Valenzuela et al.'s challenge https://www.tallipedia.org/pg-baro-challenge, and we plan to extend our approach to other applications such as scene understanding and robotic planning.

Researchers simulate the development of binary black hole systems within a surrounding medium using computer models based on Einstein's theory of gravity. By examining various initial conditions and environments, they find that the interaction between the binary and its surroundings can significantly influence the orbits of the black holes, especially if the system exists in a merger-remnant state. Additionally, existence limits for orbits with a preferred orientation in relation to their surroundings have been established, and it has been determined that such orbits can only occur when the binary is moving at speeds greater than about 0.3 times the speed of light. Furthermore, when the binary interacts with a dense field of gas and particles, even a small misalignment between their orbits and the surrounding medium can lead to short-lived orbits. This research is an important step towards better understanding how binary black holes influence their surroundings through gravitational waves, and it highlights the significance of incorporating the effects of environments on binary systems within models used to predict gravitational wave observations. Additionally, it is now possible to derive properties of the environment surrounding binary black holes solely on the basis of the gravitational wave signals they generate, providing a new tool for scientists to gain insight into the behavior of these extreme cosmic phenomena. This study is based on findings from the NCSA, where researchers employed computer models based on Einstein's theory of gravity to examine binary black hole systems within various environments, and it is now possible to visually present the results in this context. For the first time, visual representations of complex, computer-generated data related to binary black hole systems have been created, offering a new way to present existence limits, and making it easier to grasp the underlying physics. More specifically, animated videos created from this data show the preferred orientation of binary black holes existing within specific parameter ranges, and can be customized based on distinct signals detected through gravitational wave observations. This research is an important contribution to the ongoing scientific analysis of gravitational waves, and it paves the way for a deeper understanding of and better insight into the behavior of binary black holes, their surroundings, and the gravitational waves they generate. This understanding is critical for the successful interpretation of future observations, and will significantly enhance the ability to uncover subtle features of binary black holes and their environments, ultimately leading to a deeper comprehension of the fundamental principles of Einstein's theory of gravity. The color-dependent point-spread function (PSF) associated with imaging systems is a critical factor that affects the clarity and accuracy of the captured images. While the color-dependent PSF primarily impacts multispectral and hyperspectral imaging, it also has a significant influence on conventional color images. This paper introduces an innovative optimization technique to correct color-dependent PSF in both multispectral and color image processing contexts. By leveraging a regularized minimization algorithm, our proposed method accurately reconstructs the captured images by considering both the measurement noise and system's point-spread function. What sets our approach apart is that it can be applied to both compressed and uncompressed measurement data. Furthermore, our technique is adaptable to various color imaging platforms and can be executed on computationally limited devices. Comprehensive simulations and real-world experiments validate the effectiveness and practical feasibility of our proposed method. Our code is openly accessible online. 

Keywords: Color-dependent point-spread function, image reconstruction, regularized optimization, compressed sensing, multispectral and color imaging.

This paper presents a comparison between the Dirac equation in an $R$-Minkowski spacetime and its counterpart in a de Sitter spacetime. We show that the two equations are analogous, with a specific focus on the behavior of massless fermion modes in the $R$-Minkowski spacetime, which exhibit linear dispersion relations similar to those in the de Sitter spacetime. We demonstrate that the two sets of modes can be mapped onto each other using a conformal transformation of the spacetime. Additionally, we derive the associated spinor currents in both $R$-Minkowski and de Sitter spacetimes. It is found that the current in $R$-Minkowski spacetime is not conserved due to the presence of a non-integral total divergence term, which is absent in the de Sitter spacetime. We discuss the implications of these findings for the behavior of massless fermions in the $R$-Minkowski spacetime. Furthermore, we extend the analysis to the massless Dirac equation in an $R$-AdS spacetime, where we find that the equation is equivalent to that in the $R$-Minkowski spacetime, with the additional feature of bound modes with linear dispersion relations in the near-horizon region. We conclude by discussing the generalization of this analysis to higher-dimensional spacetimes. We also derive the formula for the ground state energy of a massless fermion gas in the $R$-Minkowski spacetime, which is in line with previous calculations, and find that the result holds for any number of fermion flavors. We further explore the relationship between the ground state energy and the cosmological constant in the $R$-Minkowski spacetime, where we find that the energy density is negative and proportional to the square root of the negative cosmological constant. We finally discuss the connection between the Dirac equation and the behavior of massless fermions in the $R$-Minkowski spacetime within the context of the Causal Dynamical Criticality principle. We end by highlighting the need for a more systematic understanding of the relationship between the fundamental laws of physics and the properties of the gravitational sector in the $R$-Minkowski spacetime. This understanding will not only provide insight into the behavior of massless fermions but may also reveal the underlying reasons for the specific values of fundamental physical parameters, such as the cosmological constant, within the context of the fundamental laws of physics.

Our proposed system, OctopOS, is an innovative multi-layer operating system adaptation for mobile devices, ensuring seamless security across user sessions. By independently managing each user's layer, we safeguard user data separation and prevent malicious app behavior. Additionally, we devise a pioneering dynamic binary translation approach to safeguard system calls made by apps, either by blocking untrusted calls or reverting trusted ones. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of OctopOS in containing malware damage and mitigating CoW attacks, achieving a notable improvement in performance. Moreover, our findings reveal that OctopOS incurs a minimal overhead in comparison to the default Android OS, with a average slowdown of approximately 5%. We also successfully validated the viability of OctopOS through a real-world implementation and testing on top of Android 10. Our analysis highlights various strategies to optimize performance, including the benefits of incremental compilation in binary translation. We also explore the feasibility of extending OctopOS to other operating systems and present potential paths for further research. To facilitate replication and advancement of our work, we make the full OctopOS source code freely available for download.

Using a combination of experimental data and theoretical modeling, we investigate the
electronic and magnetic properties of cubanite (β-AuAs$_2$) to illuminate the underlying
reasons for its stable charge and ferromagnetic behavior. Our analysis begins with a
5-band tight-binding model that is refined to a 10-band tight-binding model through
cluster perturbation theory. By comparing the results of tight-binding and first-principles
calculations, we establish a reliable description of the cubanite band structure. Our
theoretical model highlights the significance of orbital mixing in defining the
self-consistent potentials and magnetic moments within the material. Furthermore, we
excavate the essential features of the cubanite Hamiltonian that arise from both
nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor interactions. Through a self-consistent
analysis of our model, we successfully explain the reason behind cubanite's stable
charge and ferromagnetic behavior. Additionally, our results accurately reproduce the
peak positions observed in the density of states and effectively replicate the
ferromagnetic ground state found in experiments. Notably, our study reveals that the
exchange splitting is most pronounced at the apex of the conduction band, thus providing
a potential explanation for the odd-electron fillings observed in gold chalcogenides. 
Our findings offer a theoretical foundation for further investigation of the unique
properties of cubanite.

The current crisis resulting from the global pandemic crisis has caused significant pressure on intensive care units, leading to a severe shortage of ventilators. To tackle this issue, we have developed a method for sharing a single ventilator among multiple patients, ensuring each receives their desired tidal volume. Building on our previous work presenting mathematical models and algorithms for this issue, this paper delves deeper into computational simulations and clinical testing to validate our approach. Patient models account for respiratory mechanics and flow rate characteristics, while simulations and clinical testing demonstrate the efficacy and safety of our method. Specifically, we found that our strategy can accurately deliver desired tidal volumes even in scenarios mimicking critical conditions, and consistently met safety standards for patient protection. Furthermore, we found that our approach can provide adequate oxygen delivery to patients even in low oxygen scenarios, and that ventilator noise is minimized when using our method. Clinical testing according to international standards showed that our technique met safety and effectiveness requirements. Overall, our method presents a viable solution for sharing a single ventilator among multiple patients.

This paper introduces a new attention-based model called Dilated Dense Attention Unet, which achieves superior results in esophageal tumor segmentation. After comprehensively examining popular deep learning models, we identified their inherent flaws in capturing global context and paying close attention to critical image details. To address these limitations, we proposed modifying the well-accepted Unet framework in two ways: 1) incorporating dense convolution layers to extract rich global context features; 2) introducing dilated dense attention blocks to focus on both coarse and fine-grained details within images. By combining these innovations, Dilated Dense Attention Unet successfully combined a deep context representation with precise attention to detail, leading to exceptional segmentation performance. Experimental data from a real clinical environment confirmed the superiority of our model, with a Dice coefficient of 0.895, Sen of 0.834, Spe of 0.857, and MAE of 0.103 achieved on the ESOP-HOP challenge test dataset. Notably, our model exhibited not only high accuracy but also robustness, capable of generalizing excellent segmentation results on unseen data with a mean 0.086 increase in Dice coefficient when applied to 15 random samples. Code and model weights are available online at https://github.com/Trigone/DDAUnet for public access.

Real-time formation evaluation is crucial for on-the-fly data analysis in the oil and gas industry.  However, traditional methods face challenges when dealing with large, modern well logs.  To address this, we've developed LM-EnRML, a new technique that utilizes machine learning to quickly determine the number of layers in a well and their corresponding properties.  Building on the ensemble neural network, LM-EnRML incorporates a multi-layer sector strategy and includes a new module to produce layer-specific data.  When tested against the industry standard, LM-EnRML showed significant improvements in accuracy and layer counting.  Furthermore, LM-EnRML achieves real-time processing speeds on low-power hardware.  When applied to actual well data, LM-EnRML accurately identifies 21-25 layers with high precision, outperforming the industry standard which reports 20-22 layers.  Additionally, LM-EnRML successfully predicts layer properties within 0.12-0.16 units of uncertainty.  Developed using Python and TensorFlow, LM-EnRML demonstrates the potential for machine learning to enhance and streamline formation evaluation processes.  The code is available openly for further development and can be incorporated into existing production systems due to its real-time capability and low-power consumption.  As a result, LM-EnRML presents a promising solution for fast, efficient formation evaluation in the oil and gas industry.  The code can be found at https://github.com/cailang/LM-EnRML. This paper examines the implications of using corpus-wide data and advancements in neural networks for named entity recognition (NER) within traditional finite-state transduction frameworks. NER models are created using both zero-order and first-order maximum entropy models, both with and without corpus-level information, and these models' performances are evaluated for various languages and domains. The findings suggest that neural network-based models excel at NER, and incorporating corpus-level information has a limited but significant positive impact on model performance. Additionally, using corpus-wide data yields substantially better results than domain-specific data alone, and this paper proposes a method to leverage corpus-level information while keeping the model domain-specific. This approach involves combining corpus-wide data with domain-specific data through linear interpolation, leading to improved results and eliminating the need for extensive domain-specific labeling. The proposed method produces superior outcomes when tested on three languages and could offer a more feasible path to making existing NER models domain-adaptive. This study's largest NER data set is also introduced, comprising 20,000 unique entries from the concretely domain-ed and extensively annotated ATIS dataset. The code and data sets utilized in this research are made publicly accessible.

Researchers have long been using the Infinite Convergence Condition (ICC) to evaluate the performance of relative localization in dual-tone radar systems. However, determining the optimal transmission strategy involves complex optimization under uncertain scenarios. To address this issue, we present a novel localization approach based on the Random Convergence Condition (RCC). It works by analyzing the probability distribution of ranging data to establish a threshold for type-I and type-II errors. By fine-tuning the RCC-based filter, we aim to minimize localization error beyond this threshold. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves superior accuracy, with an average localization error (ALE) of 0.35 meters in ideal scenarios and 0.75 meters in practical environments, outperforming ICC-based methods. Furthermore, the proposed approach exhibits better robustness in presence of sensor faults and outdated data. It is also noteworthy that the ideal ALE of the RCC approach can be further improved (0.25 meters) when no faults or outdated data are considered. Additionally, our method proves superior to traditional ICC-based filtering in presence of a single fault or outdated reading (ALE of 0.85 meters compared to 1.39 meters), and impressively outperforms baseline methods (ALE of 2.12 meters) even in presence of multiple faults or outdated data. A key advantage of our method is its low computational complexity, requiring only 0.1 seconds to process a single data set compared to 15.2 seconds for ideal ICC and 5.2 seconds for RCC in ideal scenarios. It is also noteworthy that our method can localize targets up to 4000 kilometers away from the sensor, making it suitable for a wide range of applications. A key innovation of our approach is its ability to estimate type-I and type-II error probabilities, allowing it to provide confidence levels for localization results. Moreover, the proposed RCC-based filter can be adjusted to minimize localization error, and we present two strategies for fine-tuning the algorithm. Finally, we validate our approach through simulations and a real-world demonstration involving a mobile target. Although we've made significant progress in multilingual models and evaluation metrics, assessment of these systems still largely occurs in controlled settings and focuses on individualized tests. In our proposed framework, we advocate for standardized, comprehensive evaluations of multilingual NLP systems that incorporate diverse, real-world data and criteria. Specifically, we've established a set of core performance indicators and accompanying benchmark tasks in several languages to assess the performance of these systems. Our results show that currently available multilingual models perform poorly on these tasks and often struggle to surpass the baseline models trained on single languages. To further improve these systems, we've incorporated additional quality metrics and conducted additional experiments, revealing that they correlate with our core performance indicators and provide valuable insights for future research in this area. In line with our proposal for standardized evaluations, we're making our results and models publicly accessible to facilitate future comparisons and advancements in multilingual NLP systems. This study examines the idea that online users' exposure to false information is driven by their geographical and social isolation. We analyzed Twitter data and found that users living in areas with clear cultural boundaries tend to spread misinformation at a faster rate due to their limited access to opposing viewpoints. This occurs because users are confined to their own information bubbles, unreaching and unreachables. We propose a mathematical model that illustrates how these conditions give rise to the spread of false information. We further developed a metric known as the "social reachability ratio," which quantifies the extent to which users have access to opposing viewpoints. This metric provides a practical tool for assessing and comparing the vulnerability to false information in different cultural groups. We applied our model to analyze the spread of false information related to vaccination practices and found that users with limited access to opposing viewpoints are more likely to hold anti-vaccination beliefs. Our analysis highlights the complex interplay between online information fragmentation and the spread of false information, emphasizing the need for further research into the causes and consequences of online division. Human IT experts can efficiently develop and execute effective policies using their common sense, but this simplicity eludes machine learning systems, which struggle with the large cost of training and fine-tuning complex models or gathering data. In response, we present a novel approach that employs natural language processing to enable a machine learning system to create and execute policies using natural language commands, without requiring expensive model training or substantial annotation. This approach leverages a pre-trained retrieval-based model to generate policies from natural language instructions, and incorporates a simple constraint-based reasoning system to resolve ambiguities and conflicts arising from the instructions. The system is distinguished by two key aspects: first, high computational power is not necessary for its policy development to be efficient; second, extensive annotation is not needed for its policy development to be accurate. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach succeeds in developing accurate policies that minimize costs in complex settings, surpassing a basic model that relies solely on model training. Furthermore, we showcase the practical applicability of our framework in developing policies for cache management, data retention, and advertising budget allocation. In this context, speech models are trained on speech produced during demonstrations by a single expert, with both the speaker and the listener being the same person. Our findings show that these models are not only sensitive to the underlying task being demonstrated but also pick up on subtle differences in speech generated for the same task but with different instruction types and error levels. Our analysis reveals that this ability stems from the models' capacity to distinguish between concepts associated with different tasks, instruction types, and error levels. These notes outline the connections between Euler-Arnold equations and the Faddeev-Shirikov equations found in quantum field theory, specifically focusing on the monopole and instanton configurations within the SU(2) gauge theory. We then explore the application of these equations in computing semi-classical expansions of Chern-Simons invariants, using the Euler-Arnold equations to determine the minimal action monopole configurations and thus derive the 1-loop contribution for the index theorem. Furthermore, we discuss recent research findings detailing the general 1-loop contributions for the Chern-Simons invariants, obtained by combining the classical monopole configurations with the instanton configurations discussed in the appendix. These results rely heavily on the classification of the classical monopole configurations as detailed in the appendix. 

We first establish the context of these equations and configurations within quantum field theory, specifically discussing how the Euler-Arnold equations contribute to the optimization problem in quantum field theory. We then explore how these monopole and instanton configurations interact with the Dirac operator and discuss the general 1-loop contributions for the Chern-Simons invariants. These contributions take the form of a sum of the interactions between the Chern-Simons invariants and the classical monopole and instanton configurations, combined with the Dirac operator's spectral flow, and demonstrate how the index theorem yields the 1-loop contribution for the index theorem. Finally, we conclude by discussing recent related research findings.

The rise of conversational interfaces demands efficient testing frameworks for automated evaluation. However, creating and assessing these frameworks is complicated due to the inherent difficulty in replicating natural user interactions and distinguishing true positives from false negatives. Existing testing approaches, typically based on rule-driven strategies, struggle to account for the vast linguistic nuances and complexities of human conversation. To overcome these limitations, we present a data-driven approach utilizing reinforcement learning to develop a complementary testing framework. This novel framework prioritizes diverse evaluation scenarios, encouraging the training of conversational models to produce coherent and relevant responses in unexpected dialogue settings. By incorporating a diverse set of evaluation scenarios, our approach surpasses the performance of baseline models in multiple evaluation metrics, such as consistency, relevance, and coherence. The success of this method also reveals the limitations of natural language processing systems when confronted with unfamiliar topics and situations. To facilitate further research, we make our testing framework along with trained models and evaluation data publicly available. Additionally, we introduce a new benchmark for conversational model evaluation, focusing on diversity and situation-based performance, along with a comprehensive assessment including diversity metrics and human feedback on coherence and relevance. This work lays the groundwork for advanced conversational model evaluation, addressing existing challenges and providing data, methods, and benchmarks for continued development. All resources can be accessed at https://github.com/ghrua/diversity-conversational-evaluation.

Researchers explored the capabilities of using Waste Inertial Confinement Threshold (WICT) as a resource for detecting a mysterious object with significant mass in our solar system, possibly an undiscovered Earth-sized planet, in a study presented in Physical Review Letters. By leveraging the existing WICT facility at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, they determined the sensitivity of such experiments in detecting the gravitational effect on the motion of particles in a known environment, specifically in a highly controlled and isolated chamber. Under optimal conditions, they found that an unseen Earth-mass object could be detected at a distance of approximately $10^{11}$ meters, or roughly 650 astronomical units, over 90% of the sky. However, the remaining 10% is limited to about 520 astronomical units due to the specific orientation of the Earth's motion relative to the solar system. Interestingly, the WICT-based sensitivity is comparable to that of large-scale gravitational wave detectors such as LISA, offering the potential for such experiments to be considered as alternative resources for detecting the gravitational effects of an extraterrestrial planet, and potentially even other massive compact objects in our solar system. Furthermore, the study indicates that existing and future WICT facilities could potentially detect the effects of an unseen Earth-mass object within our solar system, providing a promising new area for the field to contribute to the broader astronomical research community. Finally, the study also presents the possibility of modifying the WICT experiment to focus on detecting the Gravitational Redshift, another indicator of an unseen massive object, although it would require a significantly more sophisticated sensitivity level than the current experiment. This paper introduces a cross-lingual memory retriever to supplement translation memory with parallel corpora in multiple languages. By leveraging a monolingual corpus and three other languages' corpora for fine-tuning, the retriever learns to capture similar sentence meanings across languages. This allows it to retrieve relevant sentences from target-language datasets and incorporate their corresponding meanings into the translation. Our experiments show that this method enhances translation quality compared to conventional bilingual translation memory methods. Specifically, it outperforms current state-of-the-art bilingual memory-augmented models while utilizing a significantly smaller parallel corpus. Furthermore, the proposed method achieves comparable performance to models utilizing vast quantities of parallel data but with only 1/10th of the amount of data. The results indicate that this method successfully mitigates the linguistic gap between source and target languages. Additionally, we observe an interesting multi-language effect where the model exploits similarities between languages to improve translation quality. To facilitate future research, we have made the data and code available online.

In addition, we propose a statistical test that can be used to assess the validity of these models when analyzing the cosmic microwave background radiation. This study highlights the intricate relationship between the fundamental properties of the universe and its microscopic structures, and it suggests that a deeper understanding of these relationships is necessary to uncover the underlying physics that shape the universe at its most basic level. This paper investigates the Yamabe flow under an arbitrary initial condition, where the primary finding reveals the existence of conformally transverse Jacobi field solutions to the flow equation. Additionally, we establish the decay rates for both the L^2 norm and the L^infty norm of the distance field, showing that they decrease at rates respectively defined by sqrt(1/t) and 1/t. These results are derived without the restriction of small initial data, making them more broad in applicability. Building upon this discovery, we further demonstrate the existence of conformally transverse Jacobi field solutions to the Ricci flow under an arbitrary initial condition, where the solution set is characterized by the condition of being complete in the L^2 norm over the domain [0, T). Building from this, we establish the existence of conformally transverse Jacobi field solutions to the Yamabe flow over the domain [0, T*) for any T>0, where T is defined as the maximal time interval. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence between the condition of T being a maximal time and the norm of the initial distance field being greater than zero. To tackle the challenge of adapting to novel categories from a single example or just a few examples, few-shot learning was proposed. However, FL models are vulnerable to outliers due to restricted access to training data. This has been demonstrated to lead to inaccurate predictions when encountering categories with outlier samples. To overcome this issue, an effective framework called CoSaF was proposed to reduce the impact of outlier samples by creating distinct sub-spaces for support and query samples. By doing so, models can achieve better generalization performance on novel categories. Specifically, CoSaF was tested on the popular miniImageNet and CUB-200-2011 datasets for fine-grained classification tasks. Compared to current state-of-the-art methods, CoSaF showed notable improvements when only using a single example for each category, but its performance was slightly lower than some methods using more examples. Nevertheless, CoSaF outperformed all other methods when the number of examples increased to five. Additionally, CoSaF was applied to zero-shot learning by integrating an offset function with a logarithmic operator, resulting in comparable performance to current state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, CoSaF was successful in other few-shot learning tasks such as the Oxford-102 dataset and the real-world fashion product recommendation task. In summary, CoSaF represents a groundbreaking improvement over traditional multi-sample bases methods such as prototypical networks by achieving comparable performance on certain datasets and outperforming them on others. Moreover, CoSaF's effectiveness in zero-shot learning, the Oxford-102 dataset, and real-world applications makes it a pioneering framework for various few-shot learning tasks. Additionally, the theoretical analysis of CoSaF demonstrates its optimal performance in terms of model generalization. In contrast, the negative results of the generalization analysis of multi-sample base methods such as prototypical networks provide insights into the limitations of such approaches. In particular, it was proven that prototypical networks do not generalize well to novel categories due to the overlap of distributional averages caused by included outlier samples, resulting in inaccurate estimates of the prototype and the model's poor performance. In contrast, CoSaF's successful reduction of outlier samples led to better generalization performance. Moreover, the analysis of CoSaF's performance showed that its optimal solution can be represented by the minimum spanning sub-space of the included clean samples, demonstrating the model's effectiveness. Deep learning-based recommendation models have experienced rapid growth, achieving high accuracy in various tasks including user preference prediction, product classification, and image-based recommendation. To further enhance the performance of these models, researching additional modules that effectively capture valuable information is a priority. In response to the rising demand for multi-task learning in recommendations, we introduce the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module. This innovative module is designed to integrate a preference signal from a related task by combining a preference gate and two processing paths: one for capturing common aspects and another for extracting unique aspects. We demonstrate the GAPE module's effectiveness by incorporating it into the baseline CINERACS model, which achieves superior performance compared to other multi-task learning models in the user preference prediction task for e-commerce product categorization. Additionally, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the GAPE module's properties through ablation studies, module decomposition, and case studies to provide insights into its working mechanisms and potential applications. To facilitate future research, we have made the data set used in this research, named E-commerce Product Categorization (EPC), publicly available. Recent research by hand or through simple algorithms has revealed natural formulations of exotic cones for specific problems, often comparable to extended formulations in size and complexity. This work generalizes those findings to specific problem classes and provides a deeper analysis of exotic cones within the context of polyhedral theory. Specifically, we explore the properties of exotic cones in relation to their facial structure and demonstrate the applicability of our results to extended formulations. This involves examining the dimensionality and number of facets for both exotic and extended formulations across various problem classes, focusing on monotone and non-monotone scenarios. The study includes specific examples from the design of exact algorithms and the generation of benchmark instances. Alongside generalizing previous results, this work provides a framework that enables both theoretical and practical insights into the structure of exotic cones. This framework is further illustrated by applying it to combinatorial optimization problems, instances of the stable fixed point problem, and the minimum weight perfect matching problem. This research provides a foundation for investigating the complexity of both feasible and facet-defining descriptions of exotic cones, offering new perspectives on the interplay between polyhedral structure and algorithm design. A well-established challenge in medical imaging is the development of reliable models that can accurately predict unknown MRI data from clinical images. These models typically suffer from two primary drawbacks: they are heavily influenced by their training set and often struggle to generalize to new types of data. To address this limitation, our proposed framework, known as the Multi-Task Generalizer Network (MTGN), utilizes a neural network that is trained across multiple datasets while minimizing data duplication. By sharing learned features and performing specific predictions for each dataset, MTGN demonstrates enhanced generalization performance when evaluated on new, unseen datasets, including those not presented during training. Experimental results show that MTGN surpasses the baseline model both in terms of average prediction accuracy and patient-specific output quality when assessed by human radiologists. Furthermore, MTGN exhibits a remarkable ability to generalize to new datasets created through data augmentation, outperforming the baseline model even when trained on limited datasets. A thorough analysis of MTGN's performance is investigated through experiments combining multiple datasets, different acquisition protocols, and various imaging modalities, along with an in-depth review of the underlying architecture. This paper presents a framework for solving a variety of network-based multi-agent optimization issues. The framework models these problems as time-sensitive stochastic programs within a dynamic network, where multiple agents operate independently to make decisions within their own localized sub-networks that connect to the broader network. The key innovation of the framework is an efficient two-stage solution strategy for problem instances that meet certain feasibility requirements. In the first stage, decisions are made by the agents individually, taking into account their respective objective functions and any applicable constraints. The second stage involves a centralized optimization process that considers the inherent stochastic aspects and time-sensitive factors of the problems in question. We prove that utilizing this two-stage approach yields high-quality solutions that are near-optimal under certain conditions. To demonstrate the framework's effectiveness, we apply it to a specific problem of optimizing wind power dispatch within a localized sub-network that connects to a broader grid network. The results show that the proposed solution strategy outperforms industry-standard algorithms in terms of performance. The framework is part of a larger research effort that has led to the development of a groundbreaking new algorithm, referred to as the dynamic network clearing algorithm, which serves as the foundation for solving a wide range of network-based multi-agent optimization problems. The framework is also adaptable to various dynamic network structures and is compatible with different types of network connectivity, including communication, transportation, and energy networks. The framework is particularly suited to solving optimization problems in contexts where there is a mix of centralized and decentralized decision-making, and it provides a flexible solution to various problem instances, such as supply chain management, peer-to-peer networks, and multi-agent systems, among others. To address growing memory demands, researchers are exploring ways to utilize memory modules persistently. Although some proposals exist for file systems that manage persistent memory, research specifically focusing on relaxed file systems for persistent memory modules is scarce. This paper presents NOVA-relaxed, a file system designed to work with memory modules that allow for both persistent and non-persistent operations. By accommodating both large-scale and small-scale file operations efficiently, NOVA-relaxed achieves high performance on various applications. Experimental results show that NOVA-relaxed performs up to 31 times faster than standard NOVA for small, persistent writes and demonstrates similar performance to standard NOVA for larger-scale writes. Furthermore, NOVA-relaxed performs similar to Linux Ext4 for file systems that mostly consist of large-scale writes. Additionally, NOVA-relaxed displays high extensibility and versatility, as evidenced by its ability to support various applications, including database systems, web servers, office software, and gaming, with only a 5.3% performance loss on average when using non-persistent memory. In particular, NOVA-relaxed can handle small-scale persistent applications with an average performance loss of 14.2% and large-scale applications with an average performance loss of 2.3%. Moreover, NOVA-relaxed can execute a mix of persistent and non-persistent applications while achieving an overall system performance loss of 2.3% on average. This research is compatible with various memory technologies, including spin-orbit magnetic memory, and has been evaluated using a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental testing with real memory modules. In conclusion, the development of relaxed file systems such as NOVA-relaxed provides a promising framework for the effective use of memory modules in various applications and can serve as a foundation for the exploration of novel memory technologies and operating system architectures that leverage co-design principles. This research is ongoing, and future versions of NOVA-relaxed will focus on enhancing support for special memory technologies that incorporate a form of Co they refer to as 'Co Memory'. This concept involves a cooperative approach between memory modules and system software, with an emphasis on the re-definition of traditional memory semantics. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the development of a new memory hierarchy that integrates memory modules with the processor, promoting a return to distributed memory design and making-to-order computing. This vision is supported by research into the design of memory modules with integrated arithmetic functionality and is exemplified by the proposed NOVA-relaxed design, which provides a suitable operating environment for these new types of memory modules. For the finite classical Coxeter group Bn, we analyze the exchange laws for a generalized standard element identified as the maximum element within the fundamental domain of the classical Weyl group Bn. The fundamental domain is defined by the set of elements whose Coxeter length is less than or equal to that of a given element w, and whose descent set is a subset of the set {1, 2,..., n-1}. The exchange laws for these standardized elements were first described by Brady and Devoto. We establish a connection between the standardized elements and the group Bn, and use this to derive a simpler form of the exchange laws that is directly related to the Coxeter length and descent set of an element w. This more intuitive form of the laws can be used to create an algorithm to determine whether a given element of Bn is standardized or not. Additionally, this implies that we may use this algorithm to generate all elements of Bn that are standardized, and as a result we are able to provide a more intuitive proof that the group Kn, which is known to be a subset of the standardized elements of Bn, is in fact equal to the set of elements whose Coxeter length is less than that of a given element w, and whose descent set is a subset of {1, 2,..., n-1}. We also use this new form of the laws to provide a more intuitive proof that the standardized elements of B3 are equal to the group D3. We conclude by presenting an open question related to this new form of the laws, and its possible connection to the Kn Coxeter group system. We then further explore possible applications of this new form of the laws to other Coxeter systems. Lastly, we provide an overview of the historical development of the standardized elements and their associated laws, and highlight the contributions made by various researchers in this area. We also include an appendix that contains detailed diagrams related to the standardized elements of Bn, particularly focusing on the fundamental domain and its associated structure. We further outline possible future directions of research related to the standardized elements and their associated laws. We also present an alternative proof for the equalities |Bn| = (Kn)^2, |Bn| = |Kn|^2, and |Kn| = |Bn-1|, and we also provide a new expression for the order of the group Bn that is expressed in terms of the order of the group Kn. This paper introduces a probabilistic analysis framework tailored for collocation-based numerical solutions to ordinary and partial differential equations. The associated numerical methods are typically implemented in space-based approximation systems, often with a focus on deterministic approaches. In contrast, our analytical theory is centered around mathematical spaces of stochastic functions, offering a novel perspective on the methods in question. Specifically, we investigate the convergence and related properties of the collocation methods in a probabilistic context. In doing so, our discussion can be applied to a broad range of equations and includes a detailed examination of the method's convergence based on the choice of approximation system. Moreover, we develop an approach to further enhance the method's convergence rate by integrating a non-anticipatory feedback mechanism. Key aspects of the proposed feedback method are then validated through numerical experiments. The potential applications of this feedback method suggest its utility could be equally beneficial for other spatial approximation systems. The ideas presented in this paper may serve as a foundation for advancing the collocation method through the incorporation of probabilistic analysis and feedback techniques. T-centres, a type of defect in silicon, exhibit unique optical properties including multiple optical transitions, and thus have significant potential for applications in quantum technology. However, their behavior under strain remains poorly understood, hindering efforts to control their optical characteristics. This study investigates how T-centres respond to mechanical stress in silicon, particularly at cryogenic temperatures, and reveals notable changes in their spectral features due to stress. Specifically, a stress-induced shift in energy of the $^1A$ state in relation to the $^2E$ state does not occur below 20 K, whereas phonon-assisted transitions become more pronounced under stress. Furthermore, the emergence of a zero-phonon line in the presence of stress is attributed to a mixing of states caused by the mechanical force. This research provides valuable insights into the behavior of T-centres under stress and mechanical vibration, essential for developing techniques to control their optical properties. Moreover, the findings suggest that stress may offer a means to modify the optical spectra of T-centres without the need for intricate doping processes. This could potentially enable the creation of quantum devices with tailored optical characteristics, a crucial capability for the development of scalable and functional solid-state quantum technology. This study also highlights the importance of considering the interplay between crystallographic, mechanical, and optical properties when designing stress-controlled quantum devices. This work is a preliminary step toward achieving this goal, and there is a clear need for further research in this area. This could involve exploring stress effects on other silicon defects, identifying new defect species, and developing theoretical models that account for the multifaceted responses of defects to stress and other influences. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of the interactions between stress, crystallography, mechanics, and optics will be essential for the successful development of stress-controlled quantum technology. This work is a starting point for this exciting area of research. Researchers using large spectrographic surveys to search for exoplanets through radial velocity analysis face a crucial challenge in controlling a significant source of noise, radial velocity jitter, caused by irregularities in the motion of the parent stars. To mitigate this effect, a practical approach is to eliminate brief, erratic movements by identifying and avoiding certain line lists within a given observation window. While existing methods for selecting lines are based on statistical models, a more effective strategy involves a random selection process. We examined the efficacy of this approach by comparing it to a parametric method and found a notable reduction in radial velocity jitter, a more conservative estimate of error, and a lower threshold for detecting planetary signals. Additionally, we found that even when noise levels are low, the random selection method yields better results, likely due to the presence of instrumental effects yet to be accounted for. The model fails to capture such instances, resulting in over-rejection of suitable line lists. The random selection method demonstrates superior performance and is now the standard approach used for reducing radial velocity jitter in data collected by the Apache Point Observatory. The code for this method is now publicly available and can be accessed through the ExO HPC website. The techniques discussed in this paper can also be applied to other high-resolution spectrographic surveys, such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, the SDSS-IV, the SDSS-V, and future large-scale surveys like the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope. The code is also compatible with the Multi-Object Spectrographic Observatories, specifically the MOOG and ALAMO packages. This research paper proposes a new method called Hierarchical Range Sectoring for reducing the "hidden terminal" problem in sensor networks. The "hidden terminal" problem occurs when one node transmits data to another node that is outside its detection range, causing interference. To tackle this issue, the protocol divides each sector into smaller sections based on the transmission range of each node, creating a hierarchical structure. Each section is given a unique identifier and nodes are assigned sub-identifiers accordingly. This enables efficient detection of overlapping transmissions within the same sector and facilitates seamless data communication. Theoretical analysis and a practical implementation of this method show significant reductions in packet loss and medium usage inefficiencies. The benefits of this approach include minimal overhead and robust handling of node mobility. Simulation results reveal that Hierarchical Range Sectoring outperforms existing solutions under normal to high traffic conditions. Furthermore, the protocol is adaptable to various sensor network configurations and can be an effective tool for other anti-collision applications. The method's performance is evaluated through a multi-OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access) application and the associated simulation setup. The success of this approach motivates the exploration of its applications to other communication systems prone to the "hidden terminal" problem. Different object detection methods suit different computer vision tasks and are influenced by task objectives, available resources, and the quality of segmentation annotations. To efficiently select the best object detection approach for a specific task, we propose a systematic framework that evaluates and compares various object detection algorithms. Our framework, implemented as the efficient object detection evaluator (EODETEvaluator), is designed to be modular, flexible, and adaptable to different evaluation scenarios. It can compare the performance of object detection algorithms using commonly used metrics such as mean average precision (mAP) and mean average recall (mAR), as well as tailored performance indicators that take into account the false positive rate. Furthermore, EODETEvaluator can determine the best object detection algorithm based on mAP, mean average precision at different false positive rates, and mean average recall at different false positive rates. We also provide a tool that enables the comparison of object detection algorithms in an interactive graphical user interface, facilitating the visualization of comparison results. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we compared the performance of four object detection algorithms, namely Faster R-CNN, Faster R-CNN with multi-task learning, FCN, and UNet, using the MS COCO dataset. The evaluation results show that the choice of object detection algorithm has a significant impact on the performance, and EODETEvaluator can efficiently select the best object detection algorithm based on mAP, mean average precision at false positive rates Q=2 and Q=5, and mean average recall at false positive rates Q=2 and Q=5. Moreover, EODETEvaluator identified a significant performance improvement of object detection algorithms using a large dataset with annotation, and our code is publicly available for use and customization.
