Research on the structure of ordered trees has been extensively conducted over the past several decades. To further explore the underlying properties of these trees, this study introduces a new concept known as "standard ordered trees." Specifically, a standard ordered tree is a type of ordered tree in which the rightmost leaf node has a unique edge leading to it. By analyzing standard ordered trees, this paper compares their average number of deepest nodes to that of marked ordered trees. Additionally, exact formulas are derived for the average number of deepest nodes in standard ordered trees of varying degrees, denoted as $s$ or $m$, respectively. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that when $s$ is held constant, the ratio of the average number of deepest nodes in standard ordered trees converges to the same value as the corresponding ratio in marked ordered trees. This value is found to be $\frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}$ times the total number of marked ordered trees. Building upon this ratio convergence, it can be inferred that the proportion of standard ordered trees to marked ordered trees also converges to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}$ times the proportion of $s$-ary to $m$-ary trees. By applying the methods used in this study, possible directions for analyzing other types of standard tree structures are also explored. Finally, some open questions are proposed to invite further research on standard ordered trees and related structures. This study is based on previous works by Drmota, et al., Recurrence Formulas for Standard Ordered Trees, European Journal of Combinatorics, Vol. 28, Issue 4, 2007, pp. 1015-1039, and by Janson, et al., The Number of Depths in Random Ordered Trees, Random Structures & Algorithms, Vol. 12, Issue 4, 1998, pp. 331-363. It significantly expands upon the underlying structure analysis conducted in these studies. For trees with a specific structure known as standard ordered trees, this paper explores various properties, including the distribution of their deepest nodes. By establishing a recursive formula and using it to derive an explicit expression, the study determines the average number of deepest nodes for standard ordered trees. Interestingly, when compared to marked ordered trees, standard ordered trees have a lower average number of deepest nodes, and this difference increases as the degree of the tree decreases. Interestingly, standard ordered trees and marked ordered trees share a common ratio of deepest nodes, and this ratio converges to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}$

To accurately count votes through optical character recognition, a spell-checking technique known as Levenshtein distance is employed to correct misread characters. However, a significant shortcoming of this approach is its limitation to a maximum of three corrections per recognition failure, which is often insufficient to overcome the high error rates associated with poor image quality. To mitigate this limitation, we propose an extension to the Levenshtein distance algorithm that uses a probabilistic model to generate a set of probable outputs based on the input and then ranks these probabilities according to their likelihood of being correct, effectively providing a level of flexibility beyond the traditional algorithm's constraints. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by conducting a comprehensive evaluation of the Levenshtein distance algorithm and its probabilistic model on two separate datasets comprised of optical character recognition errors, one derived from the US Ensemble Dataset and the other from the TREC Video Dataset. Our results indicate that our proposed approach not only outperforms the conventional Levenshtein distance algorithm but also exhibits a level of robustness that is unaffected by the degree of noise present in images with low quality optical character recognition. Furthermore, we showcase the practical applicability of our approach by successfully integrating it into an end-to-end vote tabulation system that incorporates optical character recognition. This system has been successfully deployed in real-world election scenarios and has a notable track record of accuracy, with a notable example being the smooth tabulation of votes in the 2020 Delaware Republican primary election. In addition, we highlight the fundamental limitations of this approach, which is constrained by the quality of the optical character recognition it is attempting to correct, and propose potential avenues for further research aimed at enhancing the algorithm's performance. We present an efficient dynamic linear model for high-dimensional data featuring non-decaying coefficients and time-varying variables. Our method, building on the ideas of positive definite matrices and Fourier transform concepts, enables the recovery of infinite-dimensional data components. In contrast to traditional approaches, our model handles non-stationary data with changing variables and no prior knowledge of parameter dimensions is required. The algorithm developed for this model minimizes a convex risk function, leading to an explicit update formula for parameter estimates. We demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy through simulated examples and real-world applications, including one involving the prediction of inflation rates and another involving the analysis of stock market indices. Furthermore, we establish an interesting connection between our model and negative sampling-based methods such as noise Contrastive Estimation. The software developed for this research is openly accessible and can be utilized for other linear models as well. Additionally, the source code for the benchmark dataset used in the paper is also publicly available. Alongside the code, comprehensive tutorial-style documentation is provided to facilitate replication of the results presented in the paper. The fundamental principle of defense in depth in safety-critical systems involves multiple layers of protection against adverse scenarios. While individual components like pressure sensors in nuclear reactors possess built-in safety mechanisms, vulnerabilities in these sensors can still pose a threat if their security is compromised. This paper delves into the potential risks posed by hacking into differential pressure sensors in nuclear reactors, specifically considering an scenario in which a reactor's recirculation system is compromised. Our analysis reveals that if the security of these sensors is breached, an attacker could create conditions leading to an uncontrolled increase in reactor temperature. This threat underscores the importance of incorporating cybersecurity measures into the safety protocols of nuclear reactors, with implications extending to other safety-critical systems. Our research also demonstrates the feasibility of hacking into these sensors using an exploitation technique called "wound round picking." This method exploits a critical flaw in the communication protocol used by these sensors, specifically in relation to their supervisory control and data acquisition system. This method's efficacy was validated through a simulation of this attack on an actual nuclear reactor's recirculation system. Our research emphasizes the value of integrating cybersecurity into the design of these safety-critical systems, given the difficulties associated with retrofitting such measures after the fact. Additionally, this research highlights the challenges associated with assessing the security risks of these complex systems due to their custom-built nature. As a result, there is an urgent need for the development of novel methods for analyzing the security risks of these complex systems. This research offers an approach to modeling the security analysis of these distributed control systems based on their individual components and their interactions with the system as a whole, which is critical for effectively mitigating cyber threats in these safety-critical systems. As the transition to a low-carbon economy gathers pace, renewal energies are rising to prominence. However, their intermittent nature demands sophisticated storage systems that require careful management to ensure optimal operation. Inflexible storage technologies exist whose risk-averse characteristics pose an interesting paradox - they risk running empty under conservative management policies, yet could be more effectively utilized through targeted demand management. Using a model that captures these dynamics, this research analyzes the behavioral response of storage technologies in low-carbon energy systems and reveals how they adapt to varying management styles. Our results show that flexible and risk-prone storage operates in sync with renewable sources, leveraging their intermittent nature. In contrast, inflexible and risk-averse storage often struggles to coexist with these sources. Notably, we find that conservative storage management can result in curtailed storage usage, especially during peak demand periods. Building on this, we explore the implications of storage flexibility on electricity prices and find that a higher level of flexibility can lead to more competitive pricing. Ultimately, this research highlights the significance of storage flexibility in low-carbon energy systems and underscores the need for more competitive pricing mechanisms that incentivize optimal operation of these systems. Through numerical analysis and case studies set in the German energy market, we demonstrate the efficacy of our model in informing policy decisions on storage investment payback periods, showing that flexible storage can recoup its costs through reduced curtailment and lower operation expenses. In addition, we examine the distributional effects of storage flexibility on electricity prices and find that a more competitive pricing system benefits low-income households the most. To further this line of inquiry, we propose a multi-objective optimization approach that balances storage profits with the desire for competitive pricing, ultimately yielding a win-win situation for all parties involved. Through practical application to the German renewable energy market, we achieve a notable increase in competitive pricing, with benefits extending to renewable energy sources and low-income households. In conclusion, this research offers an initial framework for exploring the interplay between low-carbon energy systems, storage technologies, and electricity pricing, presenting novel storage flexibility dynamics and multiple avenues for further theoretical and empirical investigation. In doing so, it provides policymakers with critical insights that can inform the design of future low-carbon energy systems. In particular, our results underscore the significance of storage flexibility, competitive pricing, and renewable energy sources, all of which are central to achieving a sustainable low-carbon economy. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a more comprehensive theory that captures the intricate interactions within low-carbon energy systems, storage technologies, and electricity

By accurately reproducing the atmospheric conditions found on Mars and incorporating a CO2 circulation pattern reminiscent of the Earth's jet stream, we successfully recreated similar storm patterns observed on Mars. These storms display a persistent, meandering shape similar to those seen on Mars, and are also capable of merging with other weather systems. By simulating the interaction between atmospheric gases and surface materials, we can better understand the chemical composition of Mars' atmosphere, and how it may be affected by incoming solar radiation, as well as the thermal effects of atmospheric circulation. This research is an important step towards a greater understanding of the complex relationships within Mars' atmosphere, and how they may be influenced by the presence of dust, as seen in the case of the Argyre dust storm. Most active learning approaches in computer vision rely on pseudo-maximum likelihood estimation to select representative samples. This strategy works well for smaller datasets but faces challenges when applied to large-scale images, such as those found in ImageNet. Current methods often choose diverse samples based on single aspects like class probability or likelihood, neglecting the complex relationships between visual features and labels. To tackle this, we propose a novel approach, Selective Active Learning, utilizing a balanced combination of probability and likelihood alongside a contrastive loss to select more informative and representative samples. We evaluate SAL on two large vision datasets, Yahoo! A9 and MS COCO, and observe a significant reduction in uncertainty and improvement in classification accuracy compared to existing methods. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that SAL can achieve comparable performance to traditional active learning methods that use vast amounts of labeled data, but with significantly fewer annotations. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yunusbetil/Selectively-Active-Learning.

The proposed work introduces a higher-dimensional algebraic multiplicity concept, referred to as the generalized algebraic multiplicity, which is grounded in the Schur operator and is applicable to matrix blocks within a matrix of arbitrary size. This generalized concept is closely related to the classical definition of algebraic multiplicity for a full matrix block, and it offers an insightful framework for analyzing the dimensionality of matrix blocks that are part of a larger matrix structure. Building upon this foundation, a specific model is then developed to study the generalized algebraic multiplicity in relation to the Schur operator's eigenvalues, and this model is shown to be effective in modeling the dynamics of a single matrix block when multiple such blocks share the same underlying structure. The proposed approach is further demonstrated through computational examples, involving both synthetic data and real-world scenarios, to illustrate the analytical insights that can be obtained from the model, especially in scenarios where the matrix structure evolves over time. The developed approach is an original contribution with potential benefits, including the identification of critical transitions in systems defined by matrices, extraction of fundamental dynamics from multi-block matrices, and determination of key performance indicators for systems where performance metrics are linked to the algebraic multiplicity of specific matrix blocks. The accompanying software enables the implementation of the proposed concepts in a computational framework. The companion paper delves into possible extensions of the generalized algebraic multiplicity concept and explores connections with other multi-dimensional invariants. The paper is accompanied by publicly accessible software that facilitates the computation of generalized algebraic multiples and the modeling of dynamic systems according to the proposed approach. Our proposal creates a two-mode squeezed state of light based on optical parametric amplification, allowing the generation of large amounts of entanglement. A key feature of this plan is using a phase-modulated drive laser to generate two-mode squeezing, which directly relates to a desired optical phase parameter of interest. To better comprehend vortex line behavior in superfluid $^3$He, a model has been developed that considers interactions between lines and points of tensionless motion within a cylindrical container. This model is solved analytically for the case of two crossing lines and points moving along lines perpendicular to the crossing point, showing that both crossing line instabilities and point motion have similar activation energies. These energies are comparable to those found in experiments, and are influenced by the strength of the line-line interaction, but are independent of the line's pinning strength. In contrast, line-line interactions have no effect on the motion of sole vortex lines, and their activation energies are the same as those moving in isolation. This difference highlights a critical distinction between the behavior of superfluid $^3$He in cylindrical and spherical containers. Furthermore, the line-line interaction is found to be stronger in the case of two lines that do not cross, involving an increase in the line's local density, and may be a key factor in the formation of quasi-long range order observed in $^3$He under stress. The line-line interaction also enhances the motion of sole vortex lines, bringing them closer to lines in $^3$He under stress, and may be a necessary step towards understanding the formation of abelian anyon excitons proposed for $^3$He under rotation and magnetic field. The proposed model is relevant not just to $^3$He but also other superfluids and systems of linear defects in other systems. The proposed model is applicable to the weak pinning regime, characterized by a small ratio of the line's pinning strength to the line's tension. The ratio of the line's pinning strength to the line's tension is the same as the correlation length of the superfluid's local density fluctuations, and therefore represents both a fundamental property of the superfluid and a potential experimental control. The line's local density fluctuations are strongly influenced by stress, but the ratio is only weakly affected, allowing for the possibility of releasing its value. Our studies revealed that the behavior of these cumulants can be classified into three distinct scenarios based on the strength of the external field: (i) at very weak fields, the normalized cumulants follow the predicted behavior of universality classes without significant deviation, (ii) at intermediate field strengths, the normalized cumulants exhibit a crossover into a new state that resembles a strong-field behavior, (iii) at strong fields, the normalized cumulants show little variation with further increases, primarily influenced by two-fold symmetry. Furthermore, our analysis of correlation lengths and magnetization also confirms the existence of these three regimes. In addition, we determined the critical temperatures for disorder and phase transitions in the presence of magnetic fields, which show a linear relationship with $h^2$, a common characteristic for strong-field behaviors on various lattices. Our findings provide direct empirical evidence for the predicted strong-field behavior of long-range cumulant and correlation properties in critical systems. In fact, our results can be seen as a direct manifestation of the strong-field behavior of universality classes, offering a new perspective on how to study strong-field physics in a system with known critical parameters, a technique we demonstrated using a cluster algorithm. Our studies also offer a more precise definition of strong-field behavior, which can be characterized by the existence of two-fold symmetry in magnetic field responses, a phenomenon that can be observed through the long-range cumulant and correlation properties. In fact, our results indicate that strong-field behavior can be studied using the magnetic field itself, rather than being an intrinsic property that needs to be derived from the determination of universality classes. Deep learning models in Natural Language Processing (NLP) have achieved great success in recent years, but they can also suffer from bias and overfitting. Data augmentation, a technique used to expand training data by subtly transforming existing data, has shown significant potential in enhancing the robustness and generalization of models in image and speech processing. However, traditional data augmentation methods such as word/character level word embeddings alterations, syntactic alterations, and token-level transformations have limited effectiveness in NLP due to the complex nature of natural languages. Moreover, the credit that a transformation receives for improving NLP models is often misallocated to the augmented data rather than the model's ability to learn. In order to overcome the limitations of current augmentation methods, this paper proposes a novel framework called Generalized Data Augmentation unifying all existing methods and allowing for enhanced performance of deep NLP models with transformer architectures on three fundamental tasks: sentiment analysis, sentence classification, and text classification. The proposed framework aggregates the training data by adding diverse transformations to the input tokens and masks the transformation credits, resulting in superior performance surpassing state-of-the-art baselines and robust generalization on multiple datasets. The theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed GDA framework boosts the performance of NLP models by mitigating the difficulty of learning invariant representations and reducing the risk of overfitting. We have developed a new iterative optimization technique to achieve this, leveraging the properties of regular tree expressions and database closure properties to increase query result precision. Furthermore, we have designed an efficient high-performance query execution engine using the Triplet-based Regular Expression Matching algorithm and 'k'-fold iteration to refine query results. In addition, we have conducted experiments and evaluations using real-world datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed framework. Our research provides a foundation for advancing query processing strategies, particularly those focused on the efficient extraction of data from structured and semi-structured sources in the absence of complete database information. The Euclid space telescope, launched in May 2023, will observe approximately one-tenth of the sky in various astronomical regions, including galaxy clusters, blending its views with those of other spacecraft. As a result, scientists anticipate significant insights from combined data, which could lead to groundbreaking findings in the fields of cosmology, planetary science, and astrophysics. However, before these insights can be realized, the data from Euclid needs to be properly processed and analyzed, which will require the development of a comprehensive software framework. This article presents an overview of the data processing system being developed by the Euclid Photometric Standard Analysis (EPSA) working group, which is responsible for converting raw images into usable data and ultimately photometric standard stars. The article focuses specifically on the component of this system responsible for converting raw images into usable data called Image Processing Pipeline (IPP), which consists of four interconnected modules that work together to refine the data. This article takes a deeper dive into the Physics-Based Pixel Level Pipeline (PBPLP) module within IPP, which utilizes linear algebra and physics-based models to enhance the quality of the data. It also explores the benefits of this approach, which include the ability to handle varying satellite orientations and observe the benefits in simulated datasets. It is essential to note that while the description of the Euclid space telescope's image processing system is ongoing, the working group welcomes feedback and suggestions from the astronomical community to ensure the most effective use of its data. This article is a starting point for an ongoing discussion aimed at ensuring the best possible analysis of the Euclid data collection. It is anticipated that the full data processing system will be fully operational by 2028; however, the working group is already exploring the benefits of the Physics-Based Pixel Level Pipeline in other image processing systems and is eager to collaborate with other spacecraft operating in the same spectral range. It is hoped that the adoption of this approach will soon be realized across other spacecraft operating in the same spectral range, leading to the integration of Euclid's data with other spacecraft, which will yield groundbreaking insights in the fields of galaxy clusters, galaxy evolution, galaxy groups, galaxy interactions, galaxy mergers, galaxy morphology, galaxy physics, galaxy surveys, galaxy formation, galaxy evolution, and cosmology. It is also anticipated that the Euclid data will provide new insights in the fields of planetary science, astrophysics, and any other field related to the Euclid mission. It is further hoped that the adoption of this approach will enable the best possible analysis of the Euclid data collection

The demand for developing reliable and user-friendly automated lane keeping systems (ALKS) is increasing as they are critically important for fully autonomous vehicles. To create effective ALKS, rigorous testing is necessary to ensure the safety and performance of these systems in various driving conditions. Conducting real-world tests is impractical and excessively expensive, so it's more feasible to use simulated environments to test the functionality of ALKS. However, existing simulation-based testing methods fail to provide challenging scenarios that can provoke system errors. To address this limitation, we propose a method to generate complex road networks that can trigger incorrect behaviors in ALKS. These generated environments can simulate unexpected situations that may arise on real roads. We utilize transfer learning and a simulation framework that incorporates physical modeling and multi-lane roads to create realistic and challenging road networks. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated by designing scenarios that can cause an ALKS to fail and comparing its performance to a state-of-the-art ALKS. The results show that our method successfully creates challenging environments that can provoke errors in ALKS, even when subjected to validation tests by human drivers. Furthermore, we found that our approach excels in simulating complex interactions between vehicles and could be applied to different ALKS systems. Additionally, we discovered that our scheme yields a high success rate in generating critical crash scenarios and outperforms a baseline method using simple rule-based logic. The methods we developed are open to public access, along with the source codes and examples available at https://github.com/yhahn17/sisus. Along with the code repository, we include a technical report that outlines the methodology, results, and discussion in greater detail. Ultimately, our method provides a powerful tool for creating rigorous tests for automated lane keeping systems in complex multi-lane roads. The code has been optimized for a single NVIDIA V100 16GB GPU. The simulation framework is based on PhysX and was customized to accommodate a highly automated driving module. The ALKS model we tested is from the OpenCV repository, but our method is compatible with other ALKS models as well. The total number of training scenarios is 5000, with 1000 samples generated for each of five challenging scenarios. The code for the generator, ALKS model, and simulation framework can be found in the accompanying technical report. The total number of parameters for the ALKS model is 216 Million. Our study presents a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme for simulating quantum effects in electronic systems, allowing us to efficiently compute nonequilibrium quantum correlations. To test the new method, we used a linearized version of the hydrodynamic equations for electron currents instead of the full Lindblad equations. The hydrodynamic approach includes dissipation in the form of damping terms, which were directly derived from the original Lindblan equations. To verify the proposed scheme, we simulated the same systems using both the linearized hydrodynamic method and the full Lindblan equations. The results showed that the linearized approach can accurately reproduce the same quantum correlations as the full Lindblan equations. To assess the performance of the linearized scheme, we measured its execution time on a single CPU core, revealing a significant speedup of the linearized approach over the full Lindblan equations. The quantum correlations computed using the linearized hydrodynamic scheme were also compared to those obtained from the quantum Boltzmann equations and quantum Lindblan equations using simulations of a p-n diode and an InGaAs quantum dot. The linearized scheme demonstrated a notable improvement in correlation computations, particularly for short times and at low temperatures, where the full Lindblan equations struggled to converge due to numerical issues. Consequently, the linearized hydrodynamic scheme offers a highly effective solution for the computational challenge of modeling quantum effects in electronic systems, enabling the efficient simulation of nonequilibrium quantum correlations. This achievement paves the way for the development of efficient device simulation tools that can accurately capture quantum phenomena. As a result, our study provides a solid foundation for exploring the performance of devices using both classical hydrodynamic and quantum simulations. Ultimately, our linearized scheme can serve as a model for a future numerical algorithm that uses a multigrid or successive domain decomposition method to achieve even faster computation times. In addition, the linearized scheme can be extended to systems that include lasers and photons, and it may also be applicable to the simulation of quantum transport in systems that exhibit strong correlations and strong coupling. As a byproduct of our research, we developed a sample numerical library that can be used to implement the linearized hydrodynamic scheme, and this library is now available for public download. As a result of our research, we can achieve a speedup of at least one order of magnitude over the full Lindblan equations. Recent advances in action proposal generation and video understanding are primarily based on deep neural networks that utilize convolutional neural networks for feature extraction. Despite achieving remarkable results, there's still significant room for improvement, thanks in part to the limited capacity of attention mechanisms used in existing methods. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN), which employs two distinct context aggregation modules that operate across spatial and temporal dimensions. The first module, the Dual Path Module, leverages two parallel streams with shared parameters to merge global and local descriptors, while the second module, the Time-Domain Module, incorporates a temporal attention mechanism to identify temporal context. By combining the output of these modules, DCAN effectively gathers both spatial and temporal context information, leading to more accurate action proposal boundaries and reduced redundancy. Exhaustive evaluation of our approach on the ActivityNet v1.3 dataset demonstrates superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods, propelled by our context aggregation module and end-to-end training strategy. The code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN. Visualize our results on ActivityNet, including ground truth annotations, on ActivityNet Analytics too. In this study, a smart surface was utilized to enhance a radar system's effectiveness in situations with poor or blocked line-of-sight connections. The associated mathematical model can be applied to various multipath scenarios, providing a framework for optimizing radar performance in diverse environments. However, this research is currently limited to narrowband signals and would require expansion to accommodate broadband signals used in radar applications. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the potential of smart surfaces to enhance radar performance in scenarios with weak or blocked line-of-sight connections and provides a design approach for optimal performance in multiple-scattering environments. Given a topological space $X$ with a trivial second homotopy group, we can define a specific subset $R_X$ of the mapping space $\mathrm{Map}_*(X, X)$ consisting of 1-homotopic maps relative to a chosen point. In this paper, we explore the fundamental properties of this subset and establish connections to both Perelman's proof of the Poincar\'e Conjecture and Thurston's sequence of conjectures. Specifically, we demonstrate that if the first homotopy group of $X$ is trivial, then $R_X$ is dense within $\mathrm{Map}_*(X, X)$. Additionally, this density result drives the classification of spaces with trivial first and second homotopy groups, leading to a classification of spaces with geometric $E_2$ action. Alongside these main contributions, this paper also examines the implications of these results to ribbon embeddings and the surgery exact sequence. Lastly, several open questions and related statements are posed for further investigation. This work is an extension of the author's PhD thesis submitted to the University of Oxford.

We examine the stability of an equilibrium point for a particular nonlinear parabolic equation in a periodic domain. The stability of an equilibrium point depends on the direction, leading to the concept of local uniform stability and local uniform asymptotic stability. To analyze the long-term behavior, we apply the Melnikov method to find an asymptotic expression for the real part of the eigenvalues, which determines the rate of convergence or divergence. However, this approach is limited to small perturbations. To study the case of large perturbations, we use the Bernoulli method to derive an explicit expression for the real part of the eigenvalues, which depends on the imaginary part and reflects the local uniform stability or asymptotic stability of the equilibrium point. Consequently, we establish the existence and uniqueness of an invariant manifold for the Bernoulli operator, and we apply this result to obtain an explicit lower bound for the real part of the eigenvalues. Finally, we illustrate our findings with numerical computations for a specific equation. This equation describes a population model with noninstantaneous diffusion, where the mobility depends on the population density, and it exhibits a complex stability pattern that cannot be analyzed using a simple linearized model. Our study provides an in-depth analysis of the stability of this equilibrium point, including both local and global aspects, and we confirm our theoretical results with numerical computations. Additionally, we discuss potential applications of our approach to other nonlinear parabolic equations. We investigate a advanced variant of Lipschitz games, which includes multiple Lipschitz constants tailored to each player. This variant is mathematically represented as maximizing the minimum of several distinct sub-optimal payoffs, and can be applied to model non-cooperative interconnections between players with diverse objective functions and constraints. A recent technique called J-K-fold cross validation is examined for enhancing the reliability of predictive model performance estimates. This involves dividing dataset D into J subsets of approximately equal size and conducting K-fold cross validation on each subset before combining the results. We investigate whether J-K-fold CV offers a greater degree of performance stability in comparison to standard K-fold CV. Our analysis indicates that, in most cases, J-K-fold CV yields a more stable performance estimate, which can be interpreted as a measure of an model's inherent efficiency. We also establish an upper limit for the degree of performance stability achieved by J-K-fold CV. Additionally, we provide guidelines for selecting optimal values of J and K based on the concept of minimum expected loss. These guidelines can be applied to a wide range of modeling scenarios, including classification, regression, and feature selection. We demonstrate the effectiveness of optimal J and K values on several real-world datasets, resulting in more accurate predictions and superior model performance. Our technique is particularly useful for monitoring the stability of performance estimates over time. For instance, we show that the stability of web click data exhibits distinct daily and weekly patterns. We also present an adapted version of the technique for assessing the stability of model performance when multiple models are used. Furthermore, we highlight the challenges associated with the technique when applied to large datasets due to increased computational costs. We address this issue by proposing a method for using a smaller subset of a dataset while maintaining a similar degree of stability, which can be used for initial model evaluations before deploying the model on the full dataset. We validate our approach by applying it to a real-world dataset involving web click data, and we provide guidance on utilizing the technique for other datasets. We have made the code for our approach publicly available to facilitate its use by other researchers. The proposed method involves a advanced teacher model that uses data augmentation to provide diverse training examples for a student model, which is further enhanced through a multi-task training process. The use of an auxiliary loss function with Sigmoid cross-entropy loss facilitates accurate prediction on various medical image datasets, which have varying class distributions. Comprehensive experiments validating our approach include evaluating highly efficient student models against state-of-the-art benchmarks on three critical medical applications: fundus lesion detection, breast cancer diagnosis, and pulmonary disease detection from chest X-rays, in addition to an evaluation of the proposed method's effectiveness in improving medical image classification accuracy. Notably, our approach proves particularly effective in correcting classification errors caused by dataset imbalances. We re-examine the concepts of jamming in frictionless and frictional systems, specifically in three-dimensional space, where asymmetry is absent. In isotropic frictionless systems, there is a critical point marked by zero sound speed and no motion; this point is distinguished by the same exponents regardless of how the system is manipulated. In such cases, the dimensions of the disorder matrix that describes the structure of a jammed state directly relates to the exponent that defines the point of jamming. We also re-evaluate the physics of shear jamming present in isotropic systems under the influence of friction. It is suggested that these systems follow different universal behaviors governed by separate critical exponents. Furthermore, we extend the physics of shear and frictionless jamming to systems where asymmetry is present, using a symmetry-reduced disorder matrix that includes the dimensions of this reduced matrix as an additional parameter that defines the point of jamming. We propose that such a model can be applied to any dimensional space. Additionally, we provide a framework for calculating the sound speed in systems located anywhere in the phase space that defines the motion of systems during their jamming process. This framework is based on the principles of rescaled volume and its relationship with the motion of systems as they jam. Finally, we apply this framework to systems where asymmetry is present, using the dimensions of the symmetry-reduced disorder matrix to determine the dimensions of the actual disorder matrix, which is crucial for understanding the sound speed in systems located near the point of shear jamming. To explore this phenomenon theoretically, we develop a framework using a Gutzwiller projection operator and apply it to a specific case study of a two-dimensional square lattice. Notably, our findings demonstrate that the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions can be adjusted through application of an external magnetic field, providing a possibility to control this interaction and, in turn, spin-triplet pairing in strontium ruthenates. Our analysis further highlights the importance of considering a two-dimensional lattice structure and the effects of hole clustering on spin-triplet pairing. Using a velocity distribution for Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) in our galaxy, which is based on measurements of gamma-ray spectra, we calculate the rate of collisions between WIMPs and atomic nuclei. We find that, at low energies, the majority of halo WIMPs have velocities that are significantly higher than those observed in a one-dimensional analysis of WIMP collisions. This discrepancy arises because the one-dimensional approach includes a larger share of the slowest-moving WIMPs, which are more likely to cause collisions that result in atomic recoils. Furthermore, we found that the one-dimensional analysis overestimates the number of these slow-moving WIMPs by a factor of about two. We also derived a lower bound on the maximum velocity of halo WIMPs, which is roughly 70 kilometers per second, and discussed how this lower bound could be tightened with the help of upgraded sensors that are capable of detecting smaller atomic recoils. Finally, we established that the current sensitivity of these experiments allows for the creation of WIMP annihilation maps of the galaxy, which could be confirmed through the detection of gamma-ray spectra in multiple energy bands. This, in turn, could lead to the development of more precise methods for predicting the intensity of WIMP annihilation in various environments. Ultimately, if the intensity of gamma-ray spectra in the galaxy's center can be increased by a factor of about 100, we believe that it will be possible to confirm the existence of WIMPs through the detection of their annihilation in this location. However, if the intensity of gamma-ray spectra in the galaxy's center cannot be increased beyond its current level by at least a factor of about 10, we predict that experiments will either have converged to a value for the WIMP's spin-conserving scattering cross-section, or they will have reached a limit where they are unable to distinguish WIMPs from other particle candidates that have similar properties. Either of these outcomes will still allow for further research into these experiments and their results. Public sector employees who frequently use search engines for work may be influenced by biased search results, which can lead to unfair decisions. This research assesses the prevalence of biased search results involving essential Web information for two common search engines, Google and Bing, in relation to high-ranking public sector jobs in the United States and Canada. We examine the frequency of search results containing negative information about prominent public figures in those countries. Specifically, we investigated 20 high-profile politicians and government officials in the U.S. and 10 in Canada. Our findings show that Google and Bing both return relevant but inaccurate negative information for some of these public figures more often than would be expected by chance. This occurs around 20-30% of the time for Google and 10-20% of the time for Bing. Our research suggests that both search engines' low bias rates are likely due to the same reason: neither uses up-to-date information to filter search results. Our study also includes an analysis of the potential causes of algorithmic bias and its potential impact on decision-making. Ultimately, our findings indicate that both Google and Bing return search results containing negative information about prominent public figures frequently enough to warrant concern. This is particularly true for Google, which returns relevant but inaccurate information around 25% of the time. This level of bias is likely sufficient to influence decisions about these public figures. Given the many high-stakes decisions that rely on search engine results, it is essential to address this issue. One possible solution could involve implementing more effective methods for managing search results, such as displaying a warning when results are outdated or incorporating more reliable information sources. Additionally, both Google and Bing could provide users with more detailed information about the credibility of search results and offer a "trust level" for search results that is based on user feedback. This not only could help reduce the negative impact of biased search results but also provide users with a greater understanding of the information they are viewing. This paper introduces rCASPR, a revised version of the Convolutional Algebraic Sampling using Partial Derivatives method, which modifies traditional linear sampling by adding second-order derivative constraints. We demonstrate that the proposed rCASPR outperforms linear sampling in terms of Point Spread Function contrast, and show that rCASPR sampled images can be represented as super-resolved high-frequency signals. Additionally, we show that rCASPR sampled data contains more information than linear sampling, allowing for increased resolution without the need for prior structures. This is achieved through an iterative Distorted Wave Propagation algorithm, which modifies the sampled data's frequency spectrum to match desired high-frequency properties. We demonstrate the effectiveness of rCASPR for limited-angle tomographic reconstructions using simulated data and a real-world clinical dataset. The proposed method's results highlight its superior performance over traditional linear sampling and some state-of-the-art deep learning-based models, particularly in limited-data scenarios. The author also provides the implementation of the proposed rCASPR method and comparative examples on GitHub. The author posits that the success of rCASPR stems from its ability to increase the sampling efficiency by capturing more information in the sampled data. The author suggests that the proposed method's high-performance results in limited-angle tomographic reconstruction make it worthy of exploration in other medical imaging applications. The author also suggests that the use of second-order derivative constraints could be an valuable strategy for improving sampling efficiency in the future. The author plans to investigate the application of the proposed rCASPR method to real-world data and explore the use of higher-order derivative constraints. The author hopes that the proposed rCASPR method can serve as a starting point for developing more advanced sampling methods that leverage the convective and algebraic properties of imaging systems. This study provides novel data insights regarding the shipping industry's shift from cartel behavior to individual competition. Our analysis of Japanese data reveals how freight rates and shipping quantities changed from 1990 to 2019, offering an examination of the Empirical Paradox within this context. Initially, during the cartel era, freight rates followed a standard breaking pattern, indicating power law behavior, whereas shipping quantities displayed Poisson distribution characteristics. In contrast, the post-cartel period exhibits extraordinary frequency fluctuations and a significant increase in shipping quantities, with time series models indicating an exponential growth component. Furthermore, our analysis discloses the existence of a fractal scaling pattern within both regimes, albeit with distinct exponents. The existence of a critical point is also confirmed, with a phase diagram illustrating the diverse dynamics based on shipping costs and the power of individual action. Our research demonstrates that the shipping industry's complex dynamics stem primarily from the interplay between competition and coordination among agents, with implications extending to the study of other multi-agent systems. Additionally, this work paves the way for empirical investigations of the shipping industry's transition using theoretical models of complex systems and critical phenomena. Specifically, we explore and analyze the consequences of launching an 'agent-based model' that mimics the industry's shift from cartel behavior to individual competition, revealing how the power of cooperation and the power of individual action can influence the emergence of complex dynamics. Lastly, we discuss potential avenues for further research, including the incorporation of technological advancements and institutional frameworks into such models. By combining theoretical and empirical analysis, this study offers an unprecedented examination of the shipping industry's complex evolution. Consequently, our analysis may offer valuable insights for policymakers seeking to manage transition dynamics in other multi-agent systems, particularly those affected by significant institutional changes. This loom space triangulation arises from a specific type of subcomplex within a construction related to loop space triangulations. Furthermore, for spaces that are neither points nor empty, their loom space triangulations have a distinct, non-trivial structure. Additionally, for some spaces, their loom space triangulations can be connected to the original space's triangulation through a continuous transformation. This relationship between loop space and loom space triangulations can be examined in the context of certain high-dimensional spaces, including orbit spaces and their associated loop and loom spaces. Consequently, this insight leads to a deeper understanding of the topological properties of loom spaces in relation to their loop spaces. This knowledge further enables the identification of specific subcomplexes within loop space triangulations and reveals the associated loom space triangulations in a more direct manner. This approach is then applied to the theoretical analysis of a particular family of loop spaces, where its loom space triangulations can be particularly simple, leading to a more straightforward analysis of the topological properties of this family of loop spaces. This research also introduces several open questions related to the relationships between loop space triangulations and loom space triangulations. Alongside this, related theoretical connections to 2-dimensional surface triangulations are explored and several examples are provided to illustrate these concepts in action. This work is a precursor to further research on the interlinkages between loop space triangulations, loom space triangulations, and their associated surface triangulations. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have consistently demonstrated superiority over traditional deep learning techniques in processing complex relational data. Researchers attribute the exceptional predictive capabilities of GNNs to their capability to leverage both node attributes and graph structure. Conversely, GNNs might only have access to a standalone graph dataset. In this paper, we explore the fundamental question of how much a GNN's performance relies on graph structure as opposed to node features. To investigate this, we develop a random graph generator that is fully independent of node attributes and incorporates it into an experimental framework. Our results indicate that graph structure accounts for a substantial 84% of a standard GNN's performance, while node features contribute the remaining 16%. Moreover, we observe that graph structure's importance fluctuates between different GNN models, and we shed light on the underlying factors influencing this variability. Ultimately, our discoveries pinpoint potential areas for further improvement in future advancements of graph neural networks. We have openly shared our code and resources at https://github.com/fghan93/How-much-GNNs-need-structure for public access.

We analyze how adaptive input affects the performance of traditional estimators in
dimensionality reduction techniques, such as PCA and MDS, when applied to network
data. By utilizing degree-based sampling and degree-based weighting, our methods
provide robust dimensionality reduction results, especially when dealing with power-law
distributions. We demonstrate theoretically and empirically that our approach
yielding adaptive input leads to more reliable estimates compared to non-adaptive
alternatives. Furthermore, our degree-based weighting technique offers an
advantage over sampling-only methods. Specifically, we observe a reduction in
estimation error and a decrease in the variance of our estimators when using
degree-based weighting. The benefits of our methods are showcased through
simulations and real-world data applications, involving co-author networks and
electroencephalogram recordings. We conclude by discussing potential applications
and future research directions for these methods. We also offer relevant software
and data at the mentioned repository link.

This paper focuses on compact subsets of a two-dimensional manifold with positive area and explores how they minimize that area under the constraint of containing a given discrete set of points. We investigate previously unknown geometric structures associated with compact, minimal areas in a neighborhood of singular points. Through specific examples and general properties, it's shown that any two such associated geometries are equivalent using a combination of cut-and-paste techniques and analytic variations. These results expand our understanding of the classification of compact, minimal areas by revealing the existence of distinct classes related to the topological properties of the underlying manifold. Moreover, the relationship between points in a discrete set can dictate the structure of associated geometries, allowing for their classification based on the combinatorial properties of that set. This research is part of a broader study aimed at identifying compact, area-minimizing sets in a two-dimensional manifold by analyzing the associated geometries with singular points. Those singular points are bounded by four distinct minimal areas, each corresponding to a distinct geometric structure. By recognizing the overlap between these areas as flat surfaces, we establish the existence of specific structures associated with compact, minimal areas by applying surgery-style arguments to previously discovered structures related to four-point sets. This research expands the current knowledge on compact, area-minimizing sets containing a given discrete set of points by providing a deeper understanding of the associated geometric structures. Additionally, it paves the way for investigating more complex discrete sets.

Using a Ginzburg-Landau model, we calculate the entropy within a vortex core in type-II superconductors and find it to be significantly lower than the entropy associated with a moving magnetic flux line. Specifically, for a London model, the entropy in the vortex core is given by $S \approx k_B T \ln(2)/(\pi \xi^2)$, where $\xi$ is the coherence length, and this can also be expressed as $S \approx \beta T^2/(2\pi)$, with $\beta$ being a dimensionless ratio of thermal energy to magnetic energy within a London penetration depth. Notably, this entropy is much smaller than the entropy associated with a moving magnetic flux line in a superconductor, and is further reduced by the superconductor's non-uniformity, effectively creating an entropy difference between up and down vortex core states. This entropy distinction leads to an energy barrier that must be overcome in order to change a vortex line's direction, and this energy barrier is found to be comparable to the thermal energy and may influence the dynamics of vortex lines at low temperatures. This concept of entropy-driven barriers may also be relevant to other systems of defects that pin magnetic flux lines, such as grain boundaries in superconducting thin films and networks. Finally, our calculations on vortex-phonon interactions suggest that vortex lines may interact with phonons not just locally within the vortex core but also more broadly along the entire length of the vortex line. This longer-range interaction could have an impact on the lattice heating and phonon emission associated with vortex lines moving under tension. Quantitative analysis in stock market prediction involves using technical indicators and historical price data, which can be combined with machine learning algorithms to enhance prediction accuracy. Deep learning neural networks are particularly suited for handling large datasets, and in this research, we investigate their potential in stock market prediction. Specifically, we examine the effectiveness of using historical price data and technical indicators in forecasting future stock prices, leveraging the capabilities of LSTM and GRU models. Our analysis yields comparable performance for both models, and surprisingly, utilizing technical indicators instead of historical price data results in similar prediction outcomes. This research offers insights into employing technical indicators and historical price data with recurrent neural networks in stock market prediction, laying the groundwork for future exploration of model configurations and predictions extending multiple days into the future. As a complementary aspect, we develop a user-friendly graphical user interface for ease of access to our dataset and predictive models via Web-based interface, making it simple for users to input stocks, select models, and retrieve predictions. By separating the Einstein equations into two independent sets of equations, Hanee and Kiyota have successfully re-expressed the conventional 2+1 dimensional lattice gravity variational principle in terms of two independent boundary observables. We extend this work to accommodate a general U(N) gauge group and demonstrate the fundamental nature of Hanee and Kiyota's findings. Furthermore, we outline a straightforward computational strategy for calculating the boundary observables directly from the original variational principle. This approach streamlines the process compared to deriving the simplified equations of motion and then calculating the boundary observables in the simplified system. Along the way, we clarify the relationship between the original variational principle and the simplified equations of motion by showing that the latter can be viewed as a particular representation of the former. We also establish a direct relationship between the two sets of boundary observables. Additionally, we explore the connection between the original variational principle and a specific gauge condition within the simplified equations of motion. This analysis enables us to define a fundamental chart for a coordinatized configuration space associated with the original variational principle. Finally, we discuss potential future directions related to this research. Those involved could benefit from further mathematical formulation and coordinate-based analysis of the configuration space, as well as potential connections to symplectic geometry. Moreover, there could be value in examining related concepts, such as the symplectic structure of the fundamental group, in the broader context of 2+1 dimensional lattice gravity. Lastly, there may be benefits to extending this research to higher-dimensional lattices and the associated Montroll-Potts model. This could provide a framework for exploring topological features of lattice gravity in those dimensions. The motion of a solid object through a granular material is influenced by the rate at which it is moved and the properties of the surrounding material. In this study, a cylindrical probe was used to measure the resistance it encountered as it moved through different layers of granular materials at varying speeds. The measurements were taken over a range of 10,000 times slower than the rate at which the grains can jump to the speed at which the grains are poured, and were compared to two existing theories used to predict how a solid object moves through a granular material. One of these theories only works when the movement is slow enough that the solid object can push through the material by moving grains out of the way one by one, and the other theory only applies when the movement is fast enough that the solid object can push through the material by displacing a layer of grains at a time. It was found that at intermediate speeds, the measurements fell somewhere in between these two extremes, and that the properties of the material played a more significant role at intermediate speeds than at very slow or very fast speeds. Additionally, the measurements were compared to simulations that took into account how the movement of the cylindrical probe affected the surrounding grains, and it was found that these simulations were able to accurately predict the measurements when the movement was fast enough that the grains had no time to respond to the movement of the surrounding layers, but not when the movement was slow enough that the grains had time to respond to the movement of the surrounding layers. Using high-resolution spectroscopy from HIRES and UVES, we analyzed a complete sample of 13 starburst galaxy candidates within 30 million light-years, which shows gas outflows induced by massive starbursts. These observations at ultraviolet and optical wavelengths help us study the ionized gas outflows and their impact on starburst galaxies. Our data show that gas outflows in these galaxies can deplete their gas supply 10 to 100 times slower than typical spiral galaxies. Furthermore, we found a correlation between the rate of gas depletion and the energy generated by the massive starbursts, which suggests that these outflows are a critical factor in how gas is used in starburst galaxies. If the outflows are oriented edge-on, which is likely due to dust, our observations suggest that we may be observing dust-obscured starburst activities in some of these galaxies, including Arp292. Our analysis also indicates that the outflows are likely caused by supernova explosions and the stellar winds from massive stars, which can lead to metal-rich gas being ejected from the galaxies. This can result in the recycling of elements essential for new star formation in the galaxies' centers, which can help explain the presence of massive young star clusters in some of these galaxies. Notably, one of the galaxies, Arp292, exhibits an unusual pair-choice behavior inspired by animal parenting, where a larger galaxy is interacting with a smaller companion that is generating a massive starburst, fueling a gas outflow, and leading to dust-lane formation due to the collision. This remarkable cosmic parent-child relationship is offering astronomers a chance to study the effects of massive starbursts on galaxy interactions and mergers. Lastly, our analysis suggests that many of these starburst galaxies with visible outflows were likely formed through major galaxy mergers. These findings can be further explored with upcoming high-resolution spectrographs like MaXXD, which will provide even more detailed spectral data for a wider range of starburst galaxy candidates. These observations will shed more light on the complex interactions between massive starbursts, galaxy interactions, and how gas and elements are circulated within these systems. Ultimately, they will contribute to a deeper comprehension of how galaxies evolved throughout the cosmos.

Configurations within specific settings are frequently evaluated using various performance metrics; however, pinpointing effective configurations that minimize costly experiments is a time-consuming process. To accelerate this search, we introduce BoAnon, an active learning approach utilizing Bayesian optimization, which leverages observational data to inform subsequent experiment designs. In a context without a ground truth objective function, BoAnon facilitates the search for optimal configurations by incorporating expert feedback into Bayesian optimization. This enables the discovery of optimal or near-optimal configurations at a fraction of the cost of random searches. Experimental results demonstrate that BoAnon speeds up the discovery process by a factor of up to $30$, as validated through experiments on performance metric configurations for memory optimization, hyperparameter tuning for neural networks, and the optimization of runtime performance metrics for memory optimization. Furthermore, BoAnon's effectiveness is showcased in a real-world application involving the optimization of runtime performance metrics for a stateful serverless computing architecture. This involves reducing latency and improving throughput; in this scenario, BoAnon reduces the number of experiments required from 2000 to just 83. Our study reveals that the transverse momentum dependence of triangular flow $v_3$ mimics the $N_{part}$-scaled dependence of elliptic flow $v_2$ when accounting for mass effects, observed in data from the Large Hadron Collider. Additionally, a comparison of $v_3$ and $v_2$ in different centrality ranges and across various particle types highlights their striking similarity. Using relativistic quantum hydrodynamics, we interpret this phenomenon as a manifestation of collective behavior in heavy ion collisions, where the initial spatial triality and ellipticity ultimately translate to specific patterns of particle emission in momentum space. A hydrodynamical analysis also enables the extraction of detailed $v_3$ and $v_2$ spectra, which exhibit remarkable agreement with experimental data. In particular, the shape of $v_3$ and $v_2$ as functions of transverse momentum reveals common trends across various particle types, centring centrality, and even holding for strange and non-strange particles. Nevertheless, the larger radius of the triality vortex compared to the elliptical one results in distinct features appearing in higher-order cumulants of $v_3$ and $v_2$. Large-scale RDF datasets pose challenges for quality assessment due to their size and interconnectedness. Existing quality evaluation techniques either focus on individual data instances or rely on time-consuming and resource-intensive approaches to determine data quality. To address these challenges, we present Quality Assessment on a Large Scale (QLS), a novel framework designed to efficiently evaluate the quality of large RDF datasets. By leveraging the properties of RDF data and applying a hierarchical evaluation strategy, QLS assigns a quality score to each dataset based on the evaluation of a limited number of key ratings. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through benchmark tests, which show QLS to be faster and more accurate than existing quality assessment techniques for large datasets. Furthermore, QLS is available online at no cost, making it an accessible quality assessment tool for researchers and practitioners working with large RDF datasets. Additionally, we provide the underlying dataset used for benchmark testing, comprising 15 well-known datasets from various domains and totaling over 3 million triples, along with their quality scores as determined by QLS. This framework is particularly suited for large-scale datasets characterized by numerous types of entities, extensive connectivity, and significant data distributions. The hierarchical approach adopted by QLS, driven by the coexistence of diverse data distributions within a single dataset, enables efficient quality assessment. The development of QLS is accompanied by a comprehensive quality evaluation dataset comprising 15 prominent RDF datasets with over 3 million triples. The evaluation results obtained from benchmarking tests validate the efficiency and accuracy of QLS, showcasing its performance superiority over existing quality assessment techniques for large datasets. The experiments conducted employ three quality assessment approaches: a leading quality assessment method along with two variations of the proposed framework. The code and quality assessment datasets are openly accessible for further research purposes. The current implementation of the proposed framework is executed on top of the Apache Jena framework via the SPARQL query language and has been successfully executed on top of the Apache Flink framework via the SPARQL ALgebra translator. The central engines of active galaxies, including quasars and blazars, release enormous amounts of energy that significantly impact their surrounding gas through powerful shocks caused by the collision of gas driven by radiation pressure and wind. As a result, shock-ionization occurs, leading to the modification of observable properties of the gas, such as temperature, abundance, and line width, which are influential factors in the formation of heavy elements and the development of magnetic fields. Utilizing a sophisticated computational approach that solves for radiation, gas, and magnetic fields simultaneously, simulations demonstrate the profound effects of shock-ionization on the distribution and properties of the gas, particularly in regions near the active galaxies within a scale of hundreds of parsecs. Furthermore, spectral analysis indicates that future observations with next-generation telescopes could detect the influence of shock-ionization on detecting massive black holes at the lower end of the known mass range. Consequently, precise measurements of the mass of smaller black holes rely heavily on distinguishing between radiation-dominated shock dynamics and magnetic field-controlled shock processes. Ultimately, this may result in more massive black holes with weaker magnetic field control, such as that seen in massive quasars, and could have notable implications for the early universe.

Using an exact Cayley tree representation, we re-express the Ising model on a lattice through group rotation operators and the lattice's structural matrix - a method that extends to finite-sized lattices a technique previously utilised for infinite Cayley trees. This approach enables us to solve the model by diagonalising a finite-sized matrix whose dimensions correspond to the number of spin interactions, in contrast to the infinite Cayley tree where only the structure of the tree is relevant. We confirm our method's validity by comparing it to existing exact results for the Ising model on a Cayley tree and also obtain novel insights for finite-sized lattices, specifically a phase transition line in the Cayley tree's parameter space for any finite number of spin interactions. Moreover, we find that the structure of a Cayley tree is equivalent to a di- bi-fractal structure consisting of local p-arboreality and b-arboreality characteristics, a concept that can be applied to any finite-sized lattice. By utilising our exact diagonalisation method, we are able to solve various finite-sized lattice versions of the Ising model that contain a Cayley tree substructure, including a mean-field like model where a Cayley tree is connected to a fully connected subgraph, a multi-layer Cayley tree where two Cayley trees are shared, and a general multi-layer lattice where different Cayley tree structures are integrated. Our results reveal that any finite-sized multi-layer lattice will experience a phase transition regardless of the layer structure due to the presence of a phase transition line in the Cayley tree's parameter space. Additionally, we find that only the di-bi-fractal structure of a Cayley tree is sufficient to explain the phase transition line, in contrast to the multi-layer lattice where the bi-fractal structure of the lattice is sufficient to do so. Our method also allows us to solve the anti-Ising model on a Cayley tree by making a simple substitution in the diagonalised matrix. Our approach provides a novel new perspective on the Ising model and its variants and we hope this will spark further research and extensions to this work.

To address the challenge of 3D object detection in far-field scenarios, this paper introduces a dual-detection framework that combines RGB and lidar-based methods. By applying a reverse perspective transform to capture the objects' potential sizes, our proposed framework classifies detected objects as either "large" or "small." A score-based validation system then filters out incorrect classifications and refines the bounding box accuracy. Experimental results using the Waymo Open Dataset showcase significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving an overall mean average precision (MAP) of 33.15% in far-field detection. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/yunsong-ai/DDFC. Additionally, we have launched a public leader board website at https://yunsong-ai.github.io/ThreeDDetect/, welcoming participation from researchers worldwide. By joining forces, we aim to advance the benchmark of 3D object detection through open competition and collaborative improvement.

While self-supervised flow estimation has achieved notable progress, significant challenges still exist in the field. Notably, current methods struggle to accommodate occlusions, a fundamental obstacle that prevents the use of flow for real-world applications. This study aims to mitigate this limitation by developing a method to estimate flow in the presence of missing data. We introduce a novel, bidirectional learning approach that incorporates and builds upon the correlations between forward and reverse flows. By doing so, we enhance the representation of occluded areas and facilitate the recovery of missing flow data. The proposed method, dubbed BiFlow, represents a significant improvement over the baseline method, OFNet, as evidenced by the significant reduction in entropy in occluded regions as captured by the improved SSIM scores. Extensive experiments and qualitative evaluations validate the effectiveness of BiFlow in addressing the challenge of occlusions and demonstrate its superior performance compared to alternative self-supervised and supervised approaches. Furthermore, BiFlow proves versatile in various real-world scenarios, including video deinterlacing, scene change detection, and occlusion boundary detection. The code and dataset will be made available at https://github.com/cg1177/BiFlow.

Deep learning techniques have achieved high accuracy in classification tasks but most of these models are power-hungry and consume significant memory. To overcome this limitation, a basic neural network called BNN is proposed in this paper. BNN aims to provide comparable performance to traditional deep neural networks at a much lower power consumption and smaller memory footprint. To achieve this, BNN uses a basic neural network structure that competes with the performance of advanced neural networks while using less resources. Additionally, this paper presents an improved training method for BNN that results in better performance and reduces the gap with traditional deep neural networks. The proposed training method is a modified version of traditional training with small noise and weight clipping. Experimental results show that BNN achieves comparable performance to traditional deep neural networks with an accuracy of over 95% on MNIST, CNNS and WGN datasets. Furthermore, BNN exhibits lower power consumption and memory usage compared to traditional deep neural networks. The proposed training method also improves the performance of BNN and reduces the gap with traditional deep neural networks. Evaluations of the classification performance of BNN and traditional deep neural networks are conducted on various datasets, demonstrating the efficacy of BNN. The code for the proposed BNN and training method is available online.

This research investigates how a strong magnetic field influences the quark matter's structure, specifically its relationship between pressure and density, for matter composed of up, down, strange quarks, and electrons. We also examine how this phenomenon changes when spin is considered and whether it could possibly override the increased pressure caused by a magnetic field at extremely high densities. Additionally, our study includes an analysis of how the structure of this type of matter is affected when it is confined to a small space and whether magnetic field can cause the formation of a charged string-like object within it. Our findings suggest that a magnetic field can stimulate the creation of a charged string-like object within this type of matter, especially when the density is high, and that its structure can be described by a relationship between the pressure and density, which includes the magnitude of the field. Even-2-factorable (E2F) is a novel graph property where there exists an edge-2-factor consisting of two disjoint cycles within the graph. Our research focuses on the E2F property for cubic graphs, exploring both the existence and form of even 2-factors. An E2F of a cubic graph can be described as two distinct cycles that cover all edges, possibly sharing no edges. We establish the relationship between the E2F property and 1-factors, examining how E2F can be derived from 1-factors. Additionally, we present a method to identify all even 2-factors by applying a specific rotation on the structure of the graph. Based on this rotation, we propose an algorithm to determine all E2Fs. We further investigate the possibility of determining all even 2-factors for cubic graphs by exploring the concept of half-edges in our previous work. Building on this foundation, we introduce new terminology to express the relationship between edges in an even 2-factor, defining the order of edges as either 'preceding' or 'following'. We leverage this new language to present a general structure for even 2-factors, enabling us to characterize all possible orders of edges. We demonstrate that all even 2-factors conform to this structure and that the order of edges can be classified into three distinct types. Furthermore, we develop a method to determine all even 2-factors by rotating the graph and examining all half-edges, as well as identifying all possible orders of edges. Our research offers an innovative approach to studying even 2-factors, allowing us to determine all even 2-factors for any given cubic graph. We conclude by presenting several specific examples to illustrate our findings, including a particular E2F for the graph known as 'Conway's road'. Lastly, we propose an open question related to the E2F property.

This paper introduces a novel technique called Timeloops, a cutting-edge system call filtering method tailored for applications written in interpreted languages such as PHP and Python. Unlike operating systems like Seaside and Hints, which focus on compiled programs, Timeloops leverages the unique characteristics of interpreted programs to devise an innovative approach to system call filtering. Unlike existing system call filtering solutions, which direct system calls to a dedicated kernel process for safe execution, Timeloops uses a novel time-based model to manage system calls and prevent security breaches. This model assigns each system call a unique time window in which it must be made; if a system call is made outside this designated time frame, it is considered malicious and blocked by the kernel. Through a case study of a web application written in PHP, we demonstrate the efficacy of Timeloops, showcasing how it successfully prevents sophisticated security breaches, including TOCTOU attacks. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that Timeloops' performance yields minimal overhead, resulting in system call filtering latency measured at less than 5 milliseconds. This suggests that Timeloops can integrate seamlessly with high-performance applications while also mitigating security risks associated with system calls.
