Deep neural network classifiers have revolutionized the field of computer science, enabling achievement of exceptional accuracy in various classification tasks. Yet, a significant flaw exists in traditional deep learning-based classification systems - they lack a mechanism to gauge prediction reliability. As a result, they cannot distinguish between highly accurate predictions and questionable ones. This concept of "prediction uncertainty" has been well-expressed quantitatively through techniques such as Bayesian neural networks and probabilistic regression models. Inspired by these ideas, our proposal incorporates uncertainty quantification into traditional deep neural network classifiers, allowing them to generate a confidence metric alongside each classification output. To enhance uncertainty estimation, our framework leverages a supplementary loss function, which is seamlessly integrated into the cross-entropy loss via a probability scaling factor. Experimental results demonstrate the significant advantages of our uncertainty-aware models in complex image classification scenarios, outperforming traditional deep learning baselines in both accuracy and uncertainty reliability. Furthermore, a intriguing phenomenon - uncertainty distribution in relation to classification error - is explored and analyzed through various datasets, revealing a key insight that uncertainty and error are closely linked in a monotonic increase pattern. To facilitate replication and further investigation, the code and dataset used in this research are available for download. In conclusion, our uncertainty-aware deep neural network classifier model has shown substantial gains over conventional deep learning baselines in complex image classification scenarios, and provides valuable insights into the relationship between uncertainty and error. To develop robust reinforcement learning algorithms, it's crucial to test them under changing conditions. Unfortunately, crafting a single comprehensive evaluation curriculum that accounts for the various scenarios is a significant challenge. As an alternative, we suggest creating a series of incremental curriculum objectives. This approach allows us to provide credit to the learned policies for both initial and updated curricula. By doing so, we can gather valuable data that can be utilized for a robust policy transfer. We applied our method to a prominent multiplayer game, and the results demonstrate impressive performance when tested against curricula not previously encountered. Notably, a notable proportion of the credit gained during training can be attributed to the ability to adapt to new objectives, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach. Moreover, compared to a static curriculum, our method yields a robust performance on unsupervised transfer trials. The code for our method is available online at https://github.com/strato-team/ multi-agent-curriculum-learning. This repository includes the code for our metric calculator, data visualization, and the multi-agent curriculum learning framework. The code is implemented using PyTorch and TensorFlow for the underlying reinforcement learning algorithms, and it can be easily integrated with other curriculum learning techniques. In the accompanying paper, we elaborate on the concepts discussed in this abstract and present additional experimental results.

This new method is particularly useful for understanding the entanglement of photons in an optical system and can be applied to analyze the spatial entanglement of photons in multiplexed systems, such as systems utilizing orbital angular momentum modes. As an example, the subdiffraction limited system, which exhibits multiple "images" or spatial modes, such as orbital angular momentum modes, is explored to demonstrate this approach, and the estimation of Schmidt number is shown to increase with the number of modes available in the system. Consequently, such a method is not only beneficial for studying the entanglement of photons but also offers insights into designing efficient multiplexing systems. In addition, it is applied to analyze the entanglement properties of an optical system utilizing a random transfer function, demonstrating its versatility. Ultimately, a comprehensive analysis of the proposed method's utility is concluded by discussing its potential to contribute to the advancement of efficient multi-photon sources. Transfer learning has become a widely adopted strategy in machine learning, enabling models to excel in multiple languages despite being initially trained on just one. We investigated the possibilities and limitations of this approach with sentiment analysis, using a pre-trained BERT model to analyze English sentiments and adapting it for use with Arabic emotions. Our experiments showed that the model successfully captured Arabic sentiments with a high degree of accuracy, surpassing baseline models and demonstrating a notable error reduction of 10% points. Additionally, we discovered that incorporating domain-specific adaptation techniques led to a further enhancement of 5% points in accuracy. Our findings also revealed the model's effectiveness in analyzing very short text samples, such as individual words, and identified key challenges that need to be addressed to achieve comparable performance with English sentiment analysis. The code and data analyses have been made publicly available, laying the groundwork for the exploration of more complex sentiment analysis tasks in Arabic.

This paper proposes a new data augmentation technique and model optimization method called Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS). By selectively eliminating unnecessary proposal boxes during training, BNPS enables the use of more complex models for Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). Our method involves generating relationships between proposal boxes and the image boundary, then discarding relationships between unrelated proposal boxes to focus on more significant negative samples. This approach simplifies the model's negative proposal classification task, allowing for the capture of more important features and improvements in detection performance. Our method further incorporates a balanced proposal sampling strategy to minimize unnecessary computation and increase training efficiency. The benefits of BNPS were tested on the Visual Relationship Detection task using the MSCOCC dataset, demonstrating enhanced performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods. The proposed approach also yields significant performance gains on the Visual Relationship Detection task for complex models, demonstrating its potential for large-scale VRD applications. The code for our method is available online at https://github.com/hjewang/BNPS. Our method's potential for other object detection tasks is also worthy of exploration in future studies.

Human motion prediction is a challenging task that is primarily studied in a supervised setting, where collecting a large amount of data is a significant issue. We investigate the action recognition process with a limited amount of training data, focusing on the implications of dataset size on prediction accuracy. Our experiments involve scaling up the training dataset from 10 to 1000 classes, and we find that the error rate drops dramatically from 69% to 15%. To address this challenge, we develop a new method called Memory-Augmented Model (MAM). This model incorporates a external memory component with a dynamic addressing mechanism, allowing individual observations to contribute specific information to the model. By incorporating a Generalized Gated Memory Cell, our model can effectively absorb a large amount of information from the training dataset. Compared to the traditional neural network, MAM exhibits enhanced performance on unseen actions and improves overall performance by a 24% gain. Notably, when trained on just 16 classes, MAM achieves an error rate of 10%, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art model trained on 100 classes with zero-shot generalization. We further explore the application of MAM to predicting new actions from unseen classes and find that it excels in cross-entropy optimization but struggles with overfitting in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we introduce an auxiliary task and a reinforcement learning framework that encourages diversity in the predicted trajectories, leading to a 27% reduction in error rate. Our method conquers the main limitation of the supervised action recognition model and facilitate its broader use in real-world scenarios. This paper describes the architecture and a Python-based simulator for the Content Addressable Parallel Processor, a historic British computer designed in the 1960s. The system consists of multiple mini-computers that can be connected to a host computer via a serial interface, and its core is made up of parallel circuits capable of searching for data, performing arithmetic operations, and updating memory content. The simulator accurately models the behavior of the real CAPP system and allows it to be used in various applications, including solving mathematical problems and simulating logical conditions for complex systems. The simulator's effectiveness is demonstrated through its execution of several real-world CAPP programs and subsequent comparison with actual system data. Furthermore, the simulator showcases the CAPP's capability to perform complex tasks, such as iterating through memory locations and applying logical operations to solve a discrete algebra problem. This paper investigates an encryption scheme with denial capability, specifically one that can reject a decrypter's identity verification. In the context of a court-compelled decryption scenario, we examine the relationship between this capability and key exchange security. Our key contribution is the analysis of Ohta and Okamoto's 1988 proposal for such an encryption scheme. Although initially considered insecure by several researchers, our assessment shows that the scheme actually meets our criteria for a denial-capable encryption system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this encryption method incorporates a non-manipulable key exchange protocol. Consequently, our findings indicate that compelling a user to decrypt data is ineffective, as the user can plausibly deny responsibility for the original encryption. This implies that the security of the Ohta-Okamoto scheme relies on the underlying problem of key exchange having the property of computational secrecy. In turn, this property is achieved when the private key is generated randomly and kept confidential during the key exchange process. Building upon our analysis of existing research, we also explore extensions to this problem, considering additional features like identity-based authentication and key exchange. Ultimately, our assessment concludes that secure denial-capable encryption systems can be realized only in scenarios where the user's secret key remains confidential throughout the key exchange process. This, in turn, is contingent upon the underlying problem of computational secrecy of the key exchange protocol being computationally intractable for the adversary. In particular, this implies that any denial-capable encryption system is secure only when the adversary lacks access to the user's secret key, a fundamental concept that underpins our review of this topic. This paper's findings provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the interplay between denial-capable encryption, key exchange security, and court-compelled decryption in various scenarios. This, in turn, is expected to yield beneficial cross-fertilization between the fields of cryptography, law, and social engineering. This paper is an independent contribution that explores the relationship between denial-capable encryption, key exchange security, and court-compelled decryption in various scenarios, offering a comprehensive framework for understanding this interplay. As such, we also outline the fundamental principles necessary to ensure the security of MDI-QKD.

Deep learning models excel in image analysis, including medical imaging, but their reliability is frequently called into question due to a lack of transparency. This study aims to investigate the relationship between the interpretability of these models and their accuracy. By utilizing a variety of interpretability techniques, such as feature importance and saliency maps, we successfully improve the performance of a convolutional neural network (CNN) in classifying breast tumor images by fine-tuning the model. The results show that the model's transparency is directly correlated with its precision and ability to detect lesions. Furthermore, we found that using the DeepCrop dataset, which contains abnormal regions marked by dermatologists, enables the model to achieve higher accuracy and transparency. This study demonstrates the value of combining performance optimization and interpretability techniques to develop more reliable and effective CNNs for medical imaging applications. Additionally, we provide an open-source implementation of the study's methods on GitHub.

This paper examines a one-dimensional transport equation occurring within a periodic domain, featuring a nonlocal flux and no dissipation, applied to odd initial conditions. We demonstrate that solutions diverge at a rate of $\frac1t$ for positive times, using the method of characteristics and an integral equation. Additionally, an issue with conserved quantities is identified, revealing that although the total mass remains constant, other invariants such as energy become distorted over time. A parallel analysis can be extended to a similar equation defined within the real numbers by modifying the nonlocal flux to rely on absolute values. This equation also experiences solutions that ultimately degenerate and characteristically fail to conserve energy across all time intervals due to an issue with an infinite propagating wave with zero amplitude. Both of these models have distinct solutions that distinguish them from each other, leading to further implications on their dynamics. This paper compares the average age of information (AoI) in discrete and continuous time systems to understand their respective age of information dynamics. To analyze AoI, we establish a framework for calculating the AoI distribution for both discrete and continuous time systems, before analyzing the stationary AoI distribution in a Poisson arrival model. Our findings show that the AoI distribution in discrete time systems follows an ergodic pattern, whereas in continuous time systems it results in a non-stationary, linearly increasing distribution. Furthermore, our results indicate that the AoI in discrete time systems is suboptimal when compared to its continuous time system counterpart, prompting us to propose a general formula for calculating the optimal AoI in discrete time systems. Through numerical simulations, we validate our analytical expressions and explore the optimal AoI in various system configurations. Notably, our proposed formula reveals that the optimal AoI in discrete time systems can be achieved through a strategy of immediate updating. We also derive a general condition for achieving optimal AoI in discrete time systems. Finally, our results highlight the suboptimal nature of the conventional uniform policy in discrete time systems.

We explore the behavior of Drinfeld twists under base change in both the classical and quantum settings, establishing conditions and results for their admissibility in set-theoretic and $q$-deformed contexts. Specifically, given a Drinfeld twist $\Psi$ for a group $G$ over a base field $k$, we examine how it evolves when extended to a larger base field $K$. Our study reveals the role of reflex fields in weeping and constructing twists, leading to the identification of suitable $k$-algebras $R$ to yield twisted Drinfeld modules. Moreover, we establish the relationship between such twists and the geometry of Drinfeld's tower of function fields over $k$. Our findings also enable us to construct a vast range of Drinfeld twists using both base change and partial base change techniques. Notably, this allows us to construct a Drinfeld twist for every group $G$ over every global function field $k$, even when $G$ is not finely generated. Additionally, our methods yield the construction of various $q$-deformed Drinfeld modules, thereby extending the classical case. Lastly, we establish a fundamental isomorphism between the Galois groups of the global function fields $k(G,\Psi)$ and $k(G',\Psi')$ for suitable pairs of Drinfeld modules $(G,\Psi)$ and $(G',\Psi')$. This is achieved through a far-reaching application of Artin-Scheier theory and the application of Grothendieck-Messing's reflex fields theory. This isometric isomorphism also establishes a tower relationship between the extensions $k(G,\Psi)/k(G)$ and $k(G')/\kappa(G)$ for some subfields $\kappa(G) \subseteq k(G')$. This, in turn, leads to an exhaustive description of the Galois groups of the global function fields $k(G,\Psi)$. This description notably reveals the occurrence of biquadratic extensions and the non-abelian gorup $A_4$ among such Galois groups. This, along with further analysis of the arithmetic of Drinfeld modules, especially their global function fields, sets the stage for new directions in research, including the study of class fields, ray class fields, and Zeta functions for Drinfeld modules. Investigating the spin exchange interaction between dopants in a silicon crystal lattice is crucial for developing reliable and scalable quantum computing systems based on silicon technology. By combining optical detection of a single spin and electrical measurement of nearby spins' influence, we studied the effect of nearby donor spins on the optical transition probability of a single charge state of a silicon spin orphan. We found that for nearest neighbor donors, the spin exchange interaction can be either strengthening or weakening the effect of a particular spin on the optical transition, depending on their relative positions, and estimated that only donors within 7 nanometers could significantly impact the optical transition due to valence band structure. Furthermore, by comparing theoretical predictions with experimental results, we found that only donors in a specific orientation could induce a spin exchange interaction, and that protons could induce a more significant effect although they are located farther away due to their unique high spin purity. These insights provide a foundation for developing strategies to mitigate or exploit the spin exchange interaction between optical and electrical spins in silicon quantum computing systems.

A convolutional neural network (CNN) based approach is presented for automatically identifying and classifying specific areas of interest in complex medical image combinations. By leveraging multi-scale encoding and decoding techniques, the proposed network effectively handles complex medical image inputs and accurately identifies boundary conditions. Two specific applications are explored: one involving automatic detection and classification of red reflexes in retinal images, and another involving segmentation and classification of premolar regions in panoramic dental images. Excellent precision and accuracy are achieved using publicly available training datasets, surpassing the effectiveness of traditional methods that rely on custom-designed features. The excellence of the proposed network is validated through comprehensive tests of various network configurations and input image resolutions. Furthermore, the introduction of multi-scale encoding and decoding techniques is shown to significantly enhance the network's performance compared to single-scale methods. The exceptional performance of the network in complex medical image analysis makes it a promising solution for other similar image processing challenges. All source code and models are available online at https://github.com/yousefis/MED-AT-UNET.

To determine whether a given set of quantum states exhibits strong quantum nonlocality, we are proposing a new, efficient method for finding the largest portion that can be found within the set when applied to multipartite systems. This proposed method specifically looks for the most substantial instance of quantum nonlocality present in a system by identifying the largest unextendible product basis (UPB) contained within the set. By doing so, we are providing a practical solution to effectively handle complex multipartite state systems. Furthermore, this novel approach enables us to generate a wide range of intriguing consequences, including a notable growth of a particular entanglement measure when applying this method to certain highly entangled states, indicating an extensive amount of quantum nonlocality present in these systems. Additionally, our proposed process is backed by detailed numerical evidence and analytical insights for certain special cases, leading to an explicit expression that directly relates the proposed measure to the original multi-qubit state system. This proposed measure is also shown to exhibit a specific pattern of growth in the Pauli-x error channel and is displayed in Table I, and we are also presenting some specific UPB examples that are overextended and their corresponding projections, providing a clearer understanding of how these complex multi-qubit state systems function. Lastly, we are proposing that our novel approach be utilized as a benchmark for evaluating the quantum nonlocality present in multipartite systems containing extended product bases.

As massive spectroscopic surveys emerge as a priority, maintaining the efficiency and safety of astrobots is crucial as they collects astronomical data across multiple arcs of sky. To tackle this challenge, we present a novel optimization framework that proactively identifies and avoids potential hazards in astrobots' trajectories. By redefining astrobots' movement as a dynamic placement problem, we develop an active sampling strategy to pinpoint optimal target observations. We enhance the framework with a hierarchical approach to manage varying observation priorities and integrate a trajectory re planning mechanism to mitigate performance decline resulting from detected obstacles. Through extensive simulations and real-world deployments, we showcase the safety and performance benefits of our method, yielding a significant improvement of up to 25% in astrobots' efficiency and safety compared to existing strategies. The enhanced efficiency further translates to a 10% to 15% decrease in data collection duration, thus facilitating faster and more reliable astronomical data acquisition. A unified deep learning framework is proposed for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction under varying data distribution conditions.  This multi-task framework leverages a common latent representation for two separate tasks: unsupervised dimensionality reduction and supervised classification.  For unsupervised learning, it uses a contrastive method to extract a compact code from input data without labels, while supervised learning utilizes two components: one generates a noisy but meaningful code and the other extracts a precise code corresponding to the class labels.  This noisy-pure decomposition of the feature extraction process allows us to factorize the encoder and two temporary codes using a method called teacher-student learning, resulting in an improved and efficient model.  Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the proposed framework's superiority over conventional methods for unsupervised learning and competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods for supervised learning.  Additionally, the proposed framework is efficient in parameter usage, achieving a reduction of up to 130x in parameters compared to supervised learning alone.  We also show that the proposed framework is robust in scenarios with limited class labels, performing better than conventional supervised methods even when only 1% of data has labels.  The code for the proposed framework is available at https://github.com/zhangqizh95/UniMulti-Task-Feature-Extraction.  The paper also includes an analysis of the method's weight sharing benefits, visualizations of the learned codes, and a discussion on the factorized learning generalization to more tasks.  We showcase the framework's superiority over conventional multi-task learning methods, achieving up to 12.2% improvement in unsupervised learning and 5.3% improvement in supervised learning. We present an infinite family of bipartite graphs, along with a subgroup of automorphisms within each graph - specifically, we show each graph's full symmetry can be divided into a direct product of two smaller groups. Additionally, for one of these families, we find the automorphism group to be isomorphic to the wreath product of smaller groups in a specific arrangement, providing something not previously documented in graph theory. Further, we construct an infinite family of connected, regular graphs, featuring the same wreath product group structure, making them distinct from earlier similar constructions. Our proof involves generating the graph members through the application of a certain linear operator to a set of initial points, using a combination of both horizontal and diagonal steps. This method enables us to establish certain properties and then analyze the graph's structure in various levels of detail. As a result, we can determine not just its automorphism group but also other key graph characteristics. Our approach yields not just the new graph families, but also a family of bipartite graphs constructed via 2-by-2 matrices, featuring an interesting self-similarity. We also explore possible connections to numerical methods. Lastly, we identify potential extensions to this construction method. This study presents an adaptation of the Group Lasso technique for both continuous and categorical variables, addressing the challenge of selecting relevant variables in high-dimensional data analysis. Based on recent advancements in non-parametric margins and accurate data modeling, our approach includes Sparsity Lasso and Fused Lasso methods. We also examine the performance of these algorithms using simulated datasets and real-world customer purchase data, comparing their effectiveness against a naive baseline approach. Our findings indicate that the Group Lasso models yield superior results, particularly in predicting unseen data, and our research provides guidelines for choosing the optimal fusion strategy. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that Model X, an extended Group Lasso framework, exhibits superior results over traditional methods and provides valuable insights into feature importance and category structure. Our methodology is applicable to any multi-dimensional categorical data and our software is freely available for public use.

Recent advancements in pre-training language models using knowledge graph triples have yielded promising results on question-answering tasks. Contrary to conventional text-based pre-training methods, knowledge graph pre-training focuses on learning representations from structural semantic information. This study delves into a comparative analysis of knowledge graph-based and traditional pre-training models in question-answering scenarios. Our knowledge graph-based models, pre-trained on large-scale factual triples, demonstrated superior performance over traditional BERT-based models in low-data settings. Furthermore, our findings reveal that combining knowledge graph-based and traditional pre-training techniques results in enhanced performance, amounting to a 9.5% boost, in a zero-shot scenario, and outperforms both standalone approaches in the more challenging few-shot setting, with a 14.2% improvement. This achievement supports the potential of knowledge graph-based pre-training as a promising technique for structural semantic representation learning. Recent advancements in computer vision have enabled the generation of high-quality images for panoramic scenes using mobile devices. Initially, this technology relied on external cameras and sensors, but recent developments in Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) have allowed them to be used as a self-contained solution. Specifically, several research projects have utilized IMUs to capture images for panoramic stitching by providing real-time orientation information. This paper examines the benefits of utilizing IMUs in this context, specifically their ability to detect rapid changes in orientation, such as those occurring during the pan operation. Furthermore, this research investigates the possibility of utilizing IMUs to monitor the baseline distance and their suitability for capturing base images. Additionally, IMU data is explored as a means to improve the accuracy of target localization and subsequent stitching process. Experimental results utilizing a smartphone equipped with an IMU and camera demonstrated the efficacy of these approaches. Finally, this research concludes by discussing potential applications and future directions for leveraging IMU data in panoramic image capture. This paper investigates the relationship between Bessel functions, Weyl group cosets, and degenerate Eisenstein series for the symplectic group in Type B. By establishing a connection to Bessel functions through Demenzl decomposition, we find that certain Weyl group cosets can be related to degenerate Eisenstein series. Additionally, this relationship enables us to examine the invariants of these cosets and their corresponding degenerate Eisenstein series, leading to explicit formulas for their absolute values. This result extends the findings of Knapp and Stern by providing a link between the spectrum of degenerate Eisenstein series and Bessel functions, offering further insights into the representation theory of the symplectic group. Furthermore, we can utilize this relationship to derive estimates for the norms of these degenerate Eisenstein series, extending a similar result obtained for the orthogonal group in Type A. Lastly, we explore a more general context involving twisted degenerate Eisenstein series and discuss potential applications of our findings. 

This work is a continuation of the authors' earlier paper, where the relationship between twisted degenerate Eisenstein series and Bessel functions was established for the orthogonal group in Type A, based on Demenzl decomposition. The current paper generalizes this result to the symplectic group in Type B, demonstrating the same underlying connection between these entities that is characterized by Weyl group cosets. The study of degenerate Eisenstein series, first introduced by Knapp and Stern, has a significant implication for the study of Bessel functions, while the established relationship is expected to facilitate the understanding of representation theory, particularly spectrum analysis, in this context. 

The primary objectives of this paper are to: 
- Establish the connection between twisted degenerate Eisenstein series and Bessel functions for the symplectic group in Type B, 
- Derive explicit formulas for the absolute values of these degenerate Eisenstein series, 
- Obtain estimates for their norms, and 
- Explore general contexts, including one involving Fubini-type sums, with potential applications.

The unique challenge of modeling Parkinson's Disease lies in its varied symptoms impacting multiple systems within the human body. This thesis outlines our approach to creating high-fidelity computational models of the brain's basal ganglia pathway using TheronTech's publicly available data set. We utilized imaging modalities like MRI and PET to build realistic simulations of brain anatomy and function. Our models consist of two components: a anatomical model representing the brain's physical structure, and a functional model showcasing brain activity through neural networks. We then incorporated them into a dynamic simulation of the brain's basal ganglia pathway using PyDSTool, a powerful tool for solving differential equations. This resulted in two different models, one with simplified neural network simulations and another with more intricate neural networks inspired by Friston's Dynamic Casual Network. To validate our approach, we compared our models to actual Parkinson's Disease patients using fMRI data and found similarities in altered brain activity patterns. Furthermore, we used our models to simulate the effects of deep brain stimulation and found them to be accurate according to the data. This research demonstrates the potential of computational models to aid in understanding and treating Parkinson's Disease. It is suggested that collaborative efforts between computer scientists, neurologists, and other medical professionals could lead to significant progress in this field. Additionally, we propose future directions for enhancing brain modeling, including the incorporation of neural network architectures and virtual reality-based validation of computational models. This could potentially allow for the testing of therapeutic interventions in a controlled virtual environment before applying them to actual human patients. This could lead to safer, more effective treatments for patients with Parkinson's Disease and other neurodegenerative disorders. A comprehensive theoretical framework for the co-evolution of galaxies and supermassive black holes is introduced in a non-linear, semi-empirical model that accounts for both the bulk properties of galaxies and the processes driving their development. This model is applied to the vast majority of the quasar population detected by SDSS, and it reproduces observed correlations at the level of galaxy clusters. It also predicts relationships between the masses of supermassive black holes and their host galaxies, both now observed in reality. Using this framework, we find that a significant fraction of quasars with outflows, observed in molecular and atomic gas, are likely caused by binary supermassive black hole mergers. These events occur over a timescale of a few ten thousand years, and they will result in the disappearance of the secondary black hole, with the remaining mass accumulating in the primary. Further, we find that binary supermassive black hole mergers produce low-ionization broad H-alpha components, as seen in some famous quasars, and that they occur frequently enough to explain the observed rate of binary black hole mergers. However, they only merge quickly, resulting in low-duty cycles. Therefore, binary black hole mergers may only occur during quasar outbursts, and they could be detected more frequently during periods of low redshift. Finally, we anticipate future observations to verify many of these theoretical predictions, and to provide greater insight into the most complex phenomena associated with supermassive black holes.

Deep neural networks like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached exceptional performance in various image classification tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to overreliance on specific image features. To mitigate this limitation, using synthetic images through data augmentation has proven effective. Nonetheless, controlling the generation process to produce relevant images involves significant challenges. In traditional methods, generating masks for specific data augmentation techniques like super pixel limiting has been demonstrated to yield desirable results. Nevertheless, a systematic approach to applying such masks across diverse image classification tasks and deep neural network architectures is lacking. To address this gap, we devise a unified framework that simultaneously trains a mask generator and a deep neural network, with the former producing target masks to be applied to image inputs. Consequently, the proposed framework yields substantial improvements in model accuracy, surpassing traditional methods that incorporate masks. Furthermore, our experiments validate the beneficial effects of mask application across different datasets and models. Notably, our findings reveal that using masks leads to improved performance even when augmented images are fed directly to the model. To facilitate further research, we publicly disclose our code and models. The benefits of mask application are attributed to the reduction of model reliance on redundant data, as evidenced by the diminished performance of models utilizing masks on clean datasets. When an atom that isn't correlated with any other interacts with a pre-existing entangled system like a cavity or a waveguide, the system's state will generally change in a way that diminishes its multi-partite entanglement. This phenomenon restricts the creation of multi-partite entanglement in complex systems composed of numerous isolated units. This occurs even if there's an effective single-partite interaction between the atom and the existing entanglement, as seen with reservoirs that cause dissipation. Nonetheless, our study reveals an exception to this rule involving a multi-partite system located within two coupled cavities. When an uncorrelated atom is placed in one of these cavities and they're not too far apart, an appreciable amount of multi-partite entanglement can still be generated. This effect utilizes the transfer of single- and multi-partite entanglements between the two cavities through photon exchange. In this case, an amount of single-partite entanglement can be transferred to the atom, which otherwise wouldn't be possible if the two cavities were highly distinct. This phenomenon occurs over a wide range of rates for the photon exchange, even when the system experiences strong dissipation within the cavities. This rules out the commonly held assumption that multi-partite entanglement among numerous units can only be created from a vacuum state using only single-partite interactions between them. This exception to the generally applicable rule of reduced multi-partite entanglement complexity could provide a foundation for the development of new techniques for multi-partite entanglement creation and transfer. This may enable the production of complex entanglements in systems composed of many isolated units by controlling the interactions between their subunits. This report highlights the design advancements and technical improvements of the upgraded detector, which included moving from 500 to 650 um layer thicknesses, and incorporating custom digital readout chips.  Furthermore, the implementation of a new readout architecture using highly parallel and customizable ASICs, led to a significant increase in data processing speed and efficiency.  The upgrade was successfully installed before 2016, and the upgraded detector showed improved performance.  However, the upgrade was short-lived, as a power glitch occurred just 100 days later, resulting in the permanent loss of data from the LHC.  Consequently, the detector remained inaccessible until the 2017 restart, during which the LHC experienced difficulties.  Hence, the upgraded detector's true potential could not be fully utilized during this period.  Ultimately, the upgrade's limitations were compensated by sophisticated software reconstruction techniques, which ensured the detector's full utilization.  The upgrade's design innovations, installed before 2016, proved robust and effective, while the permanent damage caused by the power glitch led to significant research efforts aimed at understanding the incident and mitigating similar incidents in the future. In this study, a sentiment analysis model was created to determine the public's emotional response to news stories by analyzing their Twitter comments. The model, based on long short-term memory (LSTM) neurons, effectively classified positive and negative tweets by considering the sequential structure of language. To prevent overfitting, a technique called dropout was applied, and the model's performance was optimized by gradually increasing the number of LSTM neurons and selecting the best configuration through a statistical method called cross-validation. Once the optimal model was chosen, it was tested on a random sample of tweets to evaluate its accuracy, resulting in a classification rate of 85.11%. To minimize errors, the model was refined by acknowledging the emotions expressed in the original tweets' text, which slightly improved the accuracy to 85.51%. Furthermore, the model demonstrated versatility by effectively handling an unlimited number of new tweets, thanks to its utilization of dropout. A comparison with two alternative models, naive Bayes and support vector machines, revealed that the LSTM model yielded a higher classification rate of 85.11% versus 75.37% and 79.15%, respectively. While the model was prone to a limited number of mistakes, such as misclassifying words with opposing meanings or unrelated words as essential, due to its fundamental structure. To enhance the model's performance in handling these situations, possible enhancements were proposed, including the incorporation of additional features and a different classification method called maximum entropy. This method is usually limited to observing classical behavior and may not capture unique phenomena such as entanglement and other nonclassical effects.  Our work proposes a new optical tomography that measures a specific combination of properties to image these extraordinary states and demonstrates the technique with a photon pair.  Our measurements show that the proposed tomography technique can accurately map entanglement changes, even in complex systems like the path and polarization of photons.  Our approach offers a broader understanding of optical states and can aid in developing new optical communication and metrology systems that utilize the unique properties of light. Effective management of disease pressure through economic and practical means is crucial for maintaining crop yields and profitability.  For strawberry management, precision agriculture and the potential benefits of precision agriculture, including increased efficiency and accurate real-time decision-making, have not been thoroughly assessed despite advancements in related technologies.  This study involves analyzing financial and operational consequences of precision agriculture on large commercial strawberry operations in California.  A random sampling of 21 participants yielded results after analyzing data from multiple precisions agriculture approaches including precision irrigation, precision fertilizer application, precision pest management, precision harvesting, and precision crop monitoring.  Findings show that precision agriculture can lower labor costs and chemical usage, raise yields, and ultimately increase profits.  However, implementing precision agriculture also incurs significant upfront costs and there are instances where some methods may not yield significant benefits.  Therefore, careful consideration and case-specific analysis are necessary before adopting precision agriculture methods.  This study provides a précis of the situation and sets the stage for future research aimed at evaluating the financial and operational consequences of precision agriculture on smaller strawberry operations.  This research is part of the Strawberry Precision Agriculture Research Initiative (SPARI). By creating a hierarchy of PEPOs, we increase the bond dimension requirements for approximating thermal states and time evolution from $D$ to $D^2$ in each PEPO level. In the process, we reduce the PEPO Hamiltonian's rank from $D^2$ to $D$. This improvement maintains the original model's symmetry and translational invariance properties. Notably, our approach transforms the difficult task of finding low-rank approximations to large Hamiltonians into an easier problem of finding low-rank approximations for smaller Hamiltonians with higher rank. This research builds upon the work of Holmes-Cerfon (arXiv 2005.01975) and incorporates concepts related to the PEPO framework outlined in Baker et al. (arXiv 1810.04235). Alongside, we provide detailed numerical evidence highlighting the efficacy of our proposed method. Ultimately, our hierarchical PEPO framework provides a potent tool for mitigating the difficulties associated with large Hamiltonians in quantum many-body systems. This mitigation strategy can be synergistically integrated with other techniques aimed at reducing the dimensions of Hamiltonians. In addition, our hierarchy offers a valuable paradigm for understanding the fundamental challenges and limitations of using PEPOs to model quantum many-body systems. Through this research, we also clarify the relationship between approximate Hamiltonian parameters and their corresponding effects on physical observables. Lastly, our hierarchy facilitates novel numerical demonstrations of thermal state and time-evolution approximations utilizing PEPOs, encompassing both discrete and continuous time-evolution scenarios. Our implementation is openly accessible via the Matrix-Kit framework. This work is additionally supplemented by a companion paper detailing technical aspects related to the Hamiltonian rank reduction, encompassing both conceptual foundations and intricate mathematical derivations. This secondary research is concurrently being submitted to a separate publication.

This project develops new methods for analyzing the behavior of partial differential equations in the presence of singular critical layers. By combining two approaches - conducting Taylor-based analysis and examining solutions using canonical surfaces - we provide a systematic way to identify the key dynamics governing systems with multiple layers and analyze the associated decoupling process. To demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods, we apply them to a particular partial differential equation system consisting of the Bouvier-Dulli system, and show that the proposed approach yields both the desired approximation and decoupling for this system. Consequently, we are able to establish the long-time existence and uniqueness of solutions for this system, despite the presence of rapidly oscillating terms, by leveraging the estimated boundary layer sizes. This project builds on previous work, extending the application of these methods to systems with multiple layers beyond the previously considered narrow ranges of parameter settings. Moreover, our method involves a significant refinement of the Taylor-based approach, mitigating its inherent instabilities through enhanced error estimates, and incorporating an innovative strategy for determining the optimal order of the asymptotic expansion. Consequently, we achieve a more efficient and accurate analysis of the underlying system, both individually and collectively. Ultimately, we anticipate that the developed methods will not only facilitate further exploration of the Bouvier-Dulli system but also serve as a valuable tool for analyzing other multi-layer systems exhibiting similar behavior.

The GRACE-FO trio's acceleration measurement capability was recently tested using a differential relative motion measurement method. However, unexpected rapid changes, or glitches, can occur during the flight and affect the results. A new detection and mitigation approach was developed to address this issue. Based on in-flight data, a non-parametric method was implemented to identify and remove glitches. Specifically, a 3D boundary was established to distinguish normal data fluctuations from significant changes. Any observations outside this boundary were classified as glitches and removed from the data set. This approach was successfully applied to the ISDC dataset and resulted in an improved estimation of the acceleration noise floor. Using this new technique, noise floors were re-calculated for each instrument and found to be significantly reduced, achieving an average acceleration noise level of $6.8 \times 10^{-12} g$ for SGP-A1. Additionally, glitches were found to occur at a rate of approximately one per day, with a duration of about $10^{-3}$ days. A model was developed to model glitch durations, and it was demonstrated that the proposed method can be an effective glitch detection tool. Finally, it is suggested that this method can be adapted for use in other relative motion measurement missions.

This study investigates the k-Strong Shortest Path Union Cover problem, a critical variant of the Minimum Steiner Tree problem. Given a connected graph G, vertices {s1, s2,..., sk}, and a distance metric d, the task is to find the fewest number of paths in G, covering all {s1, s2,..., sk} with respect to d, where each path has k relevant endpoints. Here, the relevance of an endpoint for a path is determined by a specific weight function ω, where the sum of weights for all endpoints is limited to 1. Here, we analyze the computational complexity of this problem under various weighted and distance metrics, showing that some special cases are solvable in polynomial time, while others are NP-hard. Additionally, we present a fixed-point search approach for solving the unweighted case with metric distances, leading to a pseudo-polynomial time algorithm. On the other hand, for weighted cases, we propose a generalization of the exact enumeration algorithm for the Steiner Tree problem, leading to a pseudo-polynomial time algorithm for the k-Strong Shortest Path Union Cover problem. We also examine the parameterized complexity of this problem, finding that it admits a parameterized algorithm with a fixed number of source vertices. Furthermore, we present a general approach for solving the k-Strong Shortest Path Union Cover problem within a factor of (1 + ε) using an exponential-time algorithm, based on the parameter ε. We also present a general approach for solving the k-Strong Shortest Path Union Cover problem within a factor of (1 + ε) using an exponential-time algorithm, based on the parameter ε, and apply this to derive a (2+ε)-approximation algorithm for the Minimum Steiner Tree problem. For the stationary version of the frog process on a tree, where there are initially no frogs, we determine the critical degree threshold $\lambda_c$ at which the process transitions from being transient to recurrent. This degree threshold is the same as the minimum degree required for percolation on the same tree, according to a recent finding by Coppersmith, Salez, and Shiraishi. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any tree whose degree is greater than $\lambda_c$, there is a unique stationary distribution for the frog process, which gives a near-zero weight to the state with no frogs. Additionally, we analyze the speed at which the process converges to this stationary distribution. For degrees greater than $\lambda_c$, the process converges according to a rate that is directly proportional to the degree, and this relationship holds even when the degree is just slightly greater than $\lambda_c$. As an example, we calculate the specific values of $\lambda_c$ for several well-known types of trees. It is interesting to note that although the process converges quickly for degrees greater than $\lambda_c$, there are cases where the process gets stuck in certain states for an extremely long time when the degree is close to $\lambda_c$. To provide further insight into these dynamics, we discuss a new algorithm that allows us to exactly compute the largest component size for a given configuration of the frog process on a random tree. This leads us to an interesting finding that, counterintively, the process tends to split into two separate components more frequently than expected, especially when the degree is close to $\lambda_c$. As an additional contribution, we derive an explicit formula for computing the stationary distribution of the frog process on a binary tree of any size. This formula emerges from an analysis of the process's dynamics on the tree, and it is distinct from the approach of applying the self-consistency equation directly to the disorder averaged process. As an even further contribution, we establish the convergence rate for a variant of the frog process that is introduced through a random activation of frogs on a binary tree. It is found that the process converges according to a rate that is directly proportional to the logarithm of the degree, and this holds even when the degree is just slightly greater than $\lambda_c$. As an even more further contribution, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the stationary distribution for a continuous-time random walk on a tree, and it is based on an analysis of the generator matrix. A popular method for black-box knowledge distillation is based on the assumption that a smaller model can mimic the behavior of a larger model. However, this approach typically requires access to the same dataset as the target model. We're introducing Decision-based Black-box Knowledge Distillation (DB3), a novel approach where the smaller model is trained to replicate the decision-making patterns of the larger model without access to shared data. In DB3, queries to the target model are treated as decisions made by an informed decision-maker, and the smaller model learns to make the same decisions based on its own observations. Experimental results show that DB3 achieves comparable performance to lattice-based methods and outperforms traditional black-box knowledge distillation methods under limited budget constraints. Furthermore, DB3 exhibits superior performance in low-budget settings, outperforming traditional methods by a significant margin. Comprehensive analyses of DB3, including studies on decision boundary learning, hard sample selection, and multiple teachers, are also provided to demonstrate the efficacy of DB3 in different scenarios. The Strong Geodetic Recognition problem is now resolved, where determining whether a given graph subset contains a unique geodetic set is equivalent to solving a minimum cover problem for the graph's edge subset, which is derived from geodetic set vertices. To achieve this, we first establish that the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem can be solved by finding the minimum number of edge covers required to cover all geodetic sets, and subsequently prove that this is equivalent to finding the minimum number of edge covers that cover all minimum vertex covers. Consequently, we can conclude that the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem has a NP-complete hardness proof based on the knowledge that the minimum edge cover problem has an NP-complete hardness proof, which is acknowledged in the literature. Furthermore, we provide a sample algorithm to solve the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem efficiently for specific types of graphs, namely chordal and interval graphs. Additionally, we provide a distinction between the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem and the Geodetic Recognition problem by proving that the latter has a co-NP completeness status based on the known co-NP completeness status of the vertex cover problem. Even with the most advanced algorithms, imitation learning (IL) often struggles to achieve comparable performance to reinforcement learning (RL). One significant issue in IL is the slow learning rate needed to stabilize training, which can result from the noisy gradients caused by training a policy to match observed trajectories. To address this problem, we introduce the TRAIL algorithm, which utilizes a unique training scheme to minimize the noise impact. In TRAIL, a regular policy is trained while an auxiliary policy is trained to mimic the observed trajectories. The two policies are integrated through a process that eliminates the introduction of noisy gradients, allowing for faster learning. Our experiments show that TRAIL achieves faster convergence and similar performance to champion RL baselines in complex domains, while significantly improving sample efficiency in simpler environments. The code for the TRAIL algorithm is available online at the specified website.

Our study delves into co-imitation learning frameworks, examining both joint and alternating optimization approaches. We analyze the connections between these frameworks and other learning methodologies. Furthermore, we investigate the application of contrast functions in co-imitation learning, exploring both positive rewards and intrinsic motivations. Our research provides a comprehensive exploration of co-imitation learning, establishing a foundation for future research in this field.

We also examine critic designs in Co-IL, covering both external experts and peer learning scenarios. Moreover, we explore contrast functions utilized in Co-IL, looking at reward-based and intrinsic contrast functions. Our research offers a thorough overview of Co-IL, establishing a foundation for future Co-IL research. 

This document is accompanied by the code for our novel Co-IL framework, called General Co-Imitation Learning via Contrastive Optimization, which can be found at this link: https://github.com/zwang84/general-co-imitation-learning.

By analyzing the properties of the polarized ensemble and decoding process, we derive a simplified expression that characterizes the error probability of the sequential decoder. Recent studies combining reinforcement learning with traditional machine translation models have achieved notable performance gains. To build upon this research, we propose a novel framework that proactively refines the action space for language model actions instead of solely relying on utility-based rewards. In an action-based paradigm, where the model selects specific actions within its vocabulary, we demonstrate significant performance benefits when optimizing the action space is integrated into the training process. Our results reveal that merely aligning the action distribution with the target label distribution achieves substantial performance improvements, amounting to +2.3 BLEU points over the baseline model. Furthermore, by introducing a transition probability penalty, we achieve an additional +0.7 BLEU points gain, ultimately yielding a +4.0 BLEU point improvement overall. Our approach also yields impressive performance in target label prediction tasks, achieving 79.5% accuracy, surpassing the baseline model's 76.4% performance. We openly share our code, data, and action datasets to facilitate future research in this area. 

Keywords: machine translation, reinforcement learning, post-processing, language models.

However, traditional CNNs are limited by their inability to adapt to changes in image shifts, leading to a decline in accuracy. To overcome this challenge, Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs) have emerged as a promising solution, integrating feedback from edge-gated layers to correct hidden states and enable robust performance. Furthermore, EG-CNNs' potential applications in image segmentation are being explored. Additionally, an exhaustive survey of EG-CNNs in image segmentation is presented, highlighting notable models and assessing their performance. The paper also discusses promising directions and potential future research avenues in EG-CNNs, especially concerns related to model flexibility, memory efficiency, and scalability. Theoretical modeling and metric-learning-based approaches are also explored, along with discussions on publicly available datasets, evaluation metrics, and the role of EG-CNNs in medical image analysis. Finally, the paper includes experimental results for semantic segmentation using EG-CNNs, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on PASCAL-12 segmentation. This paper examines current implementations of distributed transacions in noSQL databases, focusing on MongoDB's use of WiredTiger, Replicast, and ShardedCluster to manage transactions under Snapshot Isolation. By analyzing the conflict resolution strategies in these systems, we reveal inconsistencies in their behavior, leading to concurrency violations in certain transaction sequences. Furthermore, we evaluate the concurrency properties of MongoDB's transaction algorithms and explore possible improvements to achieve strict 2PL concurrency, consistent with the standards set by systems like Oracle. This analysis is set against the backdrop of MongoDB's growing influence in enterprise applications and the significance of high concurrency standards in such environments. To better understand the systems' behavior, we provide a simplified model covering the key components and then delve into a more detailed analysis of MongoDB's transaction mechanisms. Based on our findings, we suggest improving the concurrency standards in MongoDB, particularly in relation to the Two-Phase Locking algorithm, to ensure they meet the requirements of enterprise applications. To achieve this, we outline a strategy involving the selective application of lock upgrades and downgrades, inspired by systems like Oracle, to prevent concurrency violations. This strategy is feasible given MongoDB's shard-based architecture and can provide greater concurrency standards without incurring significant performance costs. As evidence, we present benchmark results showing that our proposed approach results in concurrency standards comparable to those of Oracle, with only a minimal performance difference. This indicates that the concurrency standards in MongoDB can be improved to meet the requirements of enterprise applications, and we offer our proposed approach as a starting point for this improvement. To facilitate further discussion, we are making the source code and methods used in this analysis publicly available. This analysis is part of broader research aimed at concurrently executing SQL and NoSQL transactions within a single database system. This research is timely given the increasing coexistence of SQL and NoSQL databases in real-world applications and the resulting need for better concurrency standards in these systems. A new approximate analytical solution to a highly nonlinear shock wave equation is derived, and the solution is validated through direct numerical integration in various limiting cases. For adiabatic indices greater than a critical value, specifically 5/3 for one-dimensional shocks and 4/3 for two-dimensional and three-dimensional shocks, the solution develops a singular structure at the origin, where it is dominated by a singular perturbation expansion. A more general analysis using a matched asymptotic expansion enables the derivation of a simplified model near the singularity, allowing for a deeper understanding of the shock's behavior. The model reveals a constant strain rate in the inner region, with a magnitude that can be predicted through a singular perturbation expansion of the outer solution. The highly nonlinear nature of the shock is reflected in the presence of a rarefaction wave with a singular boundary, where the temperature exhibits a singular logarithmic increase as the shock is approached. A more detailed analysis of the one-dimensional shock structure involves a inner expansion of the solution, a matching analysis, and a determination of the outer solution through a boundary layer expansion. The resulting expression for the inner region's scale factor as a function of time provides a precise description of the shock's behavior, including its initial expansion and subsequent contraction powered by an ever-increasing inner energy. This powerful phenomenon driven by the shock's own energy sources may have significant implications for the study of shock waves in highly nonlinear contexts. In addition, higher-order approximations using a higher-order matched asymptotic expansion reveal a more intricate inner structure with distinct regions, with a potential for multiple scales emerging due to the interaction of high-order terms in future applications. Although the specific adiabatic index investigated here does not yield a singularity in the one-dimensional shock wave equation, the general methodology developed can be applied to explore similar complex structures in waves resulting from other processes, such as vortex rings in Supersonic Flows, Wave- Breaking Turbulence, and High-Pressure Emissions in Ocean Dynamics. In these scenarios, where multiple scales may emerge due to high-order term interactions, a more sophisticated inner expansion with multiple layers is proposed, along with a suggested strategy for constructing outer solutions through boundary layer expansions in multiple-scale problems. In conclusion, a powerful new analytical approach is presented, enabling a deeper understanding of highly nonlinear shock waves and paving the way for further investigations into complex inner structures in wave-breaking turbulence and other nonlinear wave phenomena. To facilitate computation, we implement a hierarchical model that leverages subdomain boundary conditions to provide an efficient solution on a coarse grid, which can be refined as necessary. We found that the fraction of tidal features due to mass loss holds steady at approximately 20% across all galaxy masses, while the fraction of tidal features resulting from mergers rises from 10% among low-mass galaxies to nearly 90% among massive galaxies. This shift suggests that the most massive galaxies undergo mergers more frequently than smaller ones, and such events have significant implications for coherent stellar disks. Additionally, our analysis indicates the number of tidal features increases in proportion to galaxy mass, with each galaxy featuring multiple tidal structures. A society's distribution of opportunities has a significant impact on the economic well-being of its future generations. While individual skills and abilities are crucial, the opportunity structure plays an equally important role in determining one's chances of success. Unfortunately, many societies prioritize short-term gains over the long-term benefits of providing equal opportunities, leading to a growing wealth gap between the affluent and the underprivileged. To examine the long-term effects of varying opportunity structures, a multi-generational agent-based model is introduced, simulating how different opportunity distributions evolve over time. By applying this model to analyze income inequality, it is demonstrated that a fair share distribution leads to the most beneficial outcome, resulting in the fewest number of generations required to achieve a desired level of economic equality. Additionally, it is shown that when the opportunity structure is justly distributed, the wealth gap will eventually disappear, and the society's economic equality will be maintained for generations to come. In contrast, an unfair share distribution causes a persistent wealth gap, exacerbating inequality in the process. To provide policymakers with actionable insights, the model is used to test the effects of interventions aimed at reducing income inequality, including increased access to education and modifications to the share distribution. The results of these experiments reveal that reducing the gap between the largest and smallest opportunities can be an effective strategy in addressing inequality. Consequently, this research emphasizes the significance of monitoring opportunity distributions in societies, advocating for data-driven policies that prioritize equal access to opportunities and, in turn, the socioeconomic prosperity of future generations. Lastly, the model presented here is made publicly available to facilitate the exploration of opportunity structures in diverse societal contexts.

The creation and dissemination of deepfakes pose an emerging threat to both personal security and the credibility of information. Deepfake detection methods have consequently gained urgency, with various techniques developed in recent years. While early methods focused on specific production techniques, current models can handle multiple deepfake methods. This paper builds upon existing work by introducing a deepfake detection model capable of uniting domain-specific knowledge. We propose a novel multi-domain deepfake detection network called Cross-Stitch Deepfake Detection Network (CSDNet) that allows individual domain-specific models to share relevant features. By implementing cross-stitch connections between these models, CSDNet enhances their ability to distinguish real from deepfake images. Experimental evaluations conducted on publicly available datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing multi-domain deepfake detection techniques and matches the performance of single-domain models that require significantly more training data. Furthermore, we analyze the benefits of using cross-stitch connections and investigate the optimal unit activation function for our network. The source code for our method is available online at https://github/CSDNet. Advances in Neural Information Retrieval Systems, pp. 555-565, 2021.

A new algorithm is introduced that extends this capability to negative degree-degree correlations, enabling the creation of highly non-standard ensembles. This new algorithm is demonstrated by generating a random ensemble of degree-three codes with negative degree-degree correlation, showing that the resulting code performance can match or even surpass that of conventional low-density parity-check codes under certain conditions. A new algorithm is also introduced for approximating the distribution of degrees in a given network, which can be used to generate random graphs with complex degree distributions. As an example, an erasure channel with a particular degree-degree correlation is analyzed, resulting in a sharp phase transition at an 0.78 erasure probability, in contrast to the conventional 0.75 probability for uncorrelated degrees. It is also shown that by appropriately designing the degree distribution, codes with significantly higher tolerance to erasures can be created, with a maximum tolerable erasure probability of up to 0.88. As an added benefit, this negative degree-degree correlation can be achieved without hindering the code's performance, as evidenced by a simulation where the resulting code performance remains on the capacity achieving line for a binomial degree distribution with a degree greater than three, without negative degree-degree correlations. Notably, the widely accepted approach for achieving this involves the use of weak coherent states. A recent phenomenon observed in this field, however, involves an unusual paradox - while the proposed vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system appears secure, an eavesdropper can exploit this system's vulnerability without detection by adopting a specific strategy. In this paper, we provide an analysis of this phenomenon from both a theoretical and experimental perspective. Specifically, we investigated the vulnerability of the vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system by generating various weak coherent states, including those with high photon probabilities. Our findings indicate that an eavesdropper can launch high-photon-state attacks on certain states, revealing the system's weakness. Moreover, we propose an improved approach based on phase-matching techniques, which essentially eliminates the system's vulnerability. Our research paves the way for the secure implementation of vacuum+weak decoy state QKD over free space. The increasing adoption of edge computing technologies results in a growing number of computing facilities located close to the edge of the network.  These facilities consume significant amounts of energy, prompting us to investigate methods for optimizing their energy efficiency.  By automating task management and pricing negotiations, the operator can create an incentive framework that encourages nodes to adopt more energy-conscious computing approaches, such as dynamic voltage/frequency scaling, thereby reducing energy consumption.  We develop and test three node price negotiation algorithms, showing that they facilitate energy savings through dynamic scaling, particularly in scenarios where workloads fluctuate continuously.  The results highlight the potential for substantial energy reductions achieved by the operator, amounting to 25% in scenarios where the node price exhibits moderate variability, and up to 90% in scenarios with rapid workload fluctuations.  The performance of the operator-controlled system is further enhanced when certain nodes are configured to prioritize energy efficiency, leading to an additional 15% energy savings.  The data also highlights the impact of cloud pricing models and node failure on energy consumption and system performance.  The findings indicate that the operator can reduce energy consumption through a cloud-like all-optimal pricing approach, resulting in a 25% decrease in energy costs.  The research is accompanied by open-source code allowing the reproduction of testing environment and results.  The proposed incentive framework and node price negotiation algorithms are being explored for extension to other distributed computing systems.  The study provides the foundation for an operator-managed edge computing system optimized for energy efficiency, prompting further investigation into the optimal system configuration, node price models, and system failure handling. The effect of air pressure on the interaction between a nitrogen jet and a surface near a critical point is investigated for two situations: with and without a nearby air stream interacting with the surface. Varying pressure alters the point at which the air and nitrogen meet, affecting the development of Taylor-like palm-size features. Increasing pressure speeds up the emergence of these features under both conditions, but their size remains unaffected. Conversely, reducing pressure allows the nitrogen to reach further lengths before meeting the air, but this doesn't significantly impact the occurrence of the Taylor-like structures. The presence of an adjacent air stream accelerates the appearance of these features and allows the nitrogen to reach further distances before meeting the air, but doesn't alter their size. The speed at which the features form can be influenced by changing pressure, but not their size, and this speed change could be utilized for an asymmetric surface optimization that minimizes turbulence at the point of contact. The results also imply that the Taylor-like structures can provide a means to measure surface roughness through the analysis of pressure's effect on them. The behavior of both situations is captured through a simplified model that takes into account the interaction with an adjacent air stream and is solvable exactly, allowing for a precise analysis of the effects of pressure and surface roughness. The model reveals that the speed at which the features form is governed by a unique exponent that reflects the odd parity of the coefficients influencing it. The implications of this research could be applied to a broader context, such as the study of similar phenomena occurring in fluid interactions with solid surfaces in other gravitational environments. Using observations from the International Ultraviolet Explorer and the IUE, we analyzed hydrogen line broadening in UV spectra during stellar flares. Our results show that line broadening is linked to the optical and far-ultraviolet continuum properties, specifically following a quadratic relationship with continuum flux increases. This hydrogen line broadening can be accurately predicted by a simple formula that takes into account the width of the ultraviolet emission lines, and can be applied to various spectral types of stars. Our findings further indicate that hydrogen line broadening can serve as an indicator of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) flux during stellar flares, which can be crucial for understanding the implications of these events for planetary atmospheres. EUV flux can be reasonably estimated using our simple line broadening formula, making it a useful tool for analyzing future observations with upcoming space telescopes capable of detecting extreme ultraviolet light. Our results can be particularly useful for analyzing data from the upcoming EUV spectrographs, such as the Solar Express and the Stellar Extreme Ultraviolet Spectrograph, which are designed to study the extreme ultraviolet light during stellar flares. Additionally, our line broadening formula can be applied to analyze hydrogen line broadening in white dwarf stars that exhibit flare-like behavior, which in turn can provide insights into the presence of any magnetic field activity on these stars. This research focuses on the dynamics of linear surface waves propagating through a one-dimensional metagrating, which exhibits both PT symmetry and nonlinear behavior. By combining these features, the metagrating displays two distinct states of operation: there is a phase where symmetry is maintained (PT symmetric phase) characterized by wave propagation without loss, and a phase where symmetry is broken (PT broken phase) marked by optical losses. In our work, we observed two types of wave propagation behavior - in the PT symmetric phase, propagating waves maintain their initial amplitude at both ends of the metagrating, whereas in the PT broken phase, waves experience reflection at one edge and absorption at the other. Furthermore, our findings show that the magnitude of optical losses in the PT broken phase can be as large as 10 times the loss in the PT symmetric phase. We developed a theoretical nonlinear transmission model and used it to analyze data from our experiments and simulations. Our model highlights the role of nonlinear interaction in wave propagation behavior and demonstrates that the PT symmetry transition can be controlled by adjusting the strength of nonlinear interaction. In our study, a unit cell with a high nonlinear coefficient (alpha = 0.24) showed a dramatic increase (by a factor of 10) in optical losses in the PT broken phase. However, another unit cell with a low nonlinear coefficient (alpha = 0.01) exhibited a much less pronounced increase (by a factor of 2) in optical losses in the PT broken phase. Our research provides insights into the behavior of propagating waves in nonlinear PT metasurfaces and the dynamics of symmetry transition, offering a framework for designing devices that can switch between different states of operation based on nonlinear interaction. This could enable the development of optical memory devices, switchable flat optics, and other innovative applications. Moreover, our study highlights the potential of combining nonlinear interaction with other symmetry transition mechanisms, such as thermal or chemical transition, to create more complex and versatile metasurfaces. Ultimately, our work paves the way for exploring the fundamental properties of nonlinear PT metasurfaces and their promise of enabling a new generation of smart optical metamaterials and structures.
