The dynamical cavity method has been successful in analyzing complex systems without self-interactions, but a mathematical challenge arises when systems feature neurons that interact with themselves. By developing an alternative expression for the time-dependent variance, we overcome this obstacle and adapt the dynamical cavity method to study self-interacting Boolean networks dynamically. Utilizing this advancement, we investigate a general model that includes systems with identical inputs and those with distinct inputs, ultimately deriving mean field and quenched mean field theories for the latter category. Through our approach, we provide a theoretical framework that can be applied to a broad range of self-interacting systems, making it a valuable tool for analyzing complex networks characterized by recursive relationships between variables. Additionally, our approach facilitates a straightforward numerical implementation, enabling the efficient exploration of parameter space and the development of more refined mean field theories for systems that cannot be solved analytically. We validate our method by applying it to a press coverage network that exhibits sudden and persistent shocks in its dynamics, a phenomenon that cannot be captured by traditional mean field theories. Our study demonstrates that the cavity method can be an effective strategy for analyzing complex self-interacting systems, such as social and biological networks, in a more general context. By adapting this mathematical approach, we aim to contribute to a deeper understanding of complex dynamical systems and the emergence of critical phenomena in networks. The algorithms and models used in this study are also relevant to additional research applications, such as the analysis of binary state systems in other domains. The public data set analyzed in this study is incorporated into the package provided, along with the source code for our main findings to facilitate replication and further exploration of related research questions. Recently, point cloud models have gained popularity for 3D object recognition. Researchers initially proposed twining and projecting the models onto a unit sphere to achieve robustness against twisting transformations. Although this approach showed promise in model robustness, it came with a limited gain in certified accuracy. To build upon this research, the concept of twisting and projecting point clouds was further explored by applying the concept to sub-clouds and incorporating spherical distances. Our study introduces a new framework called Twisted Point Clouds for Complex Rotations, where the models undergo a more comprehensive twisting transformation and certification of accuracy is increased against complex rotations. Comprehensive experiments conducted across various benchmark datasets and real-world capture scenarios demonstrated notable enhancements in model certification and testing accuracy when compared to existing methods. Furthermore, our technique enabled the development of robust models capable of adapting to new viewing angles with minimal additional training. Consequently, our approach presents an effective solution for creating robust point cloud models capable of handling complex twisting transformations. Additionally, our code is publicly available for download.

In this paper, we examine Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar systems that utilize orthogonal sequential transmissions and analyze the impact of these transmissions on each other at a receiving end. We investigate how the FMCW parameters, including the number of frequency modulations within a transmission interval and the sweep rate, affect interference probabilities and system performance. By developing an accurate interference model and solving a reliability problem, we are able to determine optimal transmission strategies that minimize interference probabilities and maximize throughput in data packet transmission. In addition, we investigate the effects of radar system parameters, network behavior and target characteristics on interference probabilities and throughput. Our results show that FMCW radar systems can achieve high performance and minimize interference when using optimized transmission strategies. We also validate our theoretical findings with practical measurements conducted in an FMCW radar testbed. Temporal knowledge graph completion has seen significant advancements in recent years. A crucial aspect of this research involves developing methods to encode temporal information with minimal computational overhead. Current time-encoding techniques primarily focus on individual temporal relations rather than entire cycles. This paper presents a novel cycle-aware time-encoding scheme and demonstrates its applicability in temporal relational prime factorization and graph convolutional networks. Compared to existing time-encoding methods, our proposed approach requires fewer parameters with comparable or improved performance. We also introduce a new cycle-aware interaction attention network as an example of a model utilizing our time-encoding scheme. Experimental results show our method to be an effective way to enhance temporal information capture for temporal knowledge graph completion. The code and data are available at https://github.com/hankunht/CycleAwareTimeEncoding.

Using the RPA formalism, we re-examine the correlation pole model's representation of the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance. By directly solving the RPA equations for the ground state and a specific excited state, we obtain the pole parameters in a self-consistent manner. Our method goes beyond the conventional third-order perturbation theory employed in the correlation pole model. We calculate the self-energies employing the long-range nucleon-nucleon forces, and determine the pole parameters without making assumptions based on the correlation pole model's perturbative nature. Our results show that the model's description of the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, specifically its energy and strength, is accurate. However, the model fails to account for the double resonance structure observed in recent experiments. Additionally, our approach highlights the importance of configuration mixing in the ground state and its impact on the resonance's energy and strength. We also derive a formula connecting the resonance's energy and strength to the one-body potential's properties, and discuss the potential applications of this method to other excited states and systems. Lastly, we outline the benefits of combining this method with ab initio techniques that precisely determine nucleon-nucleon interactions and solve the RPA equations for medium-sized nuclei. This has the potential to provide a fundamental understanding of excited states' properties within the framework of quantum many-body theory.

Establishing effective sentence representations is crucial in neural text-to-sentence generation. Prior work has primarily focused on style-based generators using one-hot vectors, yielding unidimensional sentence representations. In contrast, our proposed SparseGAN technique utilizes a GAN framework to produce a high-dimensional sentence representation, encompassing a compact set of embedded meanings. By constraining this representation to be sparse, we aim to generate more semantically coherent sentences. The training process is facilitated through a supplementary dense code generation process, enabling seamless combination of the sparse sentence representation and densely encoded contextual information. Experimental evaluations on various text classification tasks demonstrate that our approach achieves enhanced performance and interpretability when incorporating pre-trained language models. Furthermore, SparseGAN exhibits capacity in dense code generation, surpassing baseline GAN scores and yielding a 1.4% improvement in accuracy when integrated with classification tasks. The technique's versatility in dense code production allows for direct application in text classification scenarios. In dense mode, SparseGAN outperforms baseline GAN scores and achieves a 1.4% improvement in accuracy when integrated with pre-trained language models for classification tasks. In addition to classification, we show that SparseGAN can produce dense codes for other tasks like summarization and paraphrasing, demonstrating its potential in these areas. The objective is to identify the minimum power required to establish k edge-disjoint paths between s and {t1, t2,..., tk}. A previous algorithm existed for solving this problem, but it had a limitation of only considering up to 2 edge-disjoint paths. The novel approach involves incrementally expanding an existing 2-edge-disjoint paths solution to accommodate additional edge-disjoint paths. The measurement of polarization in social networks is frequently conducted through the analysis of segregation among political parties, often utilizing indicators like the degree to which individuals are connected to others with the same opinions. However, a review of the current methods used for this analysis reveals significant flaws, including a lack of clear definitions and rigorous statistical methods. Furthermore, most existing studies fail to account for underlying factors that influence individual opinions and provide incomplete views of polarization within a network. In contrast, our study proposes a comprehensive framework for measuring polarization that takes into consideration both the opinions of individuals and the structure of the network, using a method that integrates parametric conditional inference to assess the degree of segregation, as well as the influence of demographic factors and network effects. Our proposed framework is applied to a dataset of Twitter users who exchanged messages during the 2012 US presidential debate, and the results demonstrate a substantial level of polarization among users who actively contributed to the discussion, with demographic factors and network effects playing a role in maintaining the segregation among party lines. Notably, our findings indicate that although opinion-based connections can foster a sense of community among individuals with the same opinions, they also facilitate the dissemination of information and promote agreement. Our method is made available online as an interactive tool that enables users to visualize and measure polarization in various social networks. Through this approach, we uncover evidence of polarization in multiple online communities, including Reddit and Twitter, and present a theoretical model that explains the mechanisms driving polarization in temporary and virtual networks, with implications for our understanding of polarization in lasting and physical contexts. In this paper, we investigate a special root in a root system that is shared by types A_l and D_l, denoted as $\alpha_{1,l}$, and analyze its unique properties. We prove that in both systems, this root $\alpha_{1,l}$ is an isolated vertex in the graph of the root system, excluding the possibility of obtaining it through the combination of other roots. Furthermore, we demonstrate that $\alpha_{1,l}$ can be obtained from the positive root $\alpha_i$ of type A_l by reflecting $\alpha_i$ across the x-axis, and that this reflection behavior does not occur for any other root in the system. We also establish the connection between the number of times $\alpha_{1,l}$ is reflected to obtain the fundamental weights as being related to the number of times the positive root $\alpha_i$ of type A_l needs to be reflected to obtain the fundamental weights of type D_l, which is in turn related to the number of fundamental weights of type D_l being greater than the number of fundamental weights of type A_l by one. This reflection behavior on the roots also leads to a similarity in behavior for the highest weight vectors of irreducible representations in these two types, and as a result, we can directly translate from the roots of type A_l to the roots of type D_l, and vice versa. This allows us to list all possible reflections of the fundamental weights of type A_l, as well as determine the possible highest weight vectors for the irreducible representations of the Lie algebra of type D_l. We conclude by considering the extension of this analysis to the Lie superalgebras of type A_(m|n).

We examine the accuracy of queue length estimation using phase-based analysis in finite capacity queues subject to various input processes, including those that are nonparametric. A new evaluation method is introduced to assess the precision of queue length predictions, and our analysis involves both theoretical and simulation-based data. We compare the performance of nonparametric and parametric methods under different scenarios, observing that nonparametric analysis often yields more accurate results than parametric methods, especially when the underlying distribution is complex. However, nonparametric analysis may struggle with short observation periods, and we suggest a minimum observation duration of two times the queue's mean service period for reliable estimates. Additionally, we found that increasing the observation period beyond this minimum does not significantly improve estimate precision. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the accuracy of predictions depends on the ratio of arrival and service rates, but is less sensitive to low utilization levels. Lastly, we investigate how traffic congestion affects the accuracy of queue length predictions and find that our proposed method performs well under various input conditions, including those resembling real-world scenarios. In conclusion, a two-times minimum observation period is recommended for reliable queue length predictions using phase-based analysis. Although this is a preliminary study, it paves the way for more in-depth research into the precision of queue length predictions under diverse scenarios. The proposed method can be applied to various complex queues, such as those with multiple input processes and finite capacities, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation examples. The new evaluation method and findings from this analysis are expected to contribute positively to the field of complex queue analysis. The associated software is available online for the convenience of researchers and practitioners in need of similar analyses.

This new approach to solving the Hamiltonian constraint in general relativity's initial value problem, where we determine the metric's conformal factor, diverges from traditional methods through the introduction of a novel minimal surface condition. In this scheme, a specific boundary value problem is formulated for the conformal factor, with the goal of estimating the factor's values across the spatial section. A key aspect of this approach is the introduction of a specific surface within the conformally transformed space, known as $\mathcal{B}^+$. Within this scheme, values of the conformal factor can be determined at $\mathcal{B}^+$ by resolving a minimal surface problem, where it is postulated that this surface has a specific relationship with another boundary value problem formulated for a massless scalar field. In this paper, we derive the minimal surface condition for the conformal factor by differentiating this relationship in time. Through an energy estimate, we demonstrate that this condition does yield an explicit expression for the conformal factor's values at $\mathcal{B}^+$. In addition, we establish the existence of a global minimal surface that satisfies this condition within a specific class of smooth metrics. Although this scheme does yield a specific expression for the conformal factor, it does not provide a means of numerically solving the Hamiltonian constraint due to an ill-posed boundary value problem. The ensemble of iterative logits from different classifiers has proven effective in various tasks, providing a straightforward improvement over individual models. By building upon this ensemble concept, our proposed Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) delivers an ensemble framework that enhances the efficacy of disparate classifiers utilizing a unique ensemble approach. In this paper, we examine how PILE can be seamlessly integrated with logit-ensemble methods, such as Pairwise Interactive Learning (PI-L) and Co-Training logit Ensemble (CTLE). Specifically, we present a novel CTLE method that leverages an unbiased estimation technique to equitably utilize the limited labeled data available for each teacher model. By incorporating an accurate bias correction method, our proposed CTLE can successfully utilize all available labeled data in the refinement process. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed methods over current state-of-the-art approaches in semi-supervised and co-training scenarios. Additionally, we showcase the broad applicability of PILE to various ensemble strategies and provide theoretical insights into the benefits it confers. Our code is openly available at https://github.com/yunshengguo/PILE.

This article examines the sobolev regularity of an obstacle in a non-autonomous obstacle problem, where the additional condition is that the obstacle's gradient meets a certain standard, resulting in the corresponding solution's gradient also meeting that standard. By leveraging an approach introduced by Schepeck and Shapiro, we prove that if the obstacle meets a specific sobolev standard in a bounded domain with smooth boundaries, then the solution also meets that standard. However, if the boundaries are not smooth, we demonstrate that only the corresponding sobolev imbedding theorem's standard is maintained by the solution. Furthermore, we analyze the solution's behavior over an unbounded domain that includes a cone. Additionally, we consider a problem defined within a cylinder, leading to a solution that reflects the sobolev standard of the obstacle while also considering the cobolev standard of the cylinder. Lastly, we discuss the implications of incorporating memory terms into the problem, resulting in the solution's sobolev standard being enhanced. This increase in sobolev standard occurs without the memory terms affecting the solution's bound or its rate of change. Quantum annealing is an experimental technique employed to solve intricate optimization problems and was initially proposed as a method to reach the ground state of a given Hamiltonian. This protocol's performance relies on slowly transforming a problem Hamiltonian from a easy-to-solve to a complex form, minimizing the likelihood of settling into a meta-stable state. We examine the impact of environmental influence on quantum annealing using a generic spin model, considering both stochastic resonance and coherent perturbation environments. Our results indicate that decoherence affects the success of quantum annealing, with the possibility of improving outcomes in certain environments. Notably, we find that decoherence can hinder the formation of a uniform up-state, a prerequisite for the target ground state, and propose this defect may be the underlying reason for the failure to solve the Ising problem via quantum annealing. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of coherent perturbations on quantum annealing, introducing a novel phase diagram that highlights distinct solutions involving coherent perturbation-driven state transfer. Our results provide a theoretical framework for understanding quantum annealing in relation to environment and suggest potential applications involving the management of coherent perturbations. We explore the idea of mesoscale flatness in relation to minimal surfaces and surfaces with bounded mean curvature. Building on previous work by Nier \& Witten, we investigate how to characterize and distinguish between different types of mesoscale flatness. Additionally, we establish a connection between these concepts and the behavior of surface directions at the mesoscale level. This enables us to analyze the surface's local structure through an expansion of Jacobi fields, which gives us a new perspective on the surface's curvature characteristics. This new perspective allows us to identify specific conditions that ensure mesoscale flatness, which we demonstrate through specific examples, including both planar surfaces and more complex constructions. Furthermore, our study reveals that mesoscale flatness is a more robust concept than mesoscale convexity, which has implications for the surface's behavior at small scales.

Recent studies utilizing local critic training for Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent Neural Networks have demonstrated notable efficiencies. By leveraging pre-trained experts and focusing on task-specific refinement, our method achieves comparable performance with significantly reduced parameters. Building on this work, we develop a unified framework for incorporating multiple experts in each module across various network layers. By extending the backpropagation algorithm to account for expert contributions, we can precisely compute the gradients for parameter updates. The key innovation is a versatile framework that enables efficient training on resource-constrained devices. To further optimize model size, we introduce an innovative strategy to dynamically prune expert parameters based on their contribution to error reduction. Combining expert parameter pruning with our unified framework leads to a significant reduction in parameters while maintaining comparable performance. To validate our method, we conduct comprehensive evaluations on image classification, speech emotion recognition, and speech classification tasks, achieving superior performance relative to baseline models in terms of accuracy and model size. Notably, our method achieves a 94.45% accuracy on the LargeWisemood dataset with fewer model parameters than the baseline multi-layer LSTM model. Moreover, our study examines the effect of expert layer configuration, pruning strategy, and activation functions on model performance. To facilitate further research, we have made our code publicly available.

By addressing these issues, we believe institutions can increase student participation within online learning environments. In response to these findings, we have revised the module's assessment strategy and are introducing additional support to enhance the online learning experience for these students. Our identities successfully capture the higher-spin symmetry present in the Toda conformal field theories, specifically for the $A_2^{(2)}$ theory, which we demonstrate through explicit applications including the derivation of screened spin-three Ward identities. Furthermore, we show that combining multiple screening charges leads to the emergence of higher-spin symmetry beyond the König-Lashkevich proposal. Specifically, we prove that the set of higher-spin currents obtained through multiple screenings forms a Virasoro algebra with central charge two. Additionally, we establish the relationship between these higher-spin currents and primary fields, presenting their expansion in terms of spin and screening levels. Lastly, we explore the multi-screening generalization of the duality between the $A_2^{(2)}$ CFT and the Goto-Gross-Witten transition in string theory on a torus. This generalization enables us to express the twisted sector of the latter in terms of the screening charges of the former. Consequently, we identify the role of higher-spin symmetry in this duality and propose its extension to other Toda CFTs and various dual transitions. This work relies heavily on the recent breakthroughs of Koehler, Lashkevich, and Konsevich regarding the higher-spin symmetry in Toda CFTs. We explore how a specific type of highly connected subgraph within a right-angled Artin group's representation on a tree can pinpoint individual group members. By analyzing this subgraph's properties, we establish conditions under which it exists in the representation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that such a subgraph's existence is equivalent to the group having a particular property called finiteness, either of the first kind when the subgraph is finite, or of the second kind when the subgraph is not finite. Additionally, we show that if the subgraph separates the tree into distinct components, it indicates that the group's action on the tree has a particular structure, leading to the group being conjugate to a subgroup of an infinite cyclic group that acts on the tree. This strategic use of subgraphs within the action on trees enables us to examine the group's overall structure. By applying this technique to various group structures, we are able to derive several results about their actions on trees. For instance, we prove that certain groups with specific subgraphs will not be able to act freely on trees. We also establish that if a group has a subgraph that splits the tree into two equal parts and this subgraph exists in every representation of the group on a tree, then the group has a particular type of finite fundamental group. This work also gives an alternative proof for a recent result showing that any group with a finite 3-arb that contains a separating 4-cycle will have a fundamental group of a finite orbifold. Moreover, we extend this result to show that if this 4-cycle contains a side of length 2, then the group's fundamental group will be finite for any tree, not just those with a specific structure. This research is based on the interaction between the group's action on the tree and the subgraph's properties, and as such, it can be seen as an extension of the 1-arb method used to study right-angled Artin groups. It also introduces new methods to analyze the group's structure by examining its action on the tree. Given its focus on the group's interaction with its own subgraph, this work can be seen as an investigation into the group's own 'geometry'. In this context, it raises several additional questions about the group's structure and its representation on trees. dynamic graph classification framework. This framework consists of multiple
subnetworks that learn to combine local representations of nodes within a graph,
training on either individual or combined data from past time steps. By
leveraging a decoder that fuses node features, DECENNT significantly outperforms
existing solutions according to experimental results, with code available at

dynamic graph classification tasks, along with dataset downloads and training
instructions. In addition, DECENNT shows substantial improvements over baseline
methods, such as a 25.4% boost in accuracy for webcast on Google Mobile Ads
and a 21.3% increase in Micro-F1 Score for Twitter-FF. This paper introduces

mechanisms, and overall technique. It also explores Decennt's Advantages over
conventional approaches like multi-task learning and graph attention networks. In
the experiments section, DECENNT is pitted against multiple graph classification
methods, including both dynamic and static models, with all code reproducible.

The development of phylogenetic analysis through stochastic processes has guided evolutionary research, offering valuable insights and reconstructing historical relationships among species. Building upon existing work, this study explores how to utilize multiple genetic signals to estimate a phylogeny, specifically focusing on the application to the evolutionary history of the cowpox virus. By incorporating a phylogeny, this research reveals the possibility of resolving the long-standing mystery surrounding the origin and dissemination of cowpox viruses in Europe and Asia. Through a stochastic model that accounts for Cowpox-related infections among rodents and the introduction of new viral strains, this study reconstructs the evolutionary history of the virus and predicts future variations, providing evidence for the coexistence of cowpox viruses with rodent hosts in Asia for an estimated 3,000 to 5,000 years. Furthermore, this model anticipates the cowpox virus will continue to evolve independently in Asia and Europe, with Asia experiencing a more rapid rate of change due to the interaction with vaccinia viruses used in vaccination efforts. As a result, this study proposes that vaccinia viruses could serve as a potential target for developing interventions aimed at controlling the cowpox virus. By leveraging multi-locus summary statistics and incorporating a phylogeny, this research offers an empirical framework with implications for accelerating methodological development for the analysis of viral genomes. Although this study employs cowpox viruses as a case study, the introduced framework is equally applicable to the investigation of other viral origins and evolutionary histories. By integrating statistical analysis and modeling of viral spread, this research aims to encourage a more comprehensive understanding of the complex dynamics underlying viral evolution and to contribute to ongoing discussions surrounding the development of improved methods for analyzing genomic data. As such, this study is freely accessible with the aim of fostering constructive discussion and paving the way for further methodological advancements. The implementation of the proposed methods is freely available for use at https://github.com/hjmhjmhjm/SPR-SCMR. The code utilized in this research, along with the data utilized in the cowpox virus analysis, can be found at https://github.com/hjmhjmhjm/SPR-SCMR/tree/main/Cowpox_virus. The parameters employed in this research, along with the results, are presented in Supplemental Material available at https://jmlb.org/submissions/20220319/2022-EM-26.Supplement.pdf. The introduced framework has the potential to bridge the gap between methodological development and the analysis of real-world viral evolution

The development of an open, unbiased analysis for the study of living systems is key to successfully addressing the inherent variability present in biological data. A crucial step in this analysis involves accurately identifying the movement of individual components within a living system from video footage. However, distinguishing this movement from the random movement of non-biological objects requires additional processing. To address this challenge, we've developed a comprehensive toolkit utilizing deep learning models to enhance the visualization and analysis of biological systems from video and image data. This toolkit includes a neural network for identifying cells within microscope images, another for predicting the trajectory of individual cells from video footage, and a method for combining these predictions with physical models to simulate the behavior of cellular movements. We've applied this toolkit to gain new insights into the dynamics of single cells and tissue coordination in developing embryos. Specifically, we've used it to improve the visualization of cellular trajectories, reveal previously unseen small-scale movement in single cells, and demonstrate how tissue coordination can lead to the formation of uniform patterns. The toolkit discussed here has the potential to accelerate the development of analysis methods for the study of living systems and is now openly available for others to use and customize. The toolkit can be accessed at: https://github.com/cubeight/CellAtlasVisualizer and the model weights at: https://github.com/cubeight/CellTrajectoryPredictor and https://github.com/cubeight/CellSegmentation. The Neumann series for inverse matrices serves as a ground truth for comparing the convergence rates of various iterative algorithms. However, its complexity as a matrix inverse grows exponentially with the number of dimensions, making it impractical for most practical applications. In contrast, the Neumann series can be effectively evaluated for multi-dimensional matrices using a recursive approach known as the Nested Neumann algorithm, with a convergence rate determined by the inception depth. By further breaking down the problem into smaller sub-problems, we can utilize multiple CPU cores to speed up the algorithm. In our experiments, we demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness by generating synthetic data and applying the Nested Neumann algorithm to image deblurring, matrix division, and sparse signal reconstruction, with significant performance improvements achieved using multiple CPU cores. Specifically, our results show that the algorithm can achieve similar accuracy as matched filter-based LMS methods but with much faster convergence. Additionally, our work includes a detailed analysis of the algorithm's sensitivity to anisotropic scaling. Notably, our research utilizes the BLAS and LAPACK libraries, which provide low-level optimizations for linear algebra operations, to achieve performance enhancements on a single CPU core. Our implementation is open-source and freely available for download. 

Keywords: Neumann series, Nested Neumann algorithm, multi-dimensional matrices, recursive evaluation, iterative algorithms, image deblurring, matrix division, sparse signal reconstruction, performance optimization, linear algebra libraries, anisotropic scaling, open-source implementation.

Recently, studies on the topological characteristics of Anderson insulators have revealed significant findings, and there's growing interest in detecting these characteristics in physical systems. Using the Jordan-Wigner transformation for spin models described by the Hamiltonian of the XXZ type in an optical lattice, we successfully obtained the diagonalized Hamiltonian and resulting eigenstates. We demonstrated that the projection of these eigenstates onto physical sites allows for the direct observation of both local and extended Anderson insulator states, which are distinguished by specific symmetry properties. We also showed that interactions between particles can induce multiple instances of the symmetry protection of topological phases, resulting in more complex phase diagrams. Furthermore, by examining the two-point correlation function, we were able to distinguish between different Anderson insulator phases based on the spatial structure of correlations. Our results provide practical methods for identifying Anderson insulators in experimental systems. Lastly, we discuss the applicability of our approach to other systems described by Hamiltonian Hamiltonian in the XX, XXZ and Ising types. This paper introduces a new statistical test to examine the presence of specific network structures within complex systems that adhere to specific patterns, referred to as MS-structures. We develop a precise method for applying this test to a broad range of network autoregressive models that encompass various well-known models, including Granger models and vector autoregressive models. Notably, our proposed method effectively mitigates the issue of non-identifiable parameters common in network autoregressive models by employing a regularisation strategy. Through numerous simulations, we demonstrate the accuracy of our proposed test, particularly when comparing it to a commonly employed alternative. Moreover, we showcase the practical utility of our proposed test by conducting an empirical analysis using the S&P 500 index composition. Our findings reveal that the most recent price movements in the network have a substantial impact on future price changes, while incorporating an exponential decay factor that lessens the impact of more distant price movements. However, we observe that the inclusion of inflation rates has a minimal effect on stock price autoregression, likely due to the limited availability of historical data and the strong co-movements among stocks, which dominate the underlying MS-structures. Consequently, our research paves the way for further investigation into the role of fundamental factors in stock price dynamics. Additionally, we offer the software used in this paper on an open-source basis via the RStudio package 'NetAR'. This package not only enables the execution of our proposed tests but also facilitates network autoregressive model estimation, forecasting, and time series network visualization. Furthermore, we outline numerous capabilities that this package offers and provide guidelines for utilizing its key features. Through the implementation of our proposed tests and the integration of network autoregressive models, we aim to contribute to the advancement of statistical research in complex systems and network dynamics. The backward pass in optimization techniques like backpropagation in neural networks and interior-point methods for linear and nonlinear programming involves computationally expensive operations that can benefit from problem structure to accelerate convergence. In specific contexts, such as training large-scale neural networks and solving large-scale linear and nonlinear programming problems, the backward pass becomes a significant performance bottleneck. We introduce a novel algorithm based on a novel differentiation technique called implicit differentiation, which applies to a broad class of optimization techniques that include neural network training, linear and nonlinear programming, and general optimization methods. The algorithm employs value functions to represent and compute the derivatives of the objective and constraint functions with respect to parameters, making it possible to leverage structure in two ways: by exploiting implicit relationships between variables and by using the algorithm to detect and utilize inactive constraints. The result is a method to further accelerate the backward pass by reducing the number of operations required. The implicit relationship exploitation leads to a factorization-based solution that results in a significant reduction in computational complexity, while the value function representation of constraints enables the detection of inactive constraints, which results in a further reduction in operations required and, in some cases, eliminates the need for sparse data structures and memory access. The algorithm can be implemented using existing solvers for the value function equations, and its benefits are demonstrated through a range of applications, including implicit differentiation of dense and sparse linear and nonlinear programming problems, and the training of large-scale neural networks, combinatorial neural networks, and graph neural networks. The results show a substantial acceleration of the backward pass, leading to total training times that are comparable to those obtained using specialized solvers for linear and nonlinear programming, and a significant reduction in training times for graph neural networks. The implicit differentiation algorithm is an accelerated backward pass solver that can be used in place of existing solvers, and it is an enabling technology for the large-scale optimization applications it targets. To study the mechanics of individual stress fibers within cells, a three-dimensional microfluidic device was used to apply precise forces to specific areas of stress fiber development.  By examining Markov Transition State Theory, our findings indicate that contractility alone cannot alone account for stress fiber mechanical properties; instead, they are influenced by the interaction between actin turnover and filament dynamics.  In particular, our results suggest that stress fibers display non-linear elasticity due to their branched structure, and that their turn-over rate significantly impacts their mechanical response, with potential applications in controlling stress fiber behavior through targeted drug delivery.  In addition, our stress fiber model can be integrated into existing cell mechanics models that consider the entire cell cytoskeleton, and such a unified framework can be used to simulate the effects of actin-related protein mutations on cell elasticity.  Through comparison with experimental data, our stress fiber model shows that its turnover-based mechanism better explains stress fiber behavior than a contractility-based approach.  In our model, stress fiber contractility is not a driving force, but rather a passive response to increased actin turnover and plus-end binding protein levels in specific regions, and it can be used to simulate stress fiber disassembly through targeted drug delivery in cells.  Our study provides new insights into stress fiber mechanics and suggest that precision force application in microfluidic devices can be an effective tool for studying the mechanics of stress fibers within cells.  Furthermore, our approach can be adapted for use in studying other cellular structures.  In addition, our stress fiber model, in conjunction with finite element analysis, can be employed to investigate the effects of stress fiber mechanics on cell behavior in response to external loads and constraints.  In our study, we demonstrate that stress fiber mechanics can be investigated at the molecular level through precision force application in microfluidic devices, and that such an approach can be used to develop targeted therapies for actin-related diseases. Cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin offer users anonymity, however, this feature also enables malicious activities such as money laundering and dark web transactions to be concealed. To combat these illicit actions, exchange and wallet institutions are required to report suspicious transactions to regulatory authorities. However, such institutions possess limited insight into the activities of individual users, prompting the development of methods that can track user behavior based on publicly available cryptocurrency data. The existing research on cryptocurrency analysis focuses primarily on identifying malicious activities within transaction history, yet real-world users continually monitor their wallets for ongoing scams. To address this gap, this paper introduces a novel approach called CGATG, utilizing a temporal transaction graph framework that captures user activities from wallet transactions and extracts hidden patterns to identify ongoing scams. The proposed framework consists of three key components: (1) a data extraction phase where wallet transactions are converted into temporal transaction graphs, (2) an intrinsic pattern learning phase that applies an advanced machine learning technique called attribute-aware graph sub-structure extraction to discover hidden cycles of activity within these graphs, (3) a scoring phase that evaluates the probability of each cycle indicating an ongoing scam based on previously reported suspicious transactions. The effectiveness of the proposed CGATG framework is validated through an evaluation of two real-world cryptocurrency datasets, showcasing significant improvement over existing solutions and the diversity of emerging cycles, including several that resemble known scams. The detailed analysis of runtime, model complexity, and scalability of the proposed CGATG framework provides valuable insights for further research, along with publicly available data and source code to support replication of the results presented. With the ability to identify suspicious activities concurrently with ongoing scams from wallet transactions, the proposed CGATG framework is poised to enhance the detection capabilities of exchange and wallet institutions, yielding a more comprehensive insight into user activities. The framework's scalability and diversity of emerging cycles in relation to conventional approaches demonstrate its potential as a solution to tackle complex cryptocurrency analysis challenges. As a result, the CGATG framework is available online at https://github.com/azamcse/CGATG. A major challenge in quantum computing is decoherence caused by the connection to their surroundings, which causes loss of information necessary for operational performance. Quantum error correction is a vital component for developing reliable quantum systems by preventing knowledge of the state from escaping into the environment. While classical programming techniques efficiently handle errors in conventional computing, similar classical algorithms can also benefit from machine learning applications that enhance decoding efficiency. This study explores the potential of reinforcement learning to develop effective and efficient decoding protocols for the protection of quantum information. Specifically, we investigate learning scenarios in which knowledge of the environment is either partially or fully accessible to the decoder. Our findings indicate that feasible decoding policies can be learned through suitable reward designs even when the environment's details are fully known, leading to significant reductions in decoding latency with minimal error increments in scenarios such as the Shor code and topological codes. Interestingly, when the environment's parameters are only partially known, observable changes in error patterns allow for efficient learning of effective decoding strategies. Most surprisingly, unlearning previous knowledge about the environment's state enables the rapid adoption of new decoding policies when code updates occur, leading to minimal latency in correction applications. These outcomes showcase the value of combining quantum computing and machine learning in the development of reliable quantum systems. Nonetheless, genuine quantum learning scenarios remain to be explored in future research.

Quantum systems can achieve highly accurate measurements by exploiting unique phenomena such as entanglement, correlation, and spontaneous transitions. A novel approach known as quantum jump metrology uses specialized feedback to make the most of these phenomena through continuous observation of quantum states and immediate correction of their dynamics. Building on previous descriptions of qubit-based systems using this approach, this paper expands on that work by examining systems involving multiple qubits and demonstrating that quantum jump metrology can provide a significant improvement in measurement performance when there is a strong correlation between qubits. Specifically, we analyze systems involving a single excited state and two excited states, showing that quantum jump metrology can achieve an optimal measurement accuracy that is 1.5 to 2 times better than traditional methods. Furthermore, we propose an feasible experimental implementation using strontium optical lattices and discuss possibilities for applying this approach to systems involving more complex interactions and multiple levels, such as chemical reaction dynamics. Our research examined the production of hadrons in Au+Au collisions at various levels of parton fragmentation, using data from RHIC experiments. By comparing measured hadron yields to theoretical predictions from Ji et al., we found significant deviations in certain cases, specifically when studying quark activity at low momentum fractions. These deviations were observed in hadron yields for various particle species, particularly pions and protons, which suggest quark contributions to hadron formation at early stages of heavy ion collisions. Furthermore, we discovered that the coherence effect, thought to influence hadron production at a certain level of parton fragmentation, may actually dominate hadron formation at lower levels of parton fragmentation, where quark behavior becomes prominent. Additionally, we investigated the balance between hadron yields and the fragmentation function in Au+Au and $e^+e^-$ collisions, finding that hadron production in heavy ion collisions is influenced more significantly by the fragmentation function than in $e^+e^-$ collisions. These findings have important implications for our understanding of hadron formation in heavy ion and $e^+e^-$ collisions. In the latter case, our research indicates that hadron production can be described by a single set of parameters, revealing a fundamental relationship between hadron yields and the fragmentation function in $e^+e^-$ collisions. This relationship may provide a basis for a more accurate description of hadron production in heavy ion collisions. In Au+Au collisions, our research indicates the need for a coherence effect to be included in the discussion of hadron production, giving further evidence for the importance of quark behavior in hadron formation. In 1970, Huard established an upper bound for the sequence of values obtained from the polynomial $x^2+x+1$, where $x$ takes on positive integers. This paper builds upon that work by expanding the upper bound limit to a higher degree, specifically for the polynomial $x^3+3x^2+1$ and its variants, and confirms that the original bound can be applied to a broader range of numbers within those increased limits. Furthermore, this paper derives upper bounds for the norm and least common multiple of the values of the polynomial $x^3+3x^2+1$, and also examines the associated sequence dynamics, confirming that the sequence remains non-reducible over its expanded upper bound limit. Additionally, this paper investigates the same sequences for the polynomials $x^2-x+1$ and $x^2+ax+1$, and provides explicit examples for non-cyclotomic polynomials of the form $x^n+1$, where $n$ is an odd prime. Last but not least, this paper proves that for any polynomial $f(x)$ of degree $d$ with coefficients in the integers, the sequence $(\alpha, \sigma(\alpha)), (\sigma(\alpha), \sigma^2(\alpha)), \ldots$ is distinct over its upper bound limit $\rho$ if and only if the sequence $\sigma, \sigma^2, \ldots$ is distinct over its upper bound limit $\sigma(\rho)$. Remote procedures calls (RPCs) in cloud-based high-performance computing (HPC) systems cause high latency and bandwidth usage due to poor optimization. This research introduces a novel RPC framework called Thunder- RPC, utilizing gRPC and asynchronous programming to significantly improve performance. By activating multiple concurrent connections and ordering RPCs by latency, Thunder-RPC reduces average latency from 1.5ms to 0.8ms and average bandwidth usage per core from 0.12GB/s to 0.08GB/s. In addition, Thunder-RPC boosts system throughput by 10-20% and minimizes memory usage per core by 10-20% in popular HPC applications. This research is now integrated into the Parrot HPC runtime system and is available open-source for community use. This is particularly relevant as cloud-based HPC systems face growing scalability and performance barriers that must be addressed innovatively. This work's performance gains can serve as a model for solving RPC-related performance challenges in cloud-based HPC systems. This paper addresses the contextual linear bandit problem under an additional assumption where the context distribution holds some prior knowledge. Specifically, we assume that the reward function can be represented by a linear combination of unknown context features and that the context distribution conforms to a specific structure, allowing us to make inferences about the structure of the reward function based on observed data. We investigate two settings: one where the structure of the context distribution is fully known in advance, known as the "identifiable" setting, and another more general setting known as the "non-identifiable" setting. For the identifiable setting with known context structure, we developed an optimal learning algorithm that adapts the linear contextual bandit strategy to the observed context features, enabling us to draw inferences about the structure of the reward function. This algorithm minimizes the expected long-term regret under weak assumptions. For the non-identifiable setting, we introduced an upper bound on the expected long-term regret under certain distribution assumptions. Interestingly, this result implies that providing the context distribution's knowledge does not necessarily reduce the bit requirements for communication, which could even increase depending on the setting. Notably, our results provide lower bounds on the expected long-term regret in both identifiable and non-identifiable settings. Moreover, we investigated a complementary problem known as the "communication optimal" problem, aiming to minimize the expected long-term regret subject to a communication constraint. This problem is particularly relevant in real-world applications where significant amounts of data need to be transmitted to agents working under contextual linear bandit problems. We established an optimal strategy for the communication optimal problem in both identifiable and non-identifiable settings, demonstrating that the optimal strategy shares key characteristics with the learning algorithm developed for the standard contextual linear bandit problem. Additionally, we investigated a special case known as the single-arm linear bandit problem, offering an alternative solution based on a different approach known as the least sensitive estimate (LSE). This approach led to an interesting comparison of the LSE's performance with our proposed algorithm, revealing that the LSE outperforms the proposed algorithm on certain context distributions, particularly those with strong structures. While many companies have successfully adapted to remote work via Scrum methodology, successfully navigating this approach poses its own challenges. To gain insight into the underlying dynamics, we propose a mathematical model that draws from systems theory and incorporates elements from the Scrum framework. By translating the model into a set of difference equations, we aim to analyze the behavioral patterns that emerge, using bifurcation diagrams to explore how the Scrum process reacts to changes brought about by working from home. Our model focuses specifically on the remote Scrum development environment described in the accompanying case study. With this model, we are able to identify how working from home can lead to unstable project schedules, and further investigate the consequences for project timelines. Additionally, we highlight potential strategies for mitigating these effects through adjustments to the Scrum process. To validate our model, we conducted a sensitivity analysis in order to assess its robustness in relation to various assumptions. Furthermore, we outline potential avenues for further research, including the extension of this model to other agile methodologies and development processes. By leveraging mathematical modeling in this way, we hope to contribute to a more in-depth understanding of the systems underlying software development, and to provide a methodological approach for analyzing other development processes. The problem of high dimensionality in value function estimation is a common challenge for policy learning. To address this, research has leveraged the idea of low-rank approximations to achieve more efficient learning. A critical issue in this context is ensuring that the estimated value function remains accurate when evaluated on new, unseen data. In response to these concerns, recent studies have developed cutting-edge methods for low-rank value function estimation, characterized by minimal sampling variance and outstanding performance on new data. Interestingly, an interesting phenomenon observed in these methods reveals that there is an optimal sample size $T$ for estimation, where an increase in $T$ does not lead to improved accuracy. Moreover, it has been discovered that when the original value function has a low rank, the optimal sample size $T$ is directly proportional to the rank, thereby significantly reducing the sampling requirement. Furthermore, an interesting connection between low-rank value function estimation and policy evaluation through linear stochastic gradient descent has been identified. Building upon these findings, this paper proposes an enhanced efficient value function estimation method -- efficient PE step (EPE) -- incorporating a regularized update formula to minimize sampling variance. Empirical evaluations across multiple scenarios have demonstrated the outstanding performance of EPE, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the paper analyzes the sampling efficiency of EPE, revealing a linear relationship between sampling efficiency and rank. The proposed method has been found applicable to various policy evaluation settings, including matrix vector settings and online EPE. The open-source code for the novel method EPE, along with the data generation program, is available on GitHub. The paper also introduces the concept of sampling efficiency and provides theoretical bounds for the proposed EPE method. The results demonstrate the outstanding performance of EPE, with the method's sample efficiency determined by the rank of the value function, leading to a significant reduction in sampling requirements when the original value function has a low rank. The paper's contributions include the development of an enhanced efficient value function estimation method EPE, the exploration of a linear stochastic gradient descent approach to PE, the examination of the sampling efficiency of EPE, the discussion of the method's applicability to online EPE, and the introduction of the concept of sampling efficiency. Our study examines the relationship between charged hadron, pion, kaon, and proton transverse momentum distributions and elliptic flow in lead-lead collisions at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. Distributions were collected by the ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC for particles with a transverse momentum greater than 0.5 GeV/c. Data at 2.76 TeV were obtained from 2015 collisions totaling 4.9 nanobarns of integrated luminosity, and data at 5.02 TeV were obtained from 2018 collisions totaling 17.4 nanobarns of integrated luminosity. Results show that the distribution ratio of higher to lower transverse momentum particles increases with transverse momentum in both energy ranges, but the proportion of particles at higher and lower transverse momentum varies between the two energy ranges. Additionally, we found that the ratio of elliptic flow in lead-lead collisions at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV is similar across different transverse momentum ranges, but transverse momentum distributions themselves differ significantly between the two energy ranges. These findings suggest that the increase in hadron production with increasing energy is more pronounced for lower transverse momentum particles, but the increase in elliptic flow is independent of energy. We also observed similar behavior in pion, kaon, and proton distributions, but the results were influenced by particle type due to varying production yields at different energies. These results provide new insights into the relationship between hadron production and elliptic flow in lead-lead collisions at the LHC. Our study also paves the way for further exploratory analyses that could shed light on the underlying mechanisms governing the interplay between particle production and collective flow behavior. Furthermore, we propose using the ratio of distribution ratios as a more sensitive indicator of variations in hadron production in different collision environments. This new quantity is particularly useful for comparing hadron production in different collisions, such as proton-proton and lead-lead collisions, and for identifying differences in hadron production in different pseudorapidity ranges. Lastly, we suggest extending this analysis to other hadrons such as hyperons and anti-hadrons, and to other collision systems such as heavy ions and proton-nucleus collisions, in order to gain a more comprehensive understanding of hadron production in high-energy collisions. To facilitate efficient computation, the paper also derives explicit formulas for both upper and lower bounds estimates of the QLCST energy. Theoretical proofs are verified through numerical examples and demonstrations using MATLAB software. The results demonstrate the quantifiable relationship between the original signals and their QLCST counterparts, providing valuable insights into the behavior of signals in both the time and frequency domains. The methods presented in this paper can be further applied to tackle fundamental challenges related to signal representation, information extraction, and data compression. The techniques discussed in this paper can be extended to explore the properties and capabilities of the QLCST in higher-dimensional signal processing applications. The authors anticipate the outcomes presented in this paper to contribute significatively to the advancement of signal processing research, offering novel methods for evaluating signals and their transforms, and providing efficient solutions for adaptive filtering challenges. Recent advancements in numerical methods for multi-phase flow simulations have utilized multiple-time-step integration algorithms, also known as implicit-explicit schemes, to accelerate computations. By segregating the update of different phases within distinct time steps, these algorithms achieve substantial speed gains without compromising stability. However, the inherent decoupling in these schemes leads to slower convergence in the iterative solution of the nonlinear equations. To address this limitation, a new multiple-time-step algorithm has been developed, where a specific phase is allowed to use implicit contributions from multiple previous time steps in an expanded nonlinear iteration scheme. This novel approach demonstrates superior convergence properties, enabling larger time steps without experiencing reduced convergence rates. Consequently, the algorithm retains the efficiency benefits of the underlying implicit-explicit methods. To demonstrate its performance, the new algorithm is applied to an exemplary problem of flowing through a narrow channel, comparing its convergence against standard implicit-explicit schemes using comprehensive parameter studies. Additionally, the optimal performance is achieved with larger time steps, leading to significant computational savings, approximately five times faster than the standard implicit-explicit method for the chosen problem. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm exhibits superior performance when implemented on multiple CPU cores, yielding further acceleration on a commercial CPU to approximately three times the standard implicit-explicit method through parallel processing. This work offers a new perspective on the potential of multiple-time-step algorithms, highlighting their potential for further investigation in complex multi-phase flow simulations. To facilitate adoption, the developed algorithm has been integrated into the public, open-source framework OpenFOAM via a contributed extension. This contribution primarily consists of the new algorithm, an expanded nonlinear iteration scheme, and a matching solver for the iterative solution of the nonlinear equations, along with suitable utility functions to streamline its usage within OpenFOAM. To utilize this contribution, the latest OpenFOAM version (2.9.x) is required, along with the most recent extensions to the solver library for multi-phase flow simulations, specifically the interFoam solver. This new algorithm is an innovative solution to the trade-off between speed and convergence, offering faster computations without compromising convergence properties. It has the potential to unlock even faster simulations for complex multi-phase flow applications by enabling larger time steps, paving the way for further research into its applications across various multi-phase flow simulations. To this end, the code developed for this project is openly available for download at https://cfdlib.org/showcase/multiple-time-step-algorithm-for-multi-phase-flow-simulations/ as part of the CFD Library, along with additional information on how to use it within OpenFOAM. Overall, the presented feedback-controlled approach yields a notable improvement in the robot's tracking performance, and its fundamental concepts have implications for the development of feedback loops in robotic hopping on various terrain types. Furthermore, the appendix presents additional analysis of the robot's motion and feedback loop behavior, supplemented with graphical illustrations of key phenomena. Additionally, it includes comparative data between simulated and actual trial results. The appendix also presents additional data and additional results not included in the main study. The presented work offers a foundational contribution to the control of impact-driven robots, addressing a critical challenge facing the development of such systems. Despite the promise they hold, robotic hoppers and other impact-driven systems face significant obstacles caused by the complex effects of repeated interaction with their surroundings. To overcome these challenges, future systems will require sophisticated feedback loops that rely on accurate sensing and modeling of the interactions between the robot and its environment. Quantum annealing's performance depends heavily on its scheduling, with various proposals nonetheless failing to pan out in actual experiments. Determining the reason behind this failure, known as the "annealing gap," is crucial to optimizing quantum annealing. One possible explanation is that certain scheduling protocols apply excessive effort to navigate the annealing gap. In this study, a new quantum annealing training method is introduced to minimize the required energy investment in relation to the annealing gap. This approach, inspired by the "cross-entropy method," efficiently finds optimal solutions while drastically reducing the necessary resources. Experimentally, the new protocol led to a 150x improvement in success rates when using only 10 kMinvestment (10,000 minority flips) on the "quantum random organizer" device developed by D-Wave. Furthermore, simulations demonstrate that this approach translates to broader applications across a variety of Hamiltonian scenarios. In addition to accelerating quantum annealing, the proposed method also yields insights into optimizing quantum annealing itself. As a result, the success of this discrete optimization technique can now serve as a benchmark for quantum annealing's performance. In this context, a 150x factor represents a substantial milestone for the technology. The COVID-19 pandemic is causing widespread infection and death, also affecting the global economy and straining healthcare systems.  To combat the pandemic's impact, governments are taking various measures including restricting personal movements, implementing curfews, and closing public places.  Accurate real-time information about infection rates, new restrictions, and essential services would be beneficial for the community's well-being, especially vulnerable populations.  Social media can provide valuable insights into public sentiment and help monitor the spread of misinformation.  In this paper, we present a multi-aspect system that leverages Twitter data to cater to the community's information needs.  Our system includes multiple sub-systems to gather data on infection rates, new restrictions, and provide sentiment analysis for fundamental human needs in real-time.  We collect and clean Twitter data using Twitter API and RAPID API, then employ NLP techniques to analyze the cleaned data.  Our system offers an interactive web interface powered by D3.js library, enabling users to explore the data and navigate easily.  We present our approach and system through a practical application, monitoring the availability of COVID-19 testing services in Scotland.  Our system is currently live at this link:  https://covid19-sentiment-website.herokuapp.com/.  In addition to the community-oriented goal, our approach can be adapted to other NLP applications that involve online data collection and require a high degree of customizability.  We open-source our approach and data collection pipeline on GitHub at this link:  https://github.com/ahmad-zahra/Twitter-DataCollection-Pipeline.  Our approach and data collection pipeline are novel, and our system addresses a pressing public health issue, providing valuable insights into public sentiment and monitoring the spread of misinformation.  In return for using Twitter API, we contributed the data collected to the COVID-19 Twitter datasets available on NASA's NLP portfolio.  In the long term, our system can serve as a foundation for a community-oriented multi-aspect monitoring system that leverages social media to cater to fundamental human needs. outer planets. Additionally, we found that larger grains can increase the

Recent research into machine learning security, fueled by growing automation and human annotation needs, has led to a surge in development and testing of hidden features known as "backdoors." While early studies on backdoors were primarily confined to static triggers and hidden classes, the field has now expanded to include more complex triggers and hidden targets. Despite significant breakthroughs, implementing robust and adaptable backdoors on complex datasets proves challenging due to issues with label data quality and classification model stability. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a novel attack called the "Dynamic Hidden Feature" which leverages a complementary classification model to trigger a hidden target by providing mislabeled samples during the training process. Specifically, the attack involves training a primary and attack model on the same dataset, where the primary model is used to generate hidden features based on differences in classification probabilities. Extensive experiments conducted on complex datasets, including the pre-trained BERT dataset, demonstrate the efficacy and adaptability of this attack in various classification tasks, revealing that even highly robust models can be vulnerable to this dynamic backdoor. Furthermore, we investigate the limitations and surprising stability of this attack in certain scenarios. To facilitate further research, we have made the code and dataset available online. Through this work, we raise fundamental security concerns regarding machine learning models' capacity to incorporate hidden features and stress the importance of implementing robust security measures to prevent such attacks. Additionally, we explore potential applications of this attack in understanding model uncertainty and activating latent targets in generative models. Overall, this paper introduces a groundbreaking dynamic backdoor attack, presents a comprehensive analysis of this issue, and paves the way for exploring this concept in machine learning security. The code and dataset developed as part of this research have been made available online.

Evaluating the performance of relational machine learning models in pharmacology, particularly in predicting drug-target interactions, requires specialized knowledge. Typically, researchers assess model accuracy by aggregating individual predictions, using the mean of all predictions for each target-drug combination. This approach is based on a assumption that each prediction has an equal level of confidence. In reality, confidence levels vary greatly, often resulting in overly conservative models that adhere to a 0.5 threshold for predicting positive interactions. To address this issue, we propose the use of confidence-based evaluation metrics that account for the degree of certainty associated with each prediction. By leveraging the effectiveness of attention mechanisms in relational machine learning models, we also explore the concept of attention scores as indicators of confidence. Our experiments demonstrate that models trained with confidence-based loss functions yield better performance and are less conservative in their predictions, with attention scores serving as reliable indicators of confidence. Through these findings, we aim to contribute to the advancement of evaluation methodologies and model performance optimization in drug-target interaction prediction. Furthermore, our research provides a foundation for exploring other applications of confidence-based evaluation metrics in pharmacology. Additionally, the pre-trained models and software developed as part of this study are available for public use, along with relevant datasets in the field of pharmacology. This includes Enzyme-Target and ToxTarget, as well as PolyPhen2, which can be utilized in conjunction with our evaluation metrics and models. A typical challenge in semi-supervised medical image segmentation involves balancing accurate initial segmentations with avoidable biases. Our research offers a innovative solution by applying interpolation-based image mixing to regularize output probabilities. The Future Extended Range Engine (FEX) is a sophisticated data processing system devised by Fermilab to manage massive amounts of data generated by the Large Hadron Collider's upcoming sensitive detectors as part of the LHC upgrade program. Specifically, the 120 TB/day processing capacity required by the CMS Level 1 trigger system and the Compact Muon Solenoid's data stream, which accounts for 30% of its total output, will be handled by the FEX. Furthermore, the FEX must also accommodate various other experimental needs for online and offline data access at a rate of at least 5 GB/s in each direction. Given its intricate design, the FEX front-end system encompasses a sophisticated software framework that efficiently allocates resources, manages memory, and facilitates seamless online and offline data transfers. In addition, the system features an innovative algorithm developed by CMS to identify potential collisions and pinpoint the precise location for further examination. This document delves into the fundamental design of the FEX system and explores its underlying software framework in detail. Moreover, it highlights the distinctive features of the FEX, including its memory management and data transfer mechanisms, as well as the unique features of the Level 1 trigger algorithm and the FEX's spatial reconstruction capabilities. Lastly, early test results and actual FEX performance data are presented, showcasing the system's capacity to process data at rates exceeding 100 MB/s and featuring a compact, industrial chassis designed for minimal footprint. The full-scale FEX prototype, comprising four custom modules and totaling four termination units, will be showcased at the conference. The designers anticipate the FEX's data processing speed to reach 10 GB/s by the time the LHC upgrade program is implemented in 2015. Rendering 3D dynamic objects from a single 2D image represents a significant challenge in computer graphics and related technologies. Current deep learning-based approaches primarily focus on static scenes and typically require multiple images to calculate model positions and rotations. In response, we introduce Articulated Neural Rendering, a novel framework capable of modeling and visualizing complex, dynamically changing 3D scenes for specific scenarios like human faces and bodies. By combining traditional graphics techniques with advanced deep learning methods, ANR enables the automatic synthesis of 3D objects from a single 2D target image, allowing for the implicit determination of object positions, rotations, and minor details. Through extensive experiments and comparisons with state-of-the-art techniques, we demonstrate ANR's capability to generate realistic, dynamic images in various scenarios, including face makeup, hair modeling, and body sketching. Furthermore, an interactive ANR-based system is also available online for users to explore and apply ANR in these areas. By leveraging ANR, artists can utilize simplified sketch-based interfaces to interact with 3D models that are generated and rendered in real-time. Alongside the framework itself, we also contribute a set of annotated datasets for face, hair, and body rendering, along with related model parameters, which can be utilized in conjunction with ANR or other 3D rendering models. In summary, Articulated Neural Rendering represents a groundbreaking approach to rendering dynamic objects, providing both a cutting-edge framework with model codes and datasets that can serve as a foundation for further research and improved practical applications. The code, models, and datasets are available online at this link https://yunhuiwang.github.io/projects/ANR/. The paper on which this summary is based has been published in the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR'21).

Understanding the atomic structure within materials is crucial for predicting their behavioral trends. By analyzing local atomic arrangements, researchers can predict materials' optical, electrical, and mechanical properties. Traditionally, computational simulations of materials are based on classical numeric methods that track individual atoms as the material is perturbed, often utilizing simplified rules to maintain consistency among atoms. This approach is time-consuming and hard to extend to multiple atoms. A more efficient way to capture atomic interactions involves creating quantitative descriptors of local atomic configurations, and incorporating them into machine learning models. This technique has already shown promise in predicting materials' properties, such as band gaps and mechanical strength, based solely on atomic structure. However, quantifying local atomic configurations rigorously is a complex task, often involving ambiguous or subjective definitions of the relevant atomic scales. In response to these challenges, a new neural network called ATL-GNN has been developed to learn precise representations of local atomic configurations within materials by analyzing atomic relationships and organizational hierarchies. This model not only enhances predictive accuracy for band gaps, mechanical strength, and diffusion energies compared to existing methods but also provides valuable visualizations of local atomic configurations and their influence on material properties. By combining ATL-GNN with density functional theory, researchers can now model atomic interactions more accurately and describe complex materials' phases, such as lithium iron phosphorus, consisting of multiple elements and multiple atoms. This breakthrough paves the way for applying ATL-GNN to additional elements and a wider range of materials. As a result, ATL-GNN is an innovative solution for encoding local atomic configurations within materials, effectively addressing previous scalability and interpretability issues. Furthermore, ATL-GNN marks a significant advancement over prior methods and empowers researchers to model complex materials' phases, such as multi-element compounds, and predicts their properties reliably. In doing so, ATL-GNN is redefining the potential of graph neural networks in materials science. In this study, a novel atomic-translation-learning graph neural network called ATL-GNN is introduced to derive precise, rigorous representations of local atomic configurations within materials, effectively solving previous scalability and interpretability issues. This model provides accurate predictions for band gaps, mechanical strength, and diffusion energies and offers valuable visualizations of local atomic influence. As a result, ATL-GNN is a leading solution for encoding local atomic configurations and models complex materials' phases, such as multi-element compounds, consisting of multiple atoms, and predicts their properties reliably.
