This paper examines the methods used for estimating discrete-time diffusion models, specifically those that involve jumping processes, by utilizing observed data up to a random time. A key aspect of our analysis involves assessing the convergence of estimators and their related statistics, which is crucial for implementing simulation-based methods. By leveraging the weak convergence of the realized measure and its components, we can establish the convergence rate of our estimators. Additionally, we derive the asymptotic distribution of a statistical test for model mispecification. Through the use of a specific example, we demonstrate the feasibility of estimating jumping processes using historical data, specifically for a stochastic population model where the population jumps in response to external shocks. Our findings convince us to employ linear diffusion models for analyzing population dynamics. By applying our methods to the real-world dataset of stock prices, we successfully model and test for jumping processes within financial markets. Our study provides a thorough exploration of the methods used for identifying jumping processes and their implementation on actual data, paving the way for future research on parameter estimation. As an extension to this paper, we have developed a comprehensive software package available online for individuals interested in this topic.

The knowledge tracing task, which predicts student progress based on previous performance, is crucial for enhancing educational delivery. Advances in deep learning have led to numerous models being developed, but evaluating these models is complicated due to a lack of access to future knowledge and assessment data. Existing evaluation metrics, such as ranking loss and cross-entropy, do not fully capture the student transition dynamics. To address this challenge, we propose the use of medical diagnosis dynamics and evaluate state-of-the-art models using this approach in our current research. By applying these models to real-world datasets with their actual future knowledge and assessment data, we assess their performance and compare the predictive power of future knowledge and current performance. Our method demonstrates that future knowledge has a more significant impact on future scores than current performance. To further evaluate these models in a more realistic setting, we introduce a new evaluation metric called cumulative cross-entropy loss, which takes into account the ongoing learning process. Using this metric, we find that recurrent models outperform static models and propose a new simple yet effective model called the Student Transition Model (STM). STM achieves the best evaluation results across all datasets and demonstrates superior performance in simulated future knowledge and assessment predictions. Our method is publicly available at https://github.com/hjdw/STM. Our current research is an initial step in modeling student transitions, and we hope STM will serve as a baseline for future knowledge tracing approaches. We examine how a key property of surjectivity among second-order elliptic differential operators behaves under composition with smooth functions in a broad context, encompassing both partial differential equations and microlocal analysis. By exploring this property in both global and local settings, we investigate its connection to surjectivity within these contexts. Specifically, we investigate how the composition of two surjective elliptic operators behaves after smooth transformations in both global and local settings, revealing that one implies the other. Furthermore, we establish a connection to the regularity of solutions to elliptic PDE under smooth coefficients, leveraging this analysis to demonstrate a composition property of surjectivity in the microlocal setting. Ultimately, we draw conclusions about the composition of two smooth functions in relation to surjectivity in the microlocal context. By extending this analysis to the behavior of non-elliptic operators under smooth transformations, we demonstrate an analogous composition property of surjectivity. Lastly, we explore implications of these findings for the study of non-elliptic differential operators. By drawing on these analyses, we propose open questions for further research.

This paper examines the capacity of transfer learning to improve cross-lingual speech recognition models using data from languages with varying degrees of similarity. We use a sequence-to-sequence model with a labeling loss to conduct experiments in speech recognition, transferring knowledge from English to Spanish and French. Our primary observation indicates that transfer learning is more effective at reducing the gap between more dissimilar languages, i.e., Spanish and French. We also discover that pre-training the model on a labeled dataset allows for better fine-tuning on data from target languages. Additionally, using an unsupervised alignment method during fine-tuning leads to better results. Our best model achieves a mean error rate of 15.3 for Spanish and 21.4 for French, representing a 11.6% and 14.5% decrease in error rates respectively, compared to models trained from scratch. However, the models we developed struggle to overcome the fundamental differences between English and the target languages, resulting in a significant disparity in error rates between similar speech sounds in different languages. This issue raises the question of whether there are more effective strategies for cross-lingual speech recognition that can more fully leverage the benefits of transfer learning.

An examination of the $B^{+}\to K^{+}K^0_S K^0_S$ decay spectrum yielded evidence for a scalar resonance at an invariant mass of approximately 774 MeV, with a width of around 152 MeV. However, this finding is subject to uncertainties related to $K^0_S K^0_S$ final-state interactions. By employing an extension of the isospin analysis to account for $S$-wave contributions, our study suggests that the observed structure in $B^{+}\to K^{+}K^0_S K^0_S$ decays is likely influenced by a scalar resonance. Under the assumption that the same scalar mechanism drives $B^0\to K^+ K^- K^+ K^-$ and $B^0\to K^0_S K^0_S K^0_S$, our analysis indicates that the $B^0\to K^+ K^- K^+ K^-$ decay spectrum features a substantial $I=2$ $S$-wave contribution, with about 50% of the total $S$-wave amplitude. Notably, this $S$-wave component is observed to be nearly spin-isospin symmetric, with an amplitude of $0.42\pm0.08\pm0.05$ neV. By constraining the $B^0\to K^0_S K^0_S K^0_S$ decay spectrum with $B^0\to K^+ K^- K^+ K^-$ information, our findings provide a more refined understanding of these four-body decays and hint at the presence of a scalar resonance contributing to $B^0\to K^0_S K^0_S K^0_S$ and $B^0\to K^+ K^- K^+ K^-$ decays. This scalar resonance, with an estimated mass and width of around 774 MeV and 152 MeV, respectively, may be related to the $\kappa$ resonance observed in $K^+ K^- $scattering or a different meson. Further research is needed to clarify the nature of this scalar resonance.

When we apply a gentle airflow, a significant distance forms between the particle and adjacent raft segments. Further examination using optical microscopy and a digital detection system reveals the mechanism behind this break-up. It appears that the competition between two processes determines raft stability: the reassembly of dispersed particles and the expansion of the surrounding fluid. As the two processes have contrasting time and length scales, the raft's behavior is governed by a simplified model. This regime is characterized by a distinct scaling for the distance phenomenon, where the ratio of the distance to the particle size varies with the square of the approach velocity. Underwater navigation is a challenging task due to its unpredictable nature, lack of global positioning systems, and limited communication. Autonomous underwater vehicles need to navigate with partially observed states, face delays in state updates, and often must make decisions without immediate reward feedback. To tackle these difficulties, we introduce a new model-free reinforcement learning algorithm, called SPGP-SARSA, based on sparse Gaussian processes. This algorithm enhances the efficiency of policy evaluation by reducing data redundancy, adapting to changing environments, and minimizing regression errors. Through simulations, we show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms traditional model-free algorithms, handling large observation spaces, delayed state updates, and sparse rewards. As a significant advancement, the proposed method achieves a notable improvement in computational time and memory usage for complex underwater navigation tasks. We also provide a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance, discussing parameters' influence and conducting a comparative study with state-of-the-art reinforcement learning methods. To facilitate replication, the code for SPGP-SARSA is available open-source. Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation metric, called the mean normalized cumulative reward, to compare algorithms in scenarios with sparse rewards. As a further contribution, we present a new approach for visualizing policy trajectories, called the reward map, to aid in understanding algorithm behavior. As water navigation is a critical application for sparse reward problems, we believe our findings provide valuable insights for tackling similar challenges. For stars where multiple fluids coexist, solving relativistic equations of state involves significant computational effort. However, many situations reveal that certain single-fluid solutions can also accommodate multiple fluids, thereby streamlining the process. Specifically, this work establishes a method to convert solutions for a single fluid of consistent entropy across different particles, into solutions for multiple fluids with the same entropy profiles. This strategy applies to fluids that follow specific equations of state, namely those of NUTty fluids described by the Misra and Prasad metric. Furthermore, we demonstrate that general relativistic solutions involving two fluids can be obtained from their single-fluid counterparts. As a practical example, we derive a solution for two fluids within a nut-like spacetime, where one fluid occupies the spacetime region surrounding the nut, while the other resides within it. Additionally, we provide solutions for fluids with varying entropy profiles. Through this approach, a vast range of nut-like spacetime solutions can be generated just by modifying the entropy profiles, rather than undergoing the nut-bar transformation. This new framework also sheds light on the relationship between scalar fields and fluid dynamics. As a result, a wide range of nut-like spacetime solutions become available, offering potential applications in various astrophysical scenarios. Lastly, we explore the possibility of applying this method to fluids within bar-like spacetime solutions. This new approach holds the potential to revolutionize our computational methods for generating solutions for multiple fluid systems within these complex spacetimes. The effect of magnetic fields on the formation of merger remnants in gas-rich major mergers is being researched to understand how they influence the process. To study this, we conducted a set of simulations that included magnetic fields and the transport of magnetic energy by gas dynamics. The results showed that adding magnetic fields to the simulations helped slow the rate at which merger remnants form. Specifically, it increased the time needed to form a stable remnant by more than two times and slowed the rate of remnant formation by about 30%. The addition of magnetic fields also led to the creation of larger, more massive halos during the pre-coalescence phase. However, the rate of star formation remained relatively similar. Additionally, we observed that adding magnetic fields reduced the efficiency of halo gas dissipation and led to an increase in magnetic energy stored in the interstellar medium due to magnetic reconnection. This led to greater variations in the density of gas across the merger site. Overall, incorporating magnetic fields and their effects on gas dynamics helped create more realistic simulations of merger Remnants. This, in turn, may offer a possible explanation for the variations in the density of gas observed in some merger Remnants. This is particularly evident in the case of the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) and the Great Attractor. The addition of magnetic fields also helped create greater density fluctuations in the gas across the merger site, contributing to greater variations in the density of gas in regions of merger activity. This is seen in the COSMOS field and within the Great Attractor, and could provide a possible explanation for the density fluctuations observed in these areas. This increase in magnetic energy storage due to magnetic reconnection could also have implications for the formation of massive stars in these areas. The severity of medical conditions such as stroke, tumor, and fracture can be difficult to pinpoint from diagnostic images due to varying quality imaging modalities and patient positions. This difficulty stems from the need for precise subspace matching to identify abnormalities, which is compromised by image manipulation. Current deep learning approaches primarily focus on enhancing model performance using data augmentation and ensembling, rather than developing innovative methods to create efficient models for severity detection. In response, we introduce the 3D Contrastive Mixup Classification network, which employs a novel contrastive learning technique to train models for severity detection in 3D diagnostic images. By incorporating a contrastive loss function alongside standard cross-entropy loss, this network can handle imbalanced data distributions effectively. Additionally, we propose a modified Mixup augmentation strategy to mimic data sampling irregularities, which results in superior performance when evaluated against baseline models and renowned datasets, including BrainMR and Isensee_2017_MSD for brain tumor segmentation, and the GRAZ-01 dataset for chest fracture detection. Notably, our approach achieves exceptional robustness when tested with limited dataset samples. The source code for the 3D CMC network is available online at https://github.com/comp-hci/3D-CMC. This study proposes a GEC adaptation technique using a modified adapter model
for sentence correction, building upon successful applications in other NLP tasks.
Our proposed method surpasses traditional multi-task transfer learning methods
in Adaptation Data efficacy, achieving notable gains of up to 8.3 F0.5 improvement.
Furthermore, the proposed adapter model excels over baseline models employing
cross-entropy loss in both label F0.5 and AUC metrics, amounting to 5.3 and 1.9 points
enhancements respectively. The proposed adapter model also demonstrates adaptability
across style transfers from E2 EN to E2 ZH, achieving 41.8 F0.5 in the challenging
Zh-En dataset. Human evaluations validate our machine-generated corrections,
yielding 83.8% acceptable scores from human assessors. The proposed adapter model
also proves capable of reducing errors in original sentences, indicating potential
value in other NLP tasks involving sentence modification. The proposed adapter
model's code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/zh-lin/GEC-Adapter.

In 2020, Japan faced a significant suicide crisis linked to the COVID-19 pandemic.
A recent study proposed a method for estimating suicide rates using aggregate
data under Poisson regression models, which considers the effect of rounding on
data. Building upon this work, a new approach is developed to address rounding
errors and their consequences on statistical inferences. Specifically, an asymptotic
theory is established to evaluate the impact of rounding on the suicide crisis,
which involves deriving a new expression for the sum of rounded variables and
establishing its asymptotic normality. To accommodate various data collection
practices, three scenarios are explored for different rounding protocols, which
are validated using simulated data and applied to analyze real-world data suicide
rates in Japan from 2010 to 2020. The implemented methods facilitate both
point and interval estimates of suicide rates, which are critical for informing
anti-suicide policies during crises fueled by data uncertainty. The introduced
methods can be extended to other applications involving aggregated count data
subject to rounding. The developed R package 'RoundingSuicide' is available by
request. 

Keywords: Anti-suicide policies, Rounding errors, Suicide rates, Statistical
inference, Surveillance data.

We present an original design for a lattice structure based on single-layer triangular prisms, where promontory edges are connected to form an equilateral triangle. This framework is realized through the arrangement of Gd$^{3+}$ ions within a GdInO$_3$ system that adopts a Delone type $h$ lattice structure. By integrating a spiral organic cation like 9-phenanthryl, these GdInO$_3$ layers are separated into individual slabs with a controlled layer thickness. A corresponding study using NMR and EPR techniques provides insights into the distinct magnetic properties of GdInO$_3$ and the effects of cation substitution, further highlighting the potential of this system for hosting exotic physics and adjusting its properties through chemical modification. Notably, our work offers a starting point for exploring other compounds sharing the GdInO$_3$ chemistry and incorporating a wide range of 3d metal ions into the lattice. By combining experimental and simulated data, we analyze the spin Hamiltonian and exchange interactions, offering a thorough understanding of the spin dynamics within these systems. Finally, our work suggests that incorporating a spiral organic cation may provide a practical way to adjust the layer thickness of these Delone type $h$ lattice materials.

In coexistence scenarios for uplink transmission, a set of coexisting links share the same communication resource. A fundamental problem arises here - how to efficiently allocate a shared channel among these links. In our research, we focus on a particular scenario where a single transmitter shares a non-regenerative capability with multiple receivers. Our objective is to develop a fair channel allocation technique without requiring prior knowledge of channel strength. Building upon existing round-robin and cut-and-choose methods, we propose an alternative fair allocation strategy. Analytically, we prove that the round-robin method guarantees at least half of the maximum possible fairness, while in simulation-based analysis, we demonstrate that our proposed cut-and-choose method achieves higher fairness guarantees compared to the round-robin method. Furthermore, we investigate the performance of these methods in relation to varying degrees of fairness and channel conditions. Our findings also reveal that multi-user decoding ability can lead to more energy-efficient allocation, where one transmission opportunity is sufficient to achieve near-maximal fairness. Through real-world implementations, we successfully apply our proposed methods to allocate channels among coexisting links in real-world scenarios. Our research provides a theoretical basis for the fair allocation of channels in coexistence scenarios, enabling the development of adaptive protocols for efficient multi-user coexistence. Ultimately, our work aims to contribute to the design of future wireless communication systems, with an adaptive protocol that efficiently manages coexistence among multiple users. This is particularly crucial as we move towards highly connected and congested future wireless networks. Our research also paves the way for an interesting direction of research, where the focus shifts from allocation to detection, involving the identification of unknown transmission channels. This new direction is supported by our discovered gain of one transmission opportunity when using the cut-and-choose method, suggesting that single-shot multi-user detection is a viable direction for further investigation. Using multiple translations of the same target image can produce consistent results, which can be harnessed for pseudo-labeling a target domain. Rather than relying on a single translation, our proposed method gathers predictions from various translations and combines them to create a single, unified pseudo-target. This approach enables pseudo-targets to capture a target image's fundamental attributes and eliminates noisy details. By doing so, pseudo-targets achieve a balance where they retain the target image's primary features while discarding its noisy aspects. As a result, the accuracy of pseudo-targets increases, leading to enhanced pseudo-labeling performance in the target domain. Using unsharp masking and advanced image processing techniques, we've sharpened high-resolution H-alpha and broad-band images to study the spiral galaxy UGC 8839. Within the central region of UGC 8839, we've identified 27 well-defined HII regions. By comparing these HII regions to mathematically simulated star clusters within a similar spiral galaxy, we found a notable discrepancy in the distribution of these HII regions when considering their average distance from the galaxy's center. While UGC 8839's HII regions are concentrated near the galaxy's outer edges, the majority of similar regions in other spiral galaxies are found closer to the galaxy's center. Additionally, UGC 8839 exhibits an open spiral arm structure, and many of its HII regions are located at the edges of molecular clouds within these arms, suggesting recent star formation activity. Using the maximum likelihood method and a grid-based approach, we determined the spatial distribution of these HII regions is best described as an extended disk with a sinusoidal component, and we estimate the rate of star formation within UGC 8839 to be about 0.46 Solar Mass per year. By analyzing the colors of these HII regions, we estimated the reddening within UGC 8839 and calculated the distances of these regions from the galaxy's center, ultimately finding that many of these HII regions reside in molecular clouds at the edges of the galaxy's spiral arms. This suggests a connection between the global potential field and the locations of these HII regions, and implies that these regions are forming in response to density waves within UGC 8839. This would place UGC 8839 among the list of spiral galaxies affected by external density waves. Further research is needed to confirm this finding, and to determine the extent of the wave and its relationship to the galaxy's central black hole.

Dark matter, a fundamental component making up approximately 27% of the universe, remains poorly understood due to its invisible nature. Direct dark matter detection is the leading scientific approach aimed at revealing the underlying physics behind this phenomenon. Existing experimental searches focus primarily on detecting dark matter at its standard, expected interaction strength, but a newly proposed detection method, known as paleo-detection, suggests the possibility of identifying evidence for dark matter in situations where its presence significantly predates human observation and is only detectable through the nuclear reactions it causes in ancient rocks and metals, potentially influencing the understanding of dark matter-nucleon interactions at low mass scales. This study explores the potential of using paleo-detection in searching for dark matter and examines various factors that influence its sensitivity, including decay processes, neutron flux calculations, anti-neutrino detection, metal alloy composition, and ancient metal production methods. Although the sensitivity of paleo-detection is ultimately constrained by conventional direct dark matter detection experiments due to underlying physics limitations, the development of new techniques and technologies could one day make paleo-detection a complementary tool in the search for dark matter. In addition, this research may also lead to breakthroughs in our understanding of nuclear decay processes, neutron flux calculations, anti-neutrino detection, metal alloy composition, and ancient metal production methods, which could have significant impacts on fundamental science and technology. Consequently, the development of paleo-detection, fueled by the intersection of particle physics, nuclear physics, archaeometallurgy, and geology, has the potential to drive innovative technological advancements and contribute significantly to the ongoing quest to uncover the nature of dark matter. Ultimately, this field may one day enable the detection of dark matter at low mass scales, significantly expanding our understanding of this enigmatic phenomenon. The rapid growth of social data and online services leads to a high demand for modern databases that make learning and prediction accessible to everyone. By providing a user-friendly interface similar to popular operating systems, modern databases have become an essential tool for individuals to update their data without needing to run complex queries. However, updating data frequently poses a risk due to sensitive information being shared publicly, such as updates to search history or browsing records. This problem focuses on securing data update histories while enabling efficient query execution and machine learning training. Building upon the work of Chen at al., we introduce a new model that incorporates differential privacy to safeguard data update histories. This model allows users to update their data privately and seamlessly, incorporating updates from multiple users with minimal overhead. Furthermore, this model supports scalable query execution and machine learning training, ensuring seamless integration with contemporary databases. We showcase the efficacy of our model through a comprehensive evaluation on real-world datasets, encompassing S3, Amazon E-commerce, and Twitter datasets. Our findings demonstrate that our model achieves a balance between data utility and privacy, surpassing the limitations of existing approaches while facilitating efficient query execution and machine learning learning. Additionally, our model empowers users to monitor the trade-off between data privacy and utility through an interactive dashboard. The exemplary implementation of our model, along with comprehensive evaluations and source code, are available at https://us.csa.ipa.cloud/paper-data-release-form for authorized access. We believe that our model will serve as a foundational building block for the next-generation databases that prioritize privacy and efficient data utilities. Moreover, our model's open-source code, along with the accompanying dataset, is readily available for download at https://us.csa.ipa.cloud/paper-data-release-form for authorized access. We look forward to collaborating with researchers and database developers who can build upon our work by contacting us directly.

Recently, deep learning techniques, specifically convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have achieved significant success in the automated segmentation of surgical instruments within complex MRI-guided surgery scenarios. However, a major challenge these methods face is maintaining focus on the target instruments, with only limited resources available to train them. To mitigate this drawback, a novel network called the Dual decoder attention network (DDANet) is proposed, comprising two decoder branches and an attention mechanism. This proposed network identifies distinct context and detail branches in the encoder, and makes use of two decoder branches with attention mechanisms to extract context and detail features, combine them, and produce a score to direct the segmentation process. Furthermore, an output layer with an attention mechanism multi-tasks with cross-section segmentation and instrument classification. Quantitative and qualitative evaluation of the proposed DDANet, compared to other advanced attention-based networks, reveals a notable improvement in segmentation accuracy and precision. Additionally, the proposed method demonstrates robustness in handling partially occluded instruments and real-time cross-section segmentation. Consequently, the DDANet is well-suited for real-time, multi-task learning applications involving the segmentation of partially occluded surgical instruments, and is thus amenable to integration with interactive surgery systems that incorporate pre-operative MRI data. This facilitates real-time cross-section guidance during surgery. Source code is available at: https://github.com/Trigiant/DDANet.

This method involves generating diverse samples for each image and applying an adaptive transformation to expand the intra-personal variable information, ultimately pruning unnecessary noise. The study utilizes two contrastive learning approaches, considering both the variable information's inherent structure and noise's arbitrary distribution. Moreover, a hierarchical approach is proposed to scale up the method for larger datasets. Notably, the new framework reduces Type II errors (missing extreme events) and consequently achieves lower VaR than GARCH models, which are prone to Type I errors (false extreme events). As a result, the new approach provides a more accurate forecast of extreme VaR events. Furthermore, the new framework includes a method to estimate the return distribution by aggregating VaR-affected returns from each GARCH model, yielding a more precise distribution than the traditional approach. An analysis of lattice QCD data from 24 distinct configurations of nearly physical ensembles has allowed for the correlation of pion properties with light and strange quark mass values. By leveraging a novel weighted linear regression method, precise relationships between the pion mass and its parts were determined. These formulas can efficiently calculate the physical pion structure parameters, given the current uncertainty in quark mass measurements. A potential extension to this method could also be applied to other two-point correlation functions. Utilizing these results at physical quark mass values, predictions for the charm-quark mass $m_c^{1/3}$ and the charm-quark lambda parameter $\lambda_c$ have been made, yielding $m_c^{1/3} = 0.6155(2)$ GeV and $\lambda_c = 0.0189(2)$. These outcomes are consistent with prior estimates and demonstrate how the behavior of pions can serve as a bridge connecting the light and heavy quark sectors. Furthermore, by integrating the partially differentiated correlation function, additional information about the charm-quark form factor was also obtained. A more detailed analysis focusing on the charm-quark sector is presented in the companion paper "Charmed quark physics from lattice QCD" by the same authors. Leveraging these results, this paper presents an overview of the broader implications for charmed meson studies. Additionally, a public database containing the extracted parameters is available online. This database includes the charm-quark mass, the charm-quark lambda parameter, the charm-quark form factor, and the charmed meson gamma parameter for several combinations of quantum numbers. By providing open access to these calculations, the possibility for further exploration and refinement is enabled, ultimately contributing to a more accurate understanding of charmed quark behavior within the framework of lattice QCD. By doing so, this research takes a significant step towards a comprehensive characterization of the charmed quark across the spectrum from light to heavy quark dynamics. Classical T Tauri stars are notable for their disk-based accretion and variability in both short and long periods. A striking feature of T Tauri stars is the massive reservoir of material accumulated in their surrounding disks, which eventually gets depleted at an extreme rate. Despite this, we find that the variability in these stars can be explained by the action of magnetized disks and stars, without needing additional factors such as the influence of binary mergers. However, if we only consider variability over short periods, there is a limitation to how much variability we can reproduce, given typical reservoir sizes, and this limitation holds true for both traditional and "superflare" variability. However, if we look at variability over longer periods, things become more complicated. In such cases, variability can indicate the discharge of a large reservoir, or alternatively, the ingestion of a massive amount of material from the disk into the star, which results from the star's gravitational influence on the disk. This study suggests that future modeling of T Tauri stars should prioritize solving the reverse problem, determining how the star's magnetic field affects its surrounding disk, rather than just trying to reproduce the stars' variability patterns. If we can achieve this, we may be able to better comprehend how these stars' magnetic fields evolve over time, and how they eventually lose their magnetic dominance as they mature. In addition, this study implies that binary mergers may have a more significant impact when the more massive component is a T Tauri star, given the enormous variability in these stars' accretion rates, which can result in massive transfers of material. Finally, this study suggests that binary systems featuring T Tauri stars should be analyzed with a greater emphasis on the complex interactions taking place within these systems, rather than simply viewing these systems as mere extensions of single-star magnetized physics. In such cases, binary systems featuring T Tauri stars may offer a unique opportunity for us to study how magnetic fields influence the accumulation and variability of material within these stars' surrounding disks, which in turn could provide valuable insights into the broader category of accreting stars across the galaxy. If we can successfully accomplish this, we may be able to tackle even more intricate questions related to these systems, such as how magnetic fields affect the replenishment of these stars' reservoirs and, ultimately, the disks themselves. In this way, binary systems featuring T Tauri stars can serve as microcosms for our investigation into the complex interplay between the accumulation of material, its variability, and the forces

People generally agree that helping the less fortunate through redistribution is a vital aspect of a fair society. However, there's less consensus on how to justify this assistance when individual fortunes are influenced by a mix of skill and luck. Using a simple economic model where chance directly impacts income, as opposed to affecting opportunities, we examine how the public's views on redistribution are shaped by these factors. Our analysis reveals that, in the context of chance affecting opportunities, people are more inclined to support policies that benefit those less fortunate, regardless of whether it's due to a lack of ability or bad luck. In contrast, when chance directly affects income, the public's views become more divided, with a greater acceptance of suffering as a necessary evil. These findings have implications for understanding the perceived fairness of economic outcomes and may also inform policy decisions aimed at mitigating inequality. Furthermore, our model suggests that inequality can persist even in a hypothetical idealized economy devoid of chance, as long as there are fundamental differences in skills among individuals. Lastly, we propose a new measure of inequality that takes into account the minimum capability required to achieve basic life goals, which provides a more comprehensive understanding of economic inequality. By exploring these concepts, our study offers a framework for investigating the complex relationships between chance, inequality, and the desire for redistribution. Ultimately, our model reveals that the divide between those who advocate for a safety net and those who embrace the idea of suffering as a necessary evil arises from a fundamental distinction, not a moral one. Rather, it stems from a difference in how we perceive the role of chance in shaping economic outcomes. In essence, our study suggests that the public's views on inequality are, in part, a reflection of their own fears of falling prey to bad luck. Consequently, this fear can lead to a greater acceptance of those less fortunate, as long as it's due to a lack of ability rather than bad luck. In the context of our model, this acceptance extends to a willingness to pay a premium to avoid suffering himself. In turn, this willingness to pay a premium to avoid suffering, even if it's not directly related to his own circumstances, stems from a desire to minimize the likelihood of experiencing true suffering in the future. Ultimately, our analysis provides a theoretical basis for understanding the complex relationships between chance, inequality, and the desire for redistribution, which can inform policy decisions aimed at mitigating inequality. This study examines the higher quantum $K$-invariants of the symmetric space $SU(2)/U(1)$ through the characteristics of certain geometric objects, specifically varieties of stable maps, for an arbitrary positive integer $n$. By establishing a relationship in quantum $K$-invariants via the divisor property, we find a correspondence between the characteristics of these stable map varieties and the quantum $K$-invariants, enabling us to compute the latter. Notably, this computation yields a representation of quantum $K$-invariants in terms of Mumford's invariant and the Griffiths volume, both of which are well-established factors in the formula for Witten's invariant. Furthermore, by exploring the properties of these stable map varieties under transformation by the fundamental group of the space $\mathbb{CP}^1$, we derive an additional relationship expressing quantum $K$-invariants in a form that includes a periodic component related to the fundamental group. This relationship especially results in a non-trivial expression for the quantum $K$-invariants in terms of Mumford's invariant and the Griffiths volume, both of which now incorporate additional factors that reflect the group action. In the final section, we illustrate the relevance of these relationships by connecting the quantum $K$-invariants to the Witten series, specifically demonstrating how they can be computed directly from the characteristics of the same stable map varieties, without needing to consider the Mumford volume. This computation specifically yields a expression for Witten's invariant that includes a factor related to the fundamental group, which provides an alternative proof of his volume formula. This study also presents the characteristics of the stable map varieties as their primary geometric object characteristics, and we anticipate that they will also be of interest in other areas of mathematical research. Furthermore, we expect that the relationships we have established between these characteristics, the quantum $K$-invariants, and Witten's invariant will prove useful in further exploring the connections between these invariants and the properties of the symmetric space $SU(2)/U(1)$. In the concluding section, we outline additional directions for future research aimed at expanding the results of this study to the case of $S^3$, the 2-sphere. This would involve computing the quantum $K$-invariants and establishing the related characteristics of the stable map varieties for this new geometric object. A machine learning model's accuracy heavily relies on high-quality input data, 
thus making data debugging a critical step in the pipeline. Simply re-training 
the model on additional data significantly elevates costs without a proportional 
increase in accuracy, especially when only a limited amount of data is involved. 
Presently, debugging involves manually sifting through data and model annotations 
in a time-consuming process. A data debugging framework like DataScope streamlines 
this process by pinpointing defective data samples responsible for model inaccuracies 
and provides actionable suggestions for remedial data to improve accuracy. 
Based on the underlying assumption that similar data samples share the same semantic 
meaning and variability, DataScope pinpoints defective data samples using a combination 
of structural and semantic embeddings. Experimental studies on three diverse datasets 
demonstrate DataScope's capability to accurately identify faulty data samples 
(around 90% accuracy) and offer effective remedial data (around 80% MRR). 
Notably, DataScope outperforms traditional approaches like cross-validation and 
model-agnostic debugging techniques by a margin of 13-14% in MRR. Furthermore, 
DataScope's debugging efficiency is a mere 0.13 seconds per query, a significant 
improvement over the current average of 15 seconds. The framework's ability to 
handle large-scale machine learning pipelines is validated through a real-world 
application involving Wikipedia's category classification. In this scenario, DataScope enhances model accuracy by around 5% following data debugging. The DataScope framework is readily available at this link: https://github.com/google-research-datascope/DataScope. The code for the baseline models utilized in the experiments can be found at the following link: https://github.com/google-research-datascope/DataScopeBaselines. The paper's supplementary material, featuring additional experimental studies and visualizations, is accessible at this link: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1QG6b6H6c1h6C5P5P5/view. DataScope's innovative approach offers a pioneering solution to efficiently addressing data debugging issues in machine learning pipelines. This paper introduces DataScope, a cutting-edge framework for data debugging. Unlike traditional methods, DataScope streamlines data debugging by pinpointing defective data samples responsible for model inaccuracies and providing actionable suggestions for remedial data to improve accuracy. Experimental studies validate DataScope's effectiveness on three diverse datasets, surpassing traditional approaches by a margin of 13-14% in MMR, as well as a real-world application

Upon re-examination of the data, two of these sources were linked to known X-ray binaries, specifically candidates for neutron star X-ray binaries or pulsars. Using the most recent observations from CHANDRA, we analyzed the X-ray spectra of these two sources, namely M22 X-2 and M22 X-5. The analysis revealed their X-ray spectra can be described by a quasi-equilibrium kinetic process involving adiabatic invariant energy distributions among electrons and non-thermal radiation components, resulting in power-law energy spectra. Combining these X-ray insights with radio observations, we developed a three-dimensional model describing the motion of these particles and predicted radio luminosities that match the observed levels, further confirming the nature of these sources as neutron star X-ray binaries or pulsars. The finding that they exhibit quasi-equilibrium kinetic processes suggests that these sources experience low levels of mass accretion, possibly relating to their low average X-ray luminosities. The study provides radio-luminosity-based criteria to identify similar globular cluster radio sources and distinguishes them from millisecond pulsars or neutron star X-ray binaries. According to these criteria, M22 X-2 and M22 X-5 are classified as neutron star X-ray binaries or pulsars, shedding light on the radio activity observed in these sources, including M22 X-5 with its variable radio behavior. The analysis also offers insights into the mass loss caused by the neutron star's rotation and the scattering of particles within the cluster's core, estimating that only a small fraction of the total energy released through X-ray radiation can be recovered as radio energy due to the large scattering loss. This paper explores the challenge of estimating high-dimensional structures, specifically hypergraphs, from their lower-dimensional projections, which can be used as a key technique in graph analysis. We discuss the methods for inferring hypergraphs from their embeddings in lower-dimensional spaces, which is crucial for visualizing and analyzing multi-dimensional data and understanding the underlying structures of a dataset. By applying hyperbolic space reconstruction to the latent variables of a deep generative model and using stochastic gradient descent to minimize reconstruction error, we demonstrate effective hypergraph inference. Our approach showcases the potential of hypere Embedding to capture important structural information from multi-dimensional data and facilitate further analysis of the underlying distributions. We highlight the potential of our method by inferring the structure of a dataset with latent dimensions and demonstrating its applicability to cross-domain data analysis through the construction of hypergraphs that combine information from different dimensions and datasets. Additionally, we explore the challenges and limitations of hypergraph inference, which is a complex and visually dynamic topic that is not well-represented through static visualizations. The benefits of SIT are highlighted through comprehensive experiments conducted on diverse data sets representing cooperative and competitive scenarios. The outcomes surpass state-of-the-art benchmarks and demonstrate the capacity of our approach to handle substantial action space dimensions. This paper investigates how single-particle entanglement affects nonlocality and quantum steering in both dichotomous and continuous cases. For dichotomous systems, our analysis reveals that entanglement begets nonlocality and quantum steering, exclusively when single-particle entanglement is present. In contrast, systems without single-pentuple entanglement cannot exhibit nonlocality or quantum steering. Furthermore, our findings indicate that single-particle entanglement is a necessary yet insufficient condition for nonlocality. In the case of systems with multiple parties, our analysis shows that single-particle entanglement alone is insufficient for nonlocality. Instead, multiple-party entanglement is required to generate nonlocal effects. In the scenario of continuous variables, our analysis indicates that single-particle entanglement is a necessary but insufficient condition for nonlocality or quantum steering, echoing the dichotomous case. Additionally, we propose a qubit system involving two parties, where single-particle entanglement fluctuates while maintaining steady multi-party entanglement, mimicking the behavior of quantum systems interacting with environments. This model exhibits oscillatory nonlocality and quantum steering in accordance with the changes in multi-party entanglement. In the context of continuous variables, our analysis shows that the soliton model proposed by Recati et al. exhibits single-particle entanglement and multi-party entanglement across all values of the two-party parameter, underscoring the unique role of single-particle entanglement in nonlocality and quantum steering. In conclusion, our analysis confirms the pivotal contribution of single-particle entanglement to nonlocality and quantum steering in both dichotomous and continuous cases, while also highlighting the distinct implications of these findings for multi-party systems. In the latter, single-particle entanglement is a necessary yet insufficient condition for nonlocality. In the former, single-particle entanglement is both necessary and insufficient for nonlocality or quantum steering, with multiple-party entanglement being the decisive factor. In the context of the dichotomous case, our analysis provides the foundation for the sole utilization of single-pentuple entanglement as a resource, as evident in the examples of entanglement swapping and the activation of superactivator gates. In the context of the soliton model for continuous variables, our analysis prompts the proposal of single-particle entanglement-based protocols that leverage multi-party entanglement, albeit stable and all-encompassing in nature.

To assess the effectiveness of individually applied quantum gates such as the Clifford gate, we create a suite of logical state preparations derived from the toric code, along with associated measurement operators. This approach allows us to accurately determine the fidelity of each individual gate by analyzing the overlap between the applied logical states and the expected outcomes, which can be efficiently calculated using the Pauli error probabilities associated with each gate. We demonstrate the practical utility of this concept by simulating the performance of a hypothetical quantum processor capable of executing parity-check measurements for the toric code, along with singly applied Clifford gates responsible for updating the logical states. This model highlights how even a small number of faulty parity-check measurements can significantly impact the fidelity of the applied logical states. Furthermore, we propose using repetitive applications of these gates to create a stabilizer code, followed by periodic parity-check measurements to provide real-time error correction and dephasing noise protection, which can enhance the fidelity of the logical states by several orders of magnitude for realistic noise scenarios. This scenario is achievable with current quantum processing systems and could serve as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of near-term quantum hardware. Alongside this, we introduce a second suite of states that can be used to evaluate the performance of measurement gates, which is essential for assessing the effectiveness of fault-tolerant logical measurements while dealing with faulty single-qubit measurements. This proposal provides a foundation for a comprehensive benchmarking framework that goes beyond the current individual gate assessment and can be utilized to evaluate the performance of coherent sequences of gates capable of maintaining stabilizer codes. This code-based benchmarking strategy is particularly valuable for evaluating the performance of quantum processing units in noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.

We investigate currents near the surface of a two-dimensional, strong anisotropic lattice, specifically in Lieb-Lattice for both bosonic and fermionic models. Anisotropy is shown to cause surface currents to become robust in two directions, while in the third direction they become robust in one direction, displaying an exotic phenomenon known as "fingerprint behavior". The magnitude of these surface currents can be heavily influenced by anisotropy, with some variations displaying a linear relationship and others displaying a saturating trend as the anisotropy strength increases. Additionally, we find that both bound states and surface currents can coexist, with the condition that the chemical potential lies within a specific range that offsets the influence of anisotropy. Our research was conducted using a tensor-based implementation of the Kubo formula for current calculations, allowing us to consider both local and non-local contributions to surface currents. This implementation enabled us to simulate a wide range of anisotropy strengths and chemical potentials. As a result, our study offers a novel framework for understanding surface currents in lattice systems. As an example, we applied this framework to study both halides and alkalides in a strong anisotropic lattice, with implications for their physical confinement. Our analysis suggests that physical confinement may not solely be a phenomenon of surface states, but rather an anisotropic effect that can manifest in currents even in the absence of strong electron interactions. As such, our study proposes a new perspective on the understanding of physical confinement in lattice systems. As an additional outcome, our research facilitates the exploration of surface currents in lattices with anisotropic couplings, providing a theoretical foundation for the analysis of current properties in a broader range of systems. As an anisotropic lattice with a unique layout, the Lieb-Lattice serves as an ideal testbed for this research, offering a two-dimensional representation of a cubic lattice with anisotropic couplings in one direction. This research investigates Brans-Dicke theory's behavior under massive scalar field perturbations, specifically in regions far from the influence of matter. To gauge Brans-Dicke theory's coherence, particularly in the absence of large-scale matter distributions, we examine its radiation patterns in this scenario. Our analysis shows that, at great distances, Brans-Dicke theory's behavior is dominated by a harmonic oscillator with a varying frequency, ultimately stabilizing to a constant value. This leads to the conclusion that photons can only escape to infinity if the initial value of the scalar field and its derivative meet certain conditions related to the direction of motion. This condition effectively limits the coherence of Brans-Dicke theory to a certain degree and reveals that, in the absence of matter, the coherence of this theory is bounded by the speed of light. This bound implies that coherent Brans-Dicke theory can only be observed at a frequency below a certain limit, further indicating that, in the absence of matter, this theory can only emit coherent gravitational waves of a particular type (typically referred to as quadratic waves). This exclusive access to quadratic waves results in a distinct energy spectrum that differs significantly from the energy spectrum associated with the decay of a harmonic oscillator in general relativity. This unique spectrum arises from the interplay between the fluctuating frequency and the asymptotic number of oscillations as the big bang's initial energy is released. Consequently, this theory's coherent nature allows us to determine the universe's total initial energy released during the big bang's early stages of expansion. This research also enables us to establish a upper bound on the coherence frequency of this theory's gravitational waves and, subsequently, a lower bound on the mass/parameter constant of this theory. Given the mass/parameter constant's current range (estimated to be approximately 0.4 to 0.7 x 10^(-5)), this upper bound would imply a coherence frequency for gravitational waves of around 10^(-12) to 10^(-11) Hz. This research sets the stage for a fresh reevaluation of Brans-Dicke theory's behavior at very low frequencies. It also highlights the unique opportunity presented by both upcoming gravitational wave detectors, which will offer a much broader spectral range for the observation of gravitational waves. This, in turn, may provide a chance to directly test Brans-Dicke theory's coherence in a fundamental sense. Understanding the evolution of ideas in scientific literature is crucial to grasping the knowledge development within the scientific community. By analyzing citation networks, researchers can examine the relationships between citations as knowledge transmissions. However, conventional metrics for transitive relations fall short in capturing the full knowledge transfer process. In our research, we introduce a new set of Quantitative Indexes of Knowledge (KQI) to provide comprehensive insights into the development of ideas within citation networks. By applying these indexes to open access literature from Physics, we present a framework for mapping knowledge progression over time, effectively visualizing the growth of scientific understanding. Our methodology can be adapted to analyze the emergence of new ideas and the strengthening of established concepts, as seen in our analysis of the distribution of alphas in citation networks. Furthermore, we utilize our method to study the co-development of concepts by calculating the correlation coefficients between indexes, revealing interesting knowledge dynamics such as the synchronized progress of concepts, the strengthening of associated concepts, and the emergence of new ideas that facilitate further knowledge development. By examining knowledge transfers in citation networks, we can identify key papers that play a central role in idea dissemination, referred to as knowledge carriers. The characteristics of these knowledge carriers, found by analyzing the structural properties of citation networks, include a high Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI) score and a critical position in the network. Our research offers a powerful framework for analyzing citation networks and understanding the development of ideas in scientific literature. Based on a general game theory framework, we modelled the power allocation problem as a non-cooperative game involving multiple coexistence scenarios. By applying an equilibrium analysis to this model, we derived strategies for optimal power allocation that consider both security and channel capacity objectives. Additionally, we numerically evaluated and compared the effectiveness of our proposed methods for different security policies and system configurations. The results showed that our secure power control approaches outperform traditional methods, achieving a significant improvement in system performance. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of fast fading on our proposed methods and found that our secure power control solutions can adapt effectively to changing fading conditions. To facilitate practical implementation, we also developed an efficient computational algorithm for solving the complex power allocation problems. The advantages of our secure power control solutions include reduced interference, improved system throughput, and increased energy efficiency. The results highlight the potential of our methods for optimizing the performance of real-world wireless communication systems. In urban settings, automated vehicles can optimize their journey by connecting to roadside infrastructure, but their trajectory planning is complicated by unknown traffic signals. To tackle this issue, we've developed an algorithm to predict signal phases, focusing on yellow and red phases, which significantly influence a vehicle's ability to clear the intersection or brake safely. By estimating the time until the traffic signal turns red, we can determine whether a clear path exists for the approaching vehicle to navigate through the intersection without encountering oncoming traffic during the red phase. In scenarios where we can't clear the intersection in time, our method identifies the minimum speed required for the vehicle to stop before entering oncoming traffic during the red phase. In conjunction with existing methods for estimating signal timing and detecting malfunctioning traffic signals, our approach can be used to enhance the accuracy of signal phase estimation. We validated our algorithm through simulations and testing on real-world data, and it's now part of the Connected Automated Vehicle Trajectory Planning system developed by General Motors. Our method has numerous applications beyond GM, and we're open to collaborating with other companies interested in utilizing our algorithm. To facilitate adoption, we're providing our code and simulation data openly, along with detailed documentation to aid integration with other companies' systems. Through cooperative development, we aim to establish a unified approach to connected vehicle trajectory planning, paving the way for the safe deployment of automated vehicles in urban environments. To that end, we invite the research community to join us in refining this code and sharing their own trajectories and experiences at the GitHub repository listed in the paper citations. By working together, we can create a celebrated grand challenge solution that can be leveraged by the connected automated vehicle industry. The code and data mentioned in this paper can be found at https://github.com/gmforacv/signal-phase-estimation and will be made publicly available upon peer review. This study investigates the potential for data augmentation to enhance NLP models' generalization in a task-agnostic setting, examining strategies like text augmentation that maintain semantic meaning and stylistic augmentation that alters visual presentation. Our experiments apply these methods to three prominent NLP tasks using widely available tools, revealing notable improvements achieved by simply combining semantic and stylistic methods. Notably, our findings demonstrate that these efficient data augmentation methods yield similar performance gains as contextualized-aware methods in several scenarios, ultimately showcasing generalization enhancements that translate to newer models. This work is made openly accessible on public repositories for replication and community feedback. Our introduced methods and guidelines for stylistic text augmentation are also shared to foster further research in this area. This study's generalization gains are anticipated to benefit various NLP tasks aided by large-scale datasets. As such, we encourage the community to build upon this work and contribute their methods for generalization augmentation, along with associated benchmarks, to benefit the NLP society as a collaborative resource. This effect is seen as a result of a new type of energy that arises from self-binding, which is a manifestation of non-linear gravity that is stronger than linear gravity. We further develop this understanding by showing that the self-binding energy can be represented in a different way, which is then used to derive a simpler condition that is equivalent to the original conjecture. This new perspective is also applicable in flat space and is consistent with the idea that the Higgs mechanism is a form of self-binding. We also discuss the possibility that this concept of self-binding may provide a more fundamental explanation for the origin of the WGC in certain theories, such as those with a large number of massless scalars. In such theories, the linear and nonlinear gravities may become distinguishable only when the number of scalar fields is large enough, which would give a new insight into the relationship between the number of degrees of freedom and the strength of gravity. We also extend our discussion to systems with multiple charged objects, which is essential for understanding how self-binding gives rise to the WGC. Finally, we present an example in AdS_4 by solving the fully nonlinear gravitational equations for a pair of fundamental strings with opposite charges. Insulating materials that support multiple quantum states with unique properties hold great potential for various technology applications. For instance, multiple magnetic states could enable the creation of magnetic memory devices, while several electric states might lead to the development of binary decision makers. Despite the promise, these concepts remain theoretical until accurately quantified and measured. Currently, measurement techniques only allow for the characterization of a single specific property at a time, which is not sufficient to identify the full range of available states. A new proposal, the model-space approach, enhances simulation simulations by introducing a set of predefined models that represent possible configurations within a system. These models are used to describe the system's expected behavior under different quantum states, which can include various phases. The simulator then uses linear least-squares minimization to find the best combination of models that fits the measured data, effectively characterizing any number of quantum states within the predefined model-space. This approach was successfully demonstrated in experiments involving the measurement of spin and charge states within individual insulating channels of Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ edges by utilizing scanning tunneling microscopy and spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy. The model-space approach can significantly contribute to the development of quantum materials by enabling the precise study of multiple quantum states in a single unit cell. The proposed technique is not limited to Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ and can be applied to any system that can be resolved at the unit cell level, offering a powerful tool for the investigation of quantum states in materials with complex structures. To tackle this issue, researchers propose a design for over-all orders in redispatch markets, based on expectations of future imbalances. This design involves a two-tier auction process: first, a grid operator procures flexible capacity from these ancient power plants in a separate auction, based on predicted imbalances and corresponding profit margins of the plants: second, the operator allocates this flexibility to meet actual imbalances in real-time, subject to minimum risk and computation requirements. Top quark pair production dominates at the Large Hadron Collider's highest luminosity levels, and it also competes with Higgs boson production in future colliders like HH and bb in High-Energy Particle Colliders. Top quark pair radiating an intermediate boson can mimic Higgs boson behavior in certain decay channels, such as when the output is examined in terms of four b-quark jets. This interference effect, which becomes more noticeable with rising energy, could either enhance (if the output exceeds the Higgs signal) or diminish (if the output falls below the Higgs signal) the detection of Higgs signals, depending on the specific working conditions and strategies employed by the experiment. A notable example where the interference effect significantly impacts the detection of Higgs signals is when searching for the decay into four b-quark jets in future High-Energy Particle Colliders. To accurately model this phenomenon, it is essential to incorporate top quark pair production and calculate the exact cross-section, taking into account the interference between the two processes. However, current versions of leading-order cross-section calculators do not account for the radiation of intermediate bosons by top quarks, and only consider the production of top quark pairs in isolation, neglecting the potential competition with Higgs boson production. As a result, these programs provide an incomplete picture of the situation and cannot be relied upon to model the full extent of this problem accurately. In contrast, state-of-the-art programs such as HHResumMMHT and SoftCollidar, which incorporate the most up-to-date understanding of high-order calculations, including the resummation of leading logarithmic cross-sections and the calculation of the soft function for the splitting of bosons into b-quark pairs, can accurately account for the presence of top quark pair production and its competing relationship with Higgs boson production, particularly in the case of decays into four b-quark jets. In this paper, the differences between these sophisticated programs and the simplified models provided by the leading-order cross-section calculators are highlighted, emphasizing the importance of considering the full complexity of this problem and the need for a deeper understanding of the interplay between these different production processes and their competing relationships with one another. In the context of future research directions, there are a number of fundamental questions that remain to be addressed, such as how the presence of top quark pair production affects the detection of Higgs boson signals in experiments and how the competition between these two processes impacts the ability to accurately model this phenomenon

To explore the fundamental properties of the Higgs boson, researchers propose using precision measurements of $pp\to \gamma\gamma$ and $pp\to \tau \tau$ at the LHC with an extended scalar sector. A theoretical framework is utilized to analyze the impact of new scalar particles on the Higgsstrahlung and $\tau \tau$ channels. The study demonstrates that precise measurements of these processes can reveal information about the mass, couplings, and quantum properties of new scalar particles, particularly if there is a significant disparity in the masses of the inert scalars or if a light pseudoscalar is present. For instance, if a heavy neutral scalar or pseudoscalar exists, with a mass gap of more than 150 GeV, the $pp\to \gamma\gamma$ measurement can exclude its existence at 95% confidence if the LHC is upgraded to a luminosity of 3000 $ab^{-1}$. Similarly, a light pseudoscalar, exchanged in the $pp\to \gamma\gamma$ channel at 95% confidence, could be within the range of 0.1 to 10 GeV, while the same is true for a heavy neutral scalar in the $pp\to \tau \tau$ channel, with a mass gap of more than 100 GeV. The study also highlights the complementary nature of these processes, emphasizing that a comprehensive understanding of the Higgs boson and its interactions necessitates the simultaneous analysis of $pp\to \gamma\gamma$ and $pp\to \tau \tau$ in the context of extended scalar sectors. The inclusion of data from future $e^+e^-$ colliders as a complement to LHC data will significantly enhance the discovery potential for light inert scalars or complex Higgs sectors. Ultimately, the integrated luminosity of 3000 $ab^{-1}$ at the LHC, coupled with an energy reach of 100 TeV and a subsequent luminosity of 100 $ab^{-1}$ at a future 100 TeV LHC, will be sufficient to thoroughly explore the fundamental properties of the Higgs boson within the framework of an extended scalar sector. However, during a follow-up observation in early 2018, a peculiar feature was observed at Saturn's south pole. Initially, researchers believed it would resemble the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV), given the expectation that it would form during the following summer of 2019. Conversely, when this expected formation failed to materialize, a thorough analysis was conducted to understand the reasons behind it. As a result, it became clear that the south polar stratosphere's behavior during the summer months is governed by a different set of rules, characterized by strong equator-to-pole wind shear that prevents the formation of a distinct vortex there. Instead, three-year-old images showed that a second, faint vortex had formed in the south polar stratosphere during the summer of 2006, and was consistent with an "antivortex" as described in a previous study. Furthermore, an examination of the NPSV's behavior over time revealed that it experiences a temporary weakening around the turn of the year, attributed to an interaction with the planet's atmospheric wave trains originating from the south polar antivortex. Ultimately, these findings underscore the unique nature of Saturn's stratospheric polar dynamics, highlighting the profound disparities between the two poles, and laying the groundwork for further exploration into the underlying causes of these complex atmospheric phenomena. The SOXI instrument played a crucial role in discovering the south polar antivortex and furnishing additional insights, made possible by a combination of infrared imaging at multiple wavelengths and spectroscopy, along with the use of high-resolution Jupiter images for comparative analysis. This paper examines how external influences affect the principle of blow-up for solutions of the Schrödinger equation in a bounded area. By analyzing local behavior near a boundary with specific conditions, we demonstrate the possibility of blow-up. In addition, we obtain an estimate for an energy concentration phenomenon occurring at the boundary due to the presence of an initial source term. Furthermore, we establish an upper limit for the life span of solutions subject to certain constraints, ultimately drawing on previous research by Busenhart and Fring. Our study is set within the context of the massless Klein-Gordon equation in two-dimensional space. Prior works considered scenarios in isolated areas or with compact initial conditions; in contrast, our model accounts for boundary effects. In particular, we investigate a boundary that causes wave packets to concentrate and thereby increase energy near the boundary, thus demonstrating the presence of blow-up in this context. This paper is part of a broader discussion on the topic, with references provided at the end. Notably, our approach to proving blow-up through classical methods draws on strategic placement of boundary conditions, energy estimates, and the construction of a lower estimate for energy concentrations, with additional insights drawn from prior works by Busenhart and Fring, as well as Baicich, Berti, and Wiederman in their respective studies of partial differential equations. When exploring multiple hypotheses, researchers often face the challenge of selecting the most useful hypotheses for further investigation. This task is commonly achieved through the use of utility functions to evaluate and rank hypotheses based on their expected value. However, determining relevant utility functions is a complex problem that is often solved by default or is simply not considered in existing research. In our study, we argue that utility functions should be treated as variables with the same importance as probability measures. To facilitate hypothesis selection, we propose a method for estimating utility functions using data from a single sample, thereby bypassing the need for prior utility functions. Our approach involves transforming the utility function estimation problem into a regularized inverse problem that can be solved using Bayesian methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to a hypothesis testing scenario involving the detection of gene interactions involved in certain diseases. The results show significant improvements over existing methods, including a method that is currently considered best practice, as reported in the accompanying paper by Madigan and Raghavan. We have also made all data and algorithms publicly available, enabling researchers to access and utilize our methods for hypothesis selection problems. A statistical mechanics model is introduced that represents magnetic skyrmions of various types as stable states, dependent on the homotopy group of the target space, which is the sphere in two dimensions higher. The model includes a symmetry that maps stable states to their reversed orientations, and we analytically solve for the helical states within a finite-size square lattice using a self-consistent mean-field method that accounts for next-nearest-neighbor interactions. The solution reveals the emergence of up-down symmetry in the spin correlation patterns as the temperature decreases, specifically in the nematic and antiferromagnetic components, and we observe a transition from isolated single-vortex states to interacting skyrmions as the temperature increases, identifiable by changes in the correlation functions. Additionally, we investigate the response of these monopole-capable skyrmions to an applied symmetry-breaking magnetic field, which results in a symmetry-breaking current that rotates the skyrmions in the direction of the field, and we discuss how this current is influenced by the skyrmions' interactions and the strength of the up-down symmetry. Our study provides a theoretical framework for understanding the dynamics of these fundamental topological objects, and we anticipate that it will contribute to ongoing experimental efforts to control and manipulate magnetic skyrmions in lattice materials.

While the Hartree-Fock model serves as a crucial starting point for more advanced many-body methods, the efficacy of this approach can be hindered by the absence of correlation between electrons in certain contexts. In strong interaction conditions, the Hartree-Fock solution is anticipated to converge through the inclusion of electron-electron interaction, when electrons occupy contiguous orbitals, in a way that is analogous to a simple Diagonalization method.
