In matrix optimization, we can transform a high-dimensional into a one-dimensional problem by factorizing the variable matrix into multiple components. However, the geodesic property in the transformed domain may not be equivalent to that in the original domain. By introducing the concepts of restricted strong convexity and smoothness, we can ensure the geodesic property in the transformed domain is similar to that in the original domain. Specifically, for an objective function meeting these conditions within a convex domain, the geodesic path in the transformed domain is equivalent to the geodesic path in the original domain. Furthermore, if the Hessian matrix of the objective function is strictly positive definite in that domain, the geodesic path in the transformed domain is the same as that in the original domain. We can apply this result to a general matrix optimization problem by defining an auxiliary variable and reformulating the problem. Finally, we can obtain a descent direction for the original matrix optimization problem by exploring the subdifferential instead of the superdifferential. By doing so, we can achieve an average gradient descent type of convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/k^2\right)$. Moreover, under strong convexity conditions of the objective function, we can establish a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(\exp(-k)/\mathcal{H}_0\right)$ for an exponential average gradient descent method. We can also extend our result to a composite matrix optimization problem by incorporating additional regularizers directly in the factorized domain. Finally, we can demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through numerical experiments on various matrix optimization problems. 

Keywords: matrix optimization, geodesic method, restricted strong convexity and smoothness, convergence rate analysis. 

This paper develops a geodesic method for matrix optimization by utilizing a factorized variable representation. A descriptive analysis is provided to highlight the benefit of this approach, specifically the adoption of restricted strong convexity and smoothness properties in the factorized domain. This leads to an enhanced understanding of the convex optimization problem, enabling the exploration of new algorithms. To illustrate the potential of this approach, a geodesic average gradient descent algorithm is proposed. We explore the convergence rate analysis of this algorithm under distinct scenarios, including non-convex and convex conditions. To further showcase its versatility, we apply the geodesic method to a composite matrix optimization problem by introducing additional regularizers in the factorized domain. Ultimately, our proposed method is evaluated through numerical experiments on multiple matrix optimization problems, highlighting its effectiveness.

In 1990, J.A. Gomez-Pando proposed a conjecture about bipartite graphs with maximum degree 3, stating that they can be colored with 2 strong edges, given that their degree sequence meets certain conditions. This conjecture was proven by S.L. Kim and J. Yang in 2019, who further extended the result to certain non-bipartite graphs. Building on these advancements, we present an additional generalization of the conjecture, with a demonstration of its applicability to a broader spectrum of graph types. Additionally, we introduce a super-strong edge-coloring scheme for certain classes of graphs that meet the original degree criteria, with results showing its efficacy. These innovations result from the application of new bijective mappings between the edges of these graphs and a specific sequence of strong edge-colors. Theoretical limitations and graph counterexamples provide further insight into the validity and scope of these new generalizations. We also explore the concept of super-strong edge-coloring in relation to its combinatorial properties and polynomi-al invariants. Consequently, several open questions remain in this area, giving rise to promising directions for future research. Our investigation focuses on helical swimmers that transition from being fully submerged to having a significant portion of their body above the water's surface as they move. We reveal how this "snowman-like" effect significantly impacts their locomotion, overriding previous assumptions about helical swimmers' behavior. As a result, we develop a new theoretical model that explains how the snowman-like structure can generate propulsion and steerage. Interestingly, we find that the most efficient swimmers in this new category actually have a larger helical curve than those in the fully submerged case, despite this seeming counterintuitive. Furthermore, we explore how surface tension can take control of helical swimmers, particularly when their surface tension-based forces outweigh those caused by viscosity. We also analyze how a helix's tightness affects its ability to navigate through different fluids, offering a simplified "locomotion number" as a key performance indicator. Ultimately, our research shows that even minimal surface tension enhancements can greatly enhance a helix's swimming speed in dense fluids, and that there are distinct transition phases depending on the relative sizes of the helix and its surrounding fluid environment. We anticipate that our theoretical model and findings will inform and guide future helical swimmer design experiments. Additionally, we anticipate that our analysis of the snowman-like effect will spark further research into the intricate interactions between fluid dynamics, surface tension, and shape in this new category of swimmers. This, in turn, may also shed light on related phenomena observed in other swimming applications. This study explores how the Hamming distance from optimal solutions evolves during
co-evolutionary learning in a simple domain, comparing two approaches: individual
learning and social learning. In the individual learning scenario, each candidate
solutions' fitness is assessed against a representative solution found through a
separate search; in the social learning scenario, the fitness of each solution is
evaluated against the best solution found so far. Our analysis reveals that Hamming
distances from optimal solutions exhibit the same pattern of growth observed in prior
work, relying on natural selection rather than learning dynamics. A theoretical
model predicts Hamming distances will increase at a rate related to the number of
variables being optimized, consistent with empirical data. Notably, social learning
results in expected Hamming distances nearly two times higher than individual learning
for both easy and difficult problems, leading to inferior performance. Our findings
also indicate that learning dynamics are key to observed behavior, while the choice
of learning mechanism has a more significant impact than algorithm parameters. In
addition, our results provide evidence that Nash Equilibrium is a suitable model for
understanding the behavior of co-evolutionary learning. Finally, we discuss the
impllications of these findings for the study of co-evolutionary learning and
suggest potential research paths. This work is a theoretical analysis of previous
empirical research conducted in (O'Neill et al. 2010, O'Neill et al. 2011, McDermid
et al. 2013, Collins and O'Neill, 2010). Although the research was inspired by
those results, this work has been developed independently of them. The main
contribution of this research has been to create a Hamming distance model, the
Nash Equilibrium model, the comparison between social and individual learning, and
the associated statistical analysis, all of which were done without the use of any
existing theoretical frameworks. The code used for this research is available online
at https://github.com/hugoac/HammingDistances. The algorithms used for this research
can be found in https://github.com/declerk/hillclimber and https://github.com/declerk/simplega. The primary goal of this research is to develop a sophisticated method using deep learning for identifying security-related concepts within written information. We present an innovative use of advanced neural network techniques, including the Bidirectional LSTM model, to demonstrate their effectiveness in concept extraction. By comparing the performance of regular and bidirectional LSTMs, we aim to investigate the benefits of using these sophisticated models. Additionally, we explore various input features to identify the most useful input data for accurate concept detection. Our best model achieves a micro-averaged F-score of 0.78 when evaluating the extracted concepts, surpassing the capacity of human security experts who achieved a micro-averaged F-score of 0.77. We also present an innovative approach utilizing our concept extraction model to monitor security-related discussions on Twitter. Our method demonstrates the potential for bidirectional LSTMs to be applied to other concept extraction tasks beyond security. We provide both the security concept dataset we developed and our concept extraction model as open resources for the community. In deep learning systems, silent data corruption can cause inaccuracies and affect the entire training process. This issue is particularly prevalent in large-scale training processes that utilize multiple machines. One effective solution to mitigate SDC's impact is to employ non-uniform data exclusion techniques. However, this approach requires a significant amount of labeled data to determine the validity of each training example. In this paper, we introduce an innovative algorithm called LExIterate, which leverages an iterative process to handle SDC's impact. This algorithm works as follows: 1) initially, it uses a limited amount of labeled data to establish a basic model; 2) it employs an unsupervised validation method to identify valid training examples based on the model's predictions and loss values; 3) it trains and refines the model using a separate subset of valid and unlabeled data; 4) this process is repeated multiple times to achieve optimal results. Our experimental findings demonstrate that LExIterate reduces SDC's impact on the test accuracy of neural networks and outperforms alternative techniques that utilize a uniform data exclusion method. Furthermore, LExIterate proves effective across multiple benchmark datasets and is particularly suited to large-scale training processes. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/yongxianfeng/Lexititerate.

In an economy, graph algorithms can help individuals make informed decisions on
an optimal network of connections. By modeling connections and conflicts between
actors as nodes and edges in a graph, a corresponding maximum weight subgraph can
be found to represent the most beneficial network. However, current graph algorithms
are often too slow to handle large-scale graphs. We introduce a new algorithm that
gradually refines a random subgraph into the maximum weight subgraph, while ensuring
each step improves the weight and keeps the subgraph connected. This algorithm is
fast enough to handle large graphs and outperforms existing connected maximum weight
subgraph algorithms. We also provide an analysis of the algorithm's performance and
verify it produces accurate results through experiments. The algorithm and its source
code are available online. By applying this algorithm to various real-world datasets,
we highlight its potential to optimize real-world connection networks.

This paper explores the generalization of the Jordanian twist from its basic form to its higher-dimensional analogues, matching the pattern observed in the generalized Yang-Baxter equation. We demonstrate that the generalized form follows from the simple Jordanian twist through a series of 'enrichment' processes, akin to matrix summations, and establish the analogous relationship between the 'enriched' and'simple' forms as seen in the Qmatrix algebra. Furthermore, we establish the algebraic form of the 'enriched' twist through 'down-shifting' of coefficients, followed by 'up-shifting' after the 'enrichment'. We also derive the 'enriched' form of the simple Jordanian twist through its enrichment, resulting in an equivalent enigmatic form first proposed by RT Kumano-go. Additionally, we confirm that this proposed form corresponds to the simple Jordanian twist upon 'down-shifting'. Finally, we establish that 'down-shifting' serves as a symbolic inversion process for the 'enrichment'. This study investigates the challenges of name tagging in low-resource languages, specifically in the context of product title classification, and introduces a novel approach using character-level neural models and a label prediction module for name detection and tagging. We test our approach on Arabic product names and observe significant improvements over existing methods and a character-level CRF model. Furthermore, our approach proves versatile and effective across languages, demonstrating excellent performance on synthetic data generated from English descriptions and extended to new names in a high-resource language, Spanish. Our code and data are openly accessible, representing a first step towards creating a comprehensive dataset for name tagging in low-resource languages. Alongside our findings, we explore the implications for name tagging in commerce and web applications. 

Additionally, our approach surpasses current standards for name tagging in Arabic, achieving 0.930 F1-score, and is equally effective on synthetic Arabic data and actual Arabic names. We also achieve comparable results to high-resource name tagging models when trained on data augmented from English and evaluated on actual Spanish names. Our approach also emerges as the top performer in name tagging among low-resource languages, outperforming models trained on data specific to the language at 0.937 F1-score. 

We make the following contributions in this study: 
- Introduce a novel approach to name tagging in low-resource languages through character-level neural models and a label prediction module for combined name detection and tagging.
- Achieve notable enhancements in name tagging in Arabic, a low-resource language, and demonstrate equitable performance on synthetic Arabic data and actual Arabic names.
- Utilize character-level models to succeed in name tagging on Spanish, a high-resource language, utilizing data generated from English and evaluate on actual Spanish names.
- Establish a new benchmark for name tagging in a low-resource language, outperforming models trained on actual data in Spanish at 0.937 F1-score.
- Provide the first dataset for name tagging in Swahili and make our code and data openly accessible, marking the beginning of comprehensive datasets for name tagging in low-resource languages. 

This research lays the groundwork for name tagging in commerce, web applications, and potentially other fields such as databases and customer relationship management. We hope our open data and code will facilitate research and advance name tagging in low-resource languages.

The growing popularity of dialog management systems necessitates accurate dialogue state tracking. Most modern models leverage neural networks, but their vulnerability to noisy data poses a challenge. The presence of incorrect labels in training data can significantly impact the performance of these models, particularly when they comprise a substantial proportion of the dataset. In this paper, we investigate the effect of noisy labels on dialogue state tracking and propose a method to mitigate their influence. By utilizing a modified loss function that incorporates a clean-probability-based penalty, we devise a way to improve model robustness. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach yields a 6.53 absolute improvement in joint goal achievement and outperforms the baseline model in most cases. Furthermore, we analyze the benefits of our proposed method for different levels of noise in the data. For further investigation, we make the code and data available for replication and advancement of dialogue state tracking techniques.

Similar to other complex systems, the spread of civil unrest within urban areas is influenced by the underlying structure of the city's infrastructure. Determining the implications of this idea, researchers have compared the topological characteristics of Barcelona's infrastructure during the 15th to 19th centuries with those of the 2007-2008 financial crisis. Conducting an in-depth analysis in the Gothic Quarter, scientists found that the city's historic districts exhibit a high degree of hierarchy, whereas areas with recent architectural development tend to be more hierarchical but also more localized in their connectivity. Furthermore, data from the 2008 crisis indicated that connected components of large size were spread across these districts, indicating their potential for future unrest. Additionally, researchers developed an mathematical model to simulate the effects of removing key infrastructure within these complexes, revealing that a small number of highly connected generators can produce large-scale instability. Conversely, in cities with more localized connectivity, smaller-scale disturbances were more prevalent. Consequently, the findings suggest that large-scale unrest may be more likely in cities characterized by hierarchical infrastructure, while smaller-scale unrest is more common in cities with more localized connectivity. The research highlights the significance of integrating the long-term development of urban infrastructure with social dynamics when analyzing the spread of civil unrest. Deep learning-based algorithms utilizing convolutional neural networks have recently achieved impressive results in various tasks, leading to increased interest in applying them to visual-inertial odometry (VIO). Inspired by the success of deep learning in computer vision, researchers have developed several deep learning-based VIO models that use learning to resolve ambiguity in equations derived from VIO. Although these approaches have shown superior performance compared to traditional VIO methods in certain scenarios, they also have limitations such as requiring large amounts of labeled data, encountering difficulties when facing significant camera movement or misalignment, and being prone to overfitting. To address these challenges, the paper proposes a deep learning-based VIO framework called DirectVIO, which processes data in a different manner than typical VIO algorithms. Unlike traditional approaches that solve optimization problems directly for parameter estimation, typical deep learning-based VIO models represent physical parameters as the combination of multiple learned features and optimize these parameters indirectly to minimize the reconstruction error in images. The proposed DirectVIO framework converts physical parameters directly into learnable features without intermediate representations, eliminating the need to jointly optimize both. To achieve this, the paper presents a novel way to build a graph neural network for inertial data processing. The learned features can then be used for two purposes: estimating the absolute orientation of the sensor and updating the state transition model. By implementing a custom optimization method with backpropagation, the paper shows that DirectVIO can learn to estimate the sensor's orientation directly from images and inertial data without iterative optimization. The results of experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of DirectVIO, a model with limited training data, against state-of-the-art deep learning-based VIO models and traditional VIO algorithms. This paper delves into the fundamental principles of Weyl semimetals in three-dimensional space, exploring their higher-order incarnations and the topological square-root models in two-dimensional systems. By converting the 3D Weyl model to a 2D representation using the Klein operator, we successfully recreate the quantum anomalous Hall insulator and the Dirac semimetal in the flat band model. This enables us to illustrate the Berry curvature and current for both 3D and 2D Weyl semimetals. Furthermore, we establish a general framework for constructing square-root topological models in 2D systems using the 3D Weyl semimetal picture. This approach simplifies the process of designing 2D topological models related to Weyl semimetals. As an example, we develop a new 2D lattice model based on this framework, demonstrating its quantitative and qualitative similarities to the honeycomb iridate model. This includes matching lattice and orbital structures, as well as overlapping flat bands in both models. Notably, both natural and artificial realizations of these 2D models are possible. This work provides a 3D Weyl semimetal perspective on the flat band and quantum anomalous Hall physics, offering a broader understanding of these phenomena. It also suggests the "square-root" topology of 2D Weyl semimetals as a distinct paradigm that encompasses flat band and quantum anomalous Hall physics. Finally, possible experimental signatures and potential connections to recent "flat band" experiments are discussed. This paper also explores the potential for lattice models related to Weyl semimetals to be used in device applications, such as quantum anomalous Hall devices, high-performance thermoelectric materials, and flat band devices in optoelectronics. This involves considering the quantization of Weyl points, anomalous Hall conductivity, flat band chemistry, lattice relaxations, and spin-orbit coupling. The feasibility of these devices relies on the ability to fabricate and manipulate 2D lattice models that mimic the flat band and quantum anomalous Hall physics of Weyl semimetals. This could enable the development of quantum anomalous Hall devices, high-performance thermoelectric materials, and flat band optoelectronic devices. This includes the possibility of creating quantum devices based on Weyl fermions, such as quantum amplifiers and quantum switches, by manipulating the transport properties of quantized Weyl points. This could provide a fundamental approach for designing new quantum devices

Although grid cells are crucial for the brain's navigational mapping system, the impact of external cues on grid cell functionality in the entorhinal cortex remains unclear. Using high-resolution recording techniques in freely navigating rats, our study reveals that grid cells are modulated by external visual cues when they don't conflict with cues from locomotion and cortical states. When the visual environment changes, the spacing of grid cells also adapts in accordance with place fields that have persistent activity in the hippocampus, suggesting a potential state-dependent placement of grid cells along navigational paths. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the adaptation of grid cells is facilitated by path integration and is subject to bounds that prevent them from becoming too large, thus maintaining the cortex's efficient use of spatial information. This is especially evident when multiple grid cells with different scales are used to represent complex navigation routes. In essence, our study shows that grid cells serve as a fundamental layer for the representation of navigation routes, and this base map can be used in various cortical states and scales to support the exploration of an environment. This multi-scale state-dependent grid cell code allows the entorhinal cortex to effectively combine the brain's internal navigation calculations with external visual cues, all while leveraging the hippocampus's persistent activity to extract meaningful information from complex navigation routes. As such, this grid cell code provides a cohesive framework for understanding how the brain's internal navigation is influenced by visual environment and is thus a hub for the integration of hippocampal navigation with the sensory cortex. This integrated code also furnishes a superior basis for the development of human navigation systems that are both efficient and effective in complex, real-world settings. Furthermore, our multidisciplinary findings offer a unified theory of grid cells and support the state-dependent grid cell model over the conflicting cues hypothesis. Ultimately, our study highlights the significance of navigating the intricate relationship between the brain's internal navigation, visual environment, and cortical states to achieve a deeper comprehension of grid cell functionality. Our research explores how kinematic dynamos impact the generation of magnetic cycles in stars with low rotation rates. Using a shell dynamo model, we find that kinematic dynamos can produce magnetic cycles in stars with moderate rotation rates. However, for slowly rotating stars, kinematic dynamos may not generate magnetic cycles, and instead produce multiple magnetic structures. These multiple structures can lead to magnetic cycles only if there is a mechanism to flush out the existing poloidal field, such as the action of the rotational shear dynamo. If this is not the case, kinematic dynamos in slowly rotating stars will only result in multiple magnetic cycles without field reversal. We also find that magnetic cycles in stars with moderate rotation rates will ultimately reach a state of stability, while in slowly rotating stars with multiple magnetic structures, this equilibrium may never be reached. These findings have implications for using magnetic cycle properties to constrain kinematic dynamo theory. For example, kinematic dynamos may only be applicable to stars with rotation rates greater than 3.5 $\times 10^5$ C, and may only be relevant to magnetic cycles in stars with rotation rates between 1.5 $\times 10^5$ C and 4 $\times 10^5$ C. Below this range, kinematic dynamos will not generate magnetic cycles, and instead produce multiple magnetic structures. These multiple structures can only lead to magnetic cycles through the action of rotational shear dynamos. Therefore, if future observations show that magnetic cycles exist in stars with rotation rates lower than 3.5 $\times 10^5$ C, this would require the action of rotational shear dynamos and cannot be explained by kinematic dynamo theory. Furthermore, if multiple magnetic cycles are observed in stars with moderate rotation rates, this would indicate that kinematic dynamos are also relevant in this range, and ultimately, both kinematic and rotational shear dynamos may be necessary to understand magnetic cycles in stars with moderate rotation rates.

We start with a family of quartic extensions from the S4 class, with the goal of determining the number of such families that contain only rank-0 or rank-1 elliptic curves for a specific range of values. To achieve this, we establish conditions for the rational rank of these extensions and develop a method to filter the families based on those conditions. By applying this approach, we identify the number of families that meet the desired criteria under the assumption that there are no additional class fields that could impact our results. To validate this assumption, we employ computational methods to examine a considerable number of instances across a broad spectrum of modulus functions. As a result, we are able to present a precise count of the families that meet our criteria standards, with this count being further confirmed through additional computational analysis. The focus of our analysis is on calculating the entropy generated over time in this system. By converting the Luttinger model to a hydrodynamic description and considering only forward-moving excitations, we establish a relationship between entropy generation, temperature changes, and chemical potential changes at different points in time and location. Ultimately, our approach allows us to determine the entropy generated at each point in time and location and demonstrate that it is directly proportional to the square of the correlation length of the system, indicating its fundamental irreversibility. According to our research, within $Q_d$, a nondegenerate regular simplex $\Delta$ exists with $k \geq \lceil (d+1)/2 \rceil$ nodes, however our study focuses on the previously unexamined cases of $k=d+1$. Our analysis involves an in-depth examination of the geometry of $Q_d$, especially its facial structure. Along with presenting new results, our paper also delves into related theories, including those concerning projection operators, vector-valued Lorentz spaces, and Kaczmarz's method for linear systems. In cancer research, understanding the disease's progression and development is crucial for effective treatment and monitoring. Machine learning methods utilized in graph neural networks have demonstrated considerable potential in analyzing complex tissue structures and their cellular components. However, most existing approaches solely focus on employing domain-specific expertise without considering important quality control measures, such as data normalization. As a result, their reliability and consistency are questionable. To address these issues, we present a novel framework that normalizes tissue data, employs graph neural networks for representation learning, and leverages supervised learning to classify sensitive information. The proposed framework comprises two primary components: a data normalization stage that uses a unique approach to create balanced node features, and a representation learning stage that incorporates a type of graph neural network. Furthermore, we incorporate a sensitive attribute prediction stage using a discriminative graph neural network, and we demonstrate the benefits of our approach through comprehensive experiments on publicly available datasets. Our findings suggest that our method achieves superior performance and consistency compared to existing cancer research applications, and we make our code publicly available to facilitate further development. Additionally, we include a comprehensive review of cancer-related research and potential future directions. Unlike other graph neural network applications that model relationships between data samples, cancer research primarily focuses on modeling connections between cellular components within tissue structures. As a result, we also introduce a new dataset called BReAst CEll (BRECE) containing detailed information about breast tissue structures and cellular components, along with cancer development progression. We conclude by outlining the key challenges associated with cancer research and propose several novel applications, including modeling breast cancer development progression, detecting cancer cells, analyzing tumor aggressiveness, and forecasting tissue structure changes. This paper develops a nonlinear version of the multi-dimensional Hawkes process, a powerful tool for analyzing interaction dynamics in complex systems represented by non-linear relationships. By transforming the process into its batch form and applying the nonlinear Hawkes process to the resulting data, we can isolate and model the interaction components. This allows us to extract specific features like short-term and long-term memory characteristics from the original data, capturing the underlying dynamics of the complex system. For parameter estimation, we propose a two-step likelihood-based method, first obtaining initial parameters through the exponential family estimation method and then refining them using the stochastic gradient descent algorithm. Through simulations and analysis of real stock price data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, the new model, and the associated estimation method. Specifically, we find that the nonlinear Hawkes process effectively models the interaction components, and the two-step estimation method efficiently yields accurate parameter estimates. Moreover, we identify significant long-term memory features in the stock price data and the implications of these findings for understanding market dynamics. Additionally, we highlight the advantages of the multi-dimensional nonlinear Hawkes process model, the limitations of the standard linear Hawkes process, and the benefits of the new model's batch form for analyzing complex systems. This work paves the way for applying the nonlinear Hawkes process to a broader range of data systems, including those with time series dependencies. Furthermore, the model's batch form provides a useful framework for analyzing complex systems, consisting of multiple interconnected components, such as social networks, financial systems, and transportation systems, and we expect this to lead to new insights into the underlying dynamics of these systems. Additionally, the model's feature learning capability can be utilized across other areas, such as computer vision and natural language processing, and we suggest potential avenues for exploring these applications. Finally, we emphasize the importance of further developing and refining the nonlinear Hawkes process, as well as the need for publicly accessible software for the associated methods. This paper introduces a novel contrastive learning algorithm for cross-anatomy domain adaptation (CS-CADA), which enables the accurate segmentation of complex anatomical structures using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). By leveraging a contrastive loss function in both unsupervised and supervised stages, CS-CADA enhances the robustness of feature representations and adapts them for target domain segmentation. To tackle the challenge of lacking direct supervised information in the target domain, we introduce an alternative prediction task and incorporate adversarial network components to produce target-domain-like images from source images, which facilitates the transfer of accurate segmentations. Comprehensive evaluation of our CS-CADA approach on two high-complexity MRI segmentation tasks demonstrates superior performance compared to existing domain adaptation techniques. Moreover, in-depth analysis of contrastive learning and adversarial image transformation components yields insightful results that help clarify the effects of these components on CS-CADA's effectiveness. Additionally, CNMF exhibits robust performance under various noise levels and temperature changes, ultimately showcasing its potential for real-world piano transcription applications. The success of machine learning models heavily relies on accurate and abundant labeled data. Obtaining sufficient labeled data is a challenging process due to the time and money it takes to manually annotate data. Selective labeling is an effective technique to acquire labeled data efficiently, where only specific, vital information is asked from annotators. To take full advantage of selective labeling, the annotation process needs to be tightly integrated with the machine learning model's training process. Although traditional methods utilize separate components for data selection and annotation, our proposed method, CoSL, simultaneously performs data selection and annotation based on the current model's predictions and a review of annotation guidelines. CoSL is designed to reduce the annotation burden and increase the effectiveness of expert annotations, where annotators review and correct the model's predictions and classify the corrections as annotations or suggestions for model updates. By incorporating a decoder decoder objective, CoSL increases the model's performance on unsupervised data and improves the quality of annotations. Experimental results demonstrate that CoSL boosts the performance of a state-of-the-art model on three datasets, specifically improvements of +2.3 in GLUE score for our primary dataset, a new dataset within the SuperGLUE dataset, and a 0.7 absolute F1-score improvement on SQuAD v2.0. Notably, expert annotations account for less than 5% of the total labeled data in CoSL, achieving the goal of reducing the annotation burden. Understanding the social determinants of health, or how living conditions influence health outcomes, is crucial for developing effective healthcare policies.  However, gathering this information on a large scale is challenging due to the expense and complexity involved.  A potential solution lies in analyzing clinical notes from patients' electronic health records, which provide detailed, individualized insights into patients' living conditions and health status.  However, these notes are often written in a style distinct from typical written language, making it difficult to extract useful information from them.  In this paper, we demonstrate the value of incorporating contextual information into models used to extract this clinical data.  We utilize a dataset of extractions from clinical notes, developed by the University of Colorado School of Medicine, to compare traditional machine learning techniques with more advanced neural network-based models.  Our analysis shows that neural network-based models yield more accurate results than traditional methods and outperform all baselines provided in the dataset itself.  Furthermore, incorporating contextual graph information into these models enhances their performance even further.  Our best model achieves an average score of 0.77 on the F1 measure for extracting social determinants of health from clinical notes.  This represents a significant improvement over baseline models and highlights the potential for widespread use of this technique within clinical settings.  We also provide an overview of the dataset itself, which includes 213 unique extraction points and is made publicly available for use by other researchers.  Along with this dataset, we include all code necessary to replicate our results, which can be utilized by researchers looking to apply similar techniques to other clinical extraction tasks.  We intend for this dataset and its associated analysis to contribute to a broader effort to enhance healthcare policy understanding through clinical record analysis. Researchers propose a theory to explain the unusual behavior of a young star called MWC 297. Located about 2,500 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia, MWC 297 is a prominent source of infrared radiation and exhibits extremely fast starlight emissions. Observations suggest the star is surrounded by a massive disk, potentially creating a massive black hole or a powerful jet system that affects the disk's structure. A computational model shows that objects migrating through the disk can cause instability near its inner parts, potentially leading to the formation of unstable regions that could result in the production of highly energetic particles and light waves. However, the model also indicates that the disk's inner sections can become stable enough to form massive chunks known as planetesimals, which could eventually develop into small stars, planets, or other celestial objects. Further analysis indicates that the disk's chemistry can produce powerful magnetic fields capable of affecting the behavior of elements like carbon, which can lead to the formation of smaller particles called dust, ultimately influencing the disk's temperature and shape. Despite its computational nature, the model faces limitations when modeling specific events, such as massive explosions observed in the disk. In its current form, the model only accounts for processes occurring over months to years, and cannot explain the origin of the massive disk itself, which is believed to have formed from the star's initial gas and matter acquired through accretion. In its study, the model is used to examine how different processes contribute to the disk's overall energy, where it finds that most energy originates from the star's gravitational pull, followed by energetic particle collisions, and then the conversion of kinetic energy from objects moving through the disk. The model also enables comparison with actual data, showing a daily variation known as the Vaiana effect, and highlights the need for even higher resolution imaging in the near infrared. The findings from this computational model contribute to a better understanding of how the disk around MWC 297 functions and ultimately may aid in the explanation of similar behaviors observed in other young stars like LL Cir. The study also includes a new high-resolution image taken with the MSX6C camera of the disk around MWC 297 in the K band, and presents various new findings presented in the form of processing techniques for the satellite data, new algorithms for analyzing spectral energy distributions, and new methods for creating artificial models from real data. This paper develops a comprehensive scattering theory that is adaptable to various symplectic algebras. Building on previous work by Witten and Hawking, we introduce an asymptotic algebra and scattering matrix to effectively capture the dynamics of scattering processes. These fundamental components enable us to derive an inductive formula for computing the scattering matrix, which can be applied to a broad range of algebras, including those associated with Minkowski, de Sitter, and anti-de Sitter spacetimes. Research into the wireless exposure caused by 5G base stations is being examined through numerical and practical assessments. When it comes to how buildings affect exposure, a key finding shows that 5G's exposure inside buildings is actually lower than previous wireless technologies, due to a feature that allows it to focus signal direction. However, when it comes to external exposures, 5G's powers can surpass previous limits, especially if optimal compensation techniques are not used. Furthermore, it's been discovered that 5G's unique characteristics, such as multi-band operation, can lead to increased exposure in certain situations. To externally monitor 5G exposure, a proposal is made to utilize existing measurement infrastructure for downlink exposures, and also propose new methods for uplink and near-field measurements. Finally, it's suggested that international exposure standards be re-evaluated in light of 5G's unique features. In addition, options for mitigating excessive exposures through new compensation techniques are also presented. In this regard, it's essential to adopt a holistic methodology that simulates and measures exposure and performance concurrently, allowing for optimization of both factors. This paper presents a novel approach to identifying the surface of water observed in video footage. A deep learning-based model, specifically a transformation matrix model combined with a U-Net, is trained on still images obtained from video frames to recover the hidden surface information - in this case, the wave's upper portion. Unlike traditional methods, the proposed approach bypasses the need for complex partial differential equations that describe wave dynamics, instead directly leveraging input images to inform the surface reconstruction. Successful applications include enhancing low-resolution surfaces, removing background objects, and handling irregular waves caused by wind. However, the model's current limitation includes only being able to analyze a single wave cycle due to a lack of temporal information in the training data. Future developments could explore enhancing the model to handle more complex scenarios. Despite this constraint, the proposed approach demonstrates significant potential for water analysis and related fields like medical imaging. The surface layer theorem is a crucial tool incorporating topological and geometric principles, primarily utilized to analyze differential forms within locally convex spaces. This article extends the surface layer theorem to saddle points by combining techniques from the regular critical point theory and hyperbolic partial differential equations. By establishing the isomorphism of Sobolev spaces for stable manifolds, we can directly obtain the surface layer operators at saddle points. This methodological approach simplifies the derivation of the operators compared to other existing methods. As a result, we can easily identify the asymptotic operator at saddle points. This breakthrough comes with a demonstration of the operator's surjectivity in certain Banach spaces. Furthermore, we explore the fundamental properties of the operator and prove the existence of quasi-orthogonal projections. These findings can be applied to the index theory for differential operators with singular points. This research is an extension of the work presented in the book 'Spatiotemporal Singularities in Nonlinear Hyperbolic Equations' by J. M. Rubin. Specifically, this article provides the theoretical foundation for the surface layer operators discussed in Chapter II of the book. This article's results solve the openness problem for stable manifolds and clarify the structure of the surface layer operators at saddle points. This paper introduces a cutting-edge navigation system for mobile platforms that utilize range sensors, specifically showing how a layer-based control system is implemented with sonar sensors in an underwater environment. The presented approach establishes separate layers for obstacle avoidance and target tracking, leveraging adaptive techniques to regulate layer interaction and learn optimal control parameters. The system's performance is highlighted through simulation and practical applications, demonstrating enhanced navigation through clutters, improved target tracking after encounters with obstacles, and robust operation in the presence of sensor faults. Furthermore, the system is evaluated using a sonar-equipped underwater robot, providing concrete evidence of its real-world effectiveness.

The spread of fake news through social media is a pressing concern, and machine learning models that can identify and counter this phenomenon are gaining importance. Most existing studies focus solely on using individual articles' content for training models, without considering the contextual information available in the form of news articles' relationships, such as posting history and interconnected topics. This study investigates the impact of incorporating contextual information on the performance of models identifying fake news from ordinary ones and proposes a novel approach that leverages contextual information through a contextualized representation model. By utilizing the contextualized representation model's ability to grasp complex semantic relationships, we can significantly improve the performance of models detecting fake news, outpacing standard models that rely solely on static representation models. Experimental results show that our proposed context-aware approach yields an absolute improvement of 2.9% in accuracy compared to static representation models and 0.8% better than models that don't consider contextual information but are trained on contextualized representations without accounting for the meaning of context. We also examine the effects of context windows size and model types for contextual representation models, along with the responsibility of context in distinguishing fake and real news. In theories of contingent reasoning, the relationship between what if questions and answers regarding a system's state is described using a non-monotonic logic called the possible worlds semantics for propositional logic. Our study translates this conceptual framework into a physical context by representing the "what if" questions as changes in a curve's geometry within a manifold. We then model the corresponding "answer" regarding the system's state as the minimal number of degrees of freedom that characterize the new microstates resulting from the change. By examining this approach in simple examples, such as circular paths in both two-dimensional space and four-dimensional flat geometry, we observe that the effect of curvature leads to an increase in the system's entropy and the emergence of hysteresis, both of which are essential features of systems with nonlinear responses that exhibit complex behavior. In these examples, the increased entropy and hysteresis arise solely as a result of the change in degrees of freedom without any energy loss, demonstrating that entropy need not necessarily be an extensive property. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the extent of hysteresis is governed by the change in entropy per cycle, which provides a fundamental understanding of this phenomenon often observed in physics but not comprehensively in other fields. Lastly, our study paves the way for applying the possible worlds semantics to controllable systems that exhibit complex, nonlinear behavior and hysteresis, such as magnetic materials with phase transitions, electric circuits with hysteresis in capacitors, chemical systems with feedback loops, biological systems with covalent bonds, and astrological systems with hysteresis in the climate's water cycle. Our research also suggests that hysteresis is an intrinsic element of contingent reasoning, offering the opportunity to bridge the gap between contingent knowledge and controllable systems that exhibit complex, nonlinear behavior. In doing so, we can utilize contingent reasoning to design, as well as adaptively control and learn from, these complex systems. Ultimately, this framework provides a theoretical foundation for applying the principles of contingent reasoning to the scientific study of controllable systems in physics and astronomy. Decentralized decision-making among self-interested agents is a common occurrence in various multi-agent systems, including distributed networks and online advertising platforms. In these settings, agents make independent decisions to minimize their own costs, often without considering the broader impact on the system as a whole. A notable problem in this domain is the decoding order selection problem, which arises when decoding concurrent transmissions in a wireless network. A recent study demonstrated that this problem exhibits strategic complexity, incorporating elements of non-verifiable message exchange and decentralized decision-making. A computationally demanding algorithm was subsequently proposed to determine a suboptimal decoding order that minimizes system-wide costs, although this solution requires significant computational resources and extensive data collection. Conversely, a new model incorporating threshold-based feedback from each receiver to the transmitter reduces the strategic complexity and computational complexity of the problem by an order of magnitude, while still yielding a suboptimal but efficient decoding order. Simulation results validate the new approach, revealing a substantial increase in concurrent transmissions and improved system performance under various traffic conditions. Furthermore, the proposed solution offers a feasible solution to the original decoding order selection problem, which previously proved computationally intractable. The new solution is also applicable to other decentralized communication problems, presenting an innovative approach to addressing complex communication challenges in self-interested networks. The proposed threshold-based feedback model and corresponding suboptimal decoding order selection algorithm are made available online for public use. The code can be found at the following repository: https://github.com/alexfeng95/decoding-order-selection. The proposed suboptimal solution reduces computational complexity from $O(2^n \cdot n^5)$ to $O(n^3)$, where n represents the number of concurrent transmissions, and is capable of handling over 100 concurrent transmissions within a second on a typical desktop computer. The new solution provides a suboptimal but near-optimal decoding order, with an average performance improvement of at least 20% under various traffic conditions. The proposed solution is adaptable to various wireless networks and can be applied to other decentralized communication problems, offering a novel approach to addressing complex communication challenges in self-interested networks. A local magnetic field affecting atomic motion in an atomic interferometer can be detected with high sensitivity, equivalent to $10^{-12}$ times the strength of the Earth's magnetic field. A demonstration of this principle involves splitting atoms using a laser and observing changes in their interference patterns following exposure to a known magnetic field. By rotating the atomic spin by 180 degrees via interaction with a hot atomic target, we significantly improve the sensitivity of this demonstration to $10^{-12}$ times the Earth's magnetic field strength, achieving this improved sensitivity in an unrotated atomic spin state scenario as well. Despite significant advancements, there are still gaps in the field, particularly in the application of entanglement concepts to machine learning for quantum physics. This paper addresses this shortage by introducing two practical approaches to implementing entanglement within neural networks, utilizing the correlator method and von-Neumann density-matrix technique. By incorporating entanglement descriptors into custom loss functions, our proposals successfully integrate the fundamental principles of quantum physics with machine learning. The efficacy of these innovative frameworks is demonstrated through comprehensive simulations of two exemplary scenarios: a quantum double well and quantum Hall physics in a parabolic well, both of which involve interplay between entanglement and quantum phase transitions. The findings reveal that quantum learning networks can accurately capture the onset of quantum entanglement and associated transitions by activating entangled representations within the network, whereas the absence of entanglement is marked by inactive channels. This research provides entanglement-enabled quantum learning networks for complex quantum systems, paving the way for a deeper understanding of quantum phenomena and the identification of entanglement in custom setups. Furthermore, the entanglement descriptors proposed here can be applied to analyze the entanglement properties of quantum states, facilitating the development of new quantum physics applications. In the context of admixture models, assigning a Dirichlet process prior to densities results in a clustering structure at different scales, reflecting both local density patterns and broader population structure. However, simply using a stick-breaking process to condition on the Dirichlet process leads to non-identifiable admixture weights. To circumvent this issue, a recent approach places a separate Dirichlet process on the weights, effectively separating the density clustering and weight clustering. This method yields independent samples of densities and corresponding weights, allowing for the recovery of admixture components unique to individual locations. In contrast, our work proposes a different strategy based on a Dirichlet process prior for densities, where the stick-breaking process is used to assign weights that are conditionally identical across different densities. This results in a single set of weights associated with distinct local densities, which can be further aggregated to obtain the corresponding admixture components for each superpopulation. Our main contribution establishes the consistency of our proposed method and provides a method for computing its asymptotic Bayes factors. This enables the inference of the number of superpopulations K from posterior distributions. Our results can be applied to a broader class of Dirichlet process mixtures by ensuring the exchangeability of densities. In the case of non-identifiable admixture weights, our approach offers an alternative to recent works focused on weight clustering. In addition, our method offers a distinct perspective on the Dirichlet process prior, facilitating the discussion of issues related to the non-identifiability of Dirichlet process mixtures. To facilitate the implementation of our method, the R package "DPAdmixture" is available online. In our experiments, our approach demonstrates comparable or superior performance to current state-of-the-art methods on both artificial and real datasets. In the context of admixture models and their extensions, our method's consistency and resulting admixture component uniqueness have significant implications for the interpretation of results. In the broader context of Dirichlet process mixtures, our work highlights the distinction between density clustering and weight clustering, raising questions about the appropriateness of separate Dirichlet processes for weights. In addition, our results raise issues about the non-asymptotic performance of our method and the Dirichlet process weight clustering. Current GPU memory allocators, including those in high-performance computing frameworks like CUDA, are largely based on simple pool management. However, the increasing size and complexity of GPU memory usage in real-world applications necessitates a more sophisticated memory management system. To address this need, we introduce DynaSOAr, a cooperative memory management system that utilizes a segment-based approach. By segmenting GPU memory into multiple independent areas and assigning each area a unique properties file, DynaSOAr enables fine-grained performance optimization and efficient memory reclamation. We showcase the benefits of DynaSOAr through various benchmarks, demonstrating a significant boost in memory usage and performance. Notably, DynaSOAr achieves a substantial memory increase of up to 5.3x and a performance improvement of up to 2.1x compared to the standard CUDA memory allocator. Moreover, DynaSOAr's memory reclamation feature reduces memory usage and improves application performance in iterative scenarios. To further highlight DynaSOAr's effectiveness, we apply it to real-world use cases and demonstrate its capability to enhance memory performance in complex scientific applications. By leveraging DynaSOAr, developers can easily optimize GPU memory usage and achieve better performance without delving into low-level memory management details. To facilitate widespread adoption, we openly disseminate DynaSOAr's code through GitHub. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive demonstration of DynaSOAr's functionality and performance at this link.

Additionally, an overview of the Morrey space and its variants, including Lebesgue-Morrey spaces, is provided to highlight their key characteristics and differentiability properties. Moreover, problem formulations are presented for further exploration within the realm of generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

for creating high-resolution segmentation masks in a coordinate-based manner. In this paper, we
propose FourierMask, a novel framework that leverages Fourier implicit functions for generating
higher-resolution segmentation masks within a frequency-based approach. Unlike existing
implicit functions that operate in a coordinate-based manner, Fourier implicit functions are
operated on grid points determined by a Fourier series, enabling efficient creation of
higher-resolution masks through a cumulative accumulation of frequency components.

output masks, facilitating supervised learning of Fourier implicit functions. Experimental
results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, as FourierMask achieves state-of-the-art
accuracy in various benchmark datasets, such as Cityscapes and KITTI. The code has been

This study explores the fundamental properties of complete, restricted minimal disks in 3D space. For a given positive value, we classify the possible configurations of such disks, where the boundary shares no points with a specific curve. This classification reveals connections to the spectrum of particular submanifolds, providing a link between the intrinsic geometry of the boundary and the extrinsic geometry of the disk. Leveraging this relationship, we establish an upper limit on the number of distinct frequency values for a given positive value. This limit specifically holds only for minimal disks in 3D space; in higher-dimensional spaces, the relationship between frequency values and the geometry of the boundary is less constrained. As a result, we demonstrate the existence of an infinite number of distinct frequency values for minimal disks in any higher-dimensional space. This existence proof is grounded in a specific construction, where a minimal disk in a higher-dimensional space is constructed to exhibit a particular symmetry, thus yielding an infinite number of distinct frequency values. This research thus provides a more general framework for previous works on this topic, addressing the non-uniqueness of minimal disks in 3D space and generalizing the framework to higher-dimensional spaces. As a byproduct, this study also addresses the regularity of minimal disks in 3D space, demonstrating that multiple solutions can exist. This implies that a minimal disk in 3D space cannot have optimal regularity. As a further result, we establish that a minimal disk with optimal regularity must be highly symmetric, a concept formalized here as being "quasi-Steiner". This insight holds not just for disks, but for all minimal submanifolds with optimal regularity in any given space. As such, the term "quasi-Steiner" may be more generally applied to any such submanifold. We have computationally examined the behavior of carbon and nitrogen within interstitial and substitutional sites within TiO2 photocatalytic materials using a method that accounts for multiple bodies and electron excitations. Our results indicate that interstitial C and N exhibit more negative charges than their counterparts in a stable state, whereas the charges for substitutional C and N are less negative. This contrast highlights the difficulty of reducing these atoms with water. To rectify this issue, we suggest modifying TiO2 by introducing interstitial C or N to enhance their reducibility. Additionally, we found that combining TiO2 with liquid water results in the formation of hydroxyl groups on the surface, which can be removed through light exposure. This observation suggests that light-driven TiO2 reduction reactions may be hindered by water coverage, emphasizing the importance of treating redox reactions in relation to the reaction environment. Notably, the formation of O2 from water on TiO2 requires a significant energy barrier, indicating that other mechanisms may be necessary for oxygen evolution reactions. By utilizing the CMS detector's properties and accounting for possible sources of uncertainty, such as the scattering of the quark within the proton and the interaction between the incident and scattered particles, as well as the resulting compound state's being detected as a single particle instead of two, we've derived limits for the branching ratios of these flavor-changing neutral current decays. The X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) on the Athena X-ray Observatory will significantly contribute to the study of intra-cluster medium turbulence. X-IFU's high spatial and spectral resolution observations will enable the determination of gas velocity fields and turbulent properties across various scales. In this paper, we examine methods for estimating turbulence characteristics from X-IFU data, applying a multidimensional spectral analysis technique called the Velocity Template Match. This analysis involves comparing observed X-ray spectra with computationally generated spectra resulting from specific velocity field and abundance patterns. The best-matching templates then provide information on the directions, amplitudes, and probabilities associated with turbulent motions, allowing for the extraction of turbulence statistics. In a simulated observation of a galaxy cluster using an X-IFU bandpass, we demonstrate the ability to recover turbulent velocity field properties, including mean velocities, dispersion, and their relationships with spatial location, up to a 100 kpc radius. Additionally, we investigate how turbulence characteristics can be interpreted in the context of MHD wave theories, assuming solar-like wave properties, and discuss the potential for detecting turbulence signatures in MHD simulations matched to X-IFU data. The techniques presented in this paper can serve as a basis for further development of turbulence analysis methods using X-IFU data, in conjunction with MHD simulations, and may be extended to other X-ray observations. Nevertheless, the success of these techniques relies heavily on the availability of high-resolution X-ray simulations of galaxy clusters. In this paper, we also outline the requirements and the proposed strategy for developing a suite of high-resolution X-ray simulations of galaxy clusters, along with their turbulent counterparts, to effectively utilize X-IFU's capabilities. This suite, along with matching analysis techniques, will provide a powerful tool for interpreting X-IFU data and extracting valuable information on the intra-cluster medium's turbulent motions. Located at the heart of our galaxy lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a vast ring-shaped area. Researchers are particularly interested in the CMZ as it resides within the massive spiral arm known as the Long Norm Arm (LNA). By using the NANTEN2 submillimeter telescope to observe the LNA, scientists have gained insight into the structure of the CMZ and the LNA by analyzing the density and anisotropy of the region. Their analysis reveals that at smaller scales (approximately 100 parsecs), the density within the CMZ and LNA follows a similar pattern, indicating a linear relationship (rho_proportional_to r^-1.2). However, at larger scales (above 200 parsecs), the density within these areas begins to follow a different pattern, showing a significant discrepancy. Furthermore, by conducting a harmonic analysis of these regions, scientists have identified a prominent 180-degree sinusoidal pattern within the CMZ, attributing it to the influence of the LNA. It is suggested that the LNA may be exerting a level of pressure on the CMZ, causing it to curve in response. By estimating the total mass associated with this curve (approximately 8 million solar masses), as well as analyzing potential bar forces and the effects of molecular cloud collisions, scientists believe that the LNA may be responsible for shaping the CMZ over the past 10 million years. Ultimately, this research provides a new perspective on the formation and structure of the CMZ and offers a framework for continued study of this galactic region. It also highlights the capabilities of using spectral line mapping in conjunction with cloud tracing techniques to analyze complex molecular regions. By using this approach, scientists can gain a more comprehensive understanding of the dynamics and structure of these areas and identify potential signatures of local and global influences. It is hoped that this approach can be applied to other molecular regions across our galaxy, offering a new perspective on the formation and evolution of these areas. It is further suggested that this approach can be used in conjunction with numerical simulations and other analytical techniques to analyze molecular regions and shed light on the global physics at play within these areas. In particular, we found that qutrits are significantly more resistant to inaccurate measurements and spontaneous photon emissions, with some scenarios indicating a mass determination error less than 10^-4 even with substantial noise, in contrast to the much greater precision achieved when there is little to no noise. We explore the convergence of polynomial diameter for groups that are not solvable, building upon recent findings by Juhasz and Praeger, who demonstrated that a large class of polycyclic groups exhibit polynomial diameter. Our research extends their results to the broader category of finite group extensions and offers an alternative, more direct proof. Additionally, we establish connections between polynomial diameter, conjugacy classes, and nilpotent subgroups, as well as upper bounds for the number of conjugacy classes within certain classes of groups that possess polynomial diameter. Furthermore, our results identify key characteristics of groups with polynomial diameter, implying that such groups must contain nilpotent subgroups of a relatively large class, thereby reinforcing the significance of the class of monomial groups. Our study also presents an infinite family of irreducible SNARLs (simple non-abelian relatively free groups), demonstrating that many of these groups exhibit polynomial diameter, whereas some members of this family exhibit an exponential number of conjugacy classes. This discovery highlights the intricate nature of polynomial diameter within the realm of finite group theory. Our research is complemented by highly interactive computer-generated proofs for numerous results, aided by the development of new algorithms to compute the diameter of groups and their conjugacy classes. Among other things, this enables the derivation of upper bounds for the polynomial degree of a group diameter, as well as determining whether a given group has polynomial diameter in a reasonable time frame. Our study is also enriched by various generalizations and open questions posed throughout the paper. In particular, we present a classification of groups with polynomial diameter of a specific degree and examine the interconnections between some of these groups and their fundamental substructures, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms driving the convergence of polynomial diameter within the context of finite group theory. In doing so, our research establishes an intriguing connection between nitpickable groups and the class of groups with polynomial diameter, yielding an intriguing framework that is both accessible and comprehensive. This framework is then applied to various categories of groups that are not solvable, including the family of Steiner triple systems. In light of these findings, we propose numerous open questions and suggest directions for further research in this area. This work describes a temperature sensor designed for accuracy in harsh industrial environments.  The sensor utilizes a resistive thermistor with inconsistent and imprecise readings, so it requires a sophisticated digital signal processing platform based on an ADSP-21469 ARM Cortex-A9 dual-core MPU.  The algorithm converts the analog data at various temperatures and voltages applied to the thermistor, and a precise digital temperature reading is obtained by fitting a curve to the data using a mathematical technique called least-squares.  Exhaustive simulations and practical tests show that the proposed method yields highly accurate results, compatible with ISO/IEC 61131-2 for type K thermocouples, and produces a reliable reading in less than 5 milliseconds.  Developed in a MATLAB environment, the algorithm was successfully ported to the processing platform without modifications.  In addition to temperature measurement, the proposed sensor can also estimate the ambient temperature by processing data over a certain period, thus providing an advantage over conventional temperature sensors that offer only a single reading.  In terms of accuracy, the proposed sensor meets or exceeds typical sensor specifications found in the industry, and is an effective solution for controlling and monitoring industrial processes that involve high temperatures and electrical signals.  In combination with its low cost and high performance, this temperature sensor presents a compelling alternative to commercial temperature sensors and can also be applied to other thermal sensing applications, such as those involving thermocouples and bolometers.  Furthermore, the algorithm developed for this project can be adapted for use in medical temperature sensing applications by employing more sophisticated signal processing techniques that account for changes in blood flow and heat transfer between organs, thus providing a more accurate estimation of organ temperatures.  In this work, the algorithm was applied to estimate gastrointestinal temperatures, and simulations indicated a high degree of accuracy, but further research is required to validate these results in actual organ temperatures.  In order to facilitate replication and further development of the algorithm, the MATLAB code utilized in this project is included as supplementary material.  Additionally, the ADSP-21469 ARM Cortex-A9 dual-core MPU software platform used in this project is also available from the manufacturer as an open-source reference design.  In summary, this paper presents an innovative digital temperature sensor that utilizes a sophisticated algorithm to provide highly accurate readings for industrial applications, and the code developed in this project can be adapted for use in medical temperature sensing applications, such as estimating organ temperatures. This involves establishing a categorial correspondence between gerbes and their underlying groupoid extensions, which enables a morphism between two gerbes to be described as a homomorphism between their underlying groupoid extensions. Using the 1.3 cm [CI] radio line surveys of the Central Molecular Zone conducted by the ATLASGAL and the SFR survey of the Milky Way, a sample of 1037 massive protostar candidates was identified within 3.5 kpc of the Galactic Center. By examining the mass growth of 313 molecular cores associated with these protostar candidates, researchers found that about 30% of core mass increases due to accretion exceed the limits imposed by the Eddington limit, resulting in a mass growth rate that is directly proportional to time. This mass accumulation rate is highly unstable and can lead to the formation of massive stars. It is suggested that the Eddington limit plays a crucial role in regulating the core mass growth and star formation, implying that the Eddington limit could be a fundamental limit on the growth of molecular core mass. Researchers also found a maximum mass growth rate in low-density environments, and it decreases with increasing density. Consequently, highly dense core masses are limited by the birth of massive stars, while lower density core masses can either become massive stars or be consumed by the wind. This finding provides a possible solution to the massive core mass function paradox. It is proposed that the relationship between the Eddington limit and the birth of massive stars, accompanied by wind loss, could hold not just within our galaxy but also across the universe, as indicated by recent observations of distant galaxies. As a result, it is suggested that density-regulated star formation based on the Eddington limit could be a fundamental process affecting the mass scales of both molecular cores and stars. Furthermore, it is proposed that this process could lead to the formation of massive starless cores, and that the mass growth rate could lead to the formation of binary and multiple systems. Finally, it is suggested that this model could be applied to other galaxies across the universe.

Finite Godel algebras are intimately connected with finite forest languages, which are closed under preimage under morphisms. We establish that the duality between these algebras and forest languages is restricted to finite instances, yet still captures the fundamental nature of infinite Godel algebras within their infinite forest counterparts. Additionally, we prove that within the realm of infinite forest languages, those corresponding to Godel algebras contain no uncountable elements. This overarching framework allows us to classify several other mathematical systems, including Jonsson algebras, canonical algebras, and algebras of forests with specific properties. We then employ this classification to exhibit an ongoing complexity equivalence between the satisfiability problem for these systems and Godel algebras. This demonstrates a particular computational barrier within the realm of finite mathematical structures. We also explore the implications of our findings to the existing theory of finite Godel algebras and their corresponding forest languages. Moreover, we present an alternative approach to defining the complexity of a mathematical system based on the complexity of its underlying forest language. This new perspective enables us to establish a complexity hierarchy among various algebraic systems, including Jonsson algebras and canonical algebras, which can be based on the complexity of their corresponding forest languages. This hierarchy provides an equivalent structure to the existing Birkhoff's finite base theorem within the context of finite Godel algebras. We conclude by discussing an open question related to the computational properties of forest languages. This discussion is accompanied by a forest language that satisfies a certain condition and is computationally intractable, yet its underlying algebraic system has a computationally efficient description. This counterexample not only sheds light on the nature of forest languages but also implies that the complexity of an algebraic system is an incomplete measure of the computational intractability of its corresponding forest language. This perspective is further illuminated through the presentation of a family of finite Godel algebras whose complexities fluctuate erratically despite their underlying forest languages remaining computationally intractable across all members of this family. This phenomenon highlights the distinction between computational intractability within the context of forest languages and the computational intractability within the context of algebraic systems, thereby validating our new approach to defining the complexity of mathematical systems based on the complexity of their corresponding forest languages. This new framework also enables us to establish an infinite hierarchy of finite Godel algebras whose complexities are equivalent to any depth k of the arithmetical hierarchy. This achievement is made possible by our earlier results

Notably, our context-aware model achieved significant precision gains of up to 35% when considering individual classes, highlighting the importance of contextual information for LiDAR data classification. We also found that using neighbor information allowed for reduced sensor data at half the amount without compromising accuracy, thus implying potential battery life increases for mobile LiDAR sensors. Moreover, our context-aware approach proved adaptable to different data sampling rates and models, showing potential benefits for other LiDAR-based computer vision tasks. Finally, we found minimal performance degradation even with substantial changes in scene composition, suggesting our model's robustness in real-world applications. To facilitate replication and advancement of our research, we are providing the associated code and data in an open-source repository.
