In this research, the impact of classical differentiation and integration on the positivity of zonal functions is thoroughly examined. Furthermore, specific formulas are derived to compute the repeated derivatives and integrals of zonal functions in spherical coordinates. In addition, the study proves the uniqueness of approximating zonal functions through a series of circular buffers in a high-dimensional Euclidean space. Theoretical estimates and a special formula for the volume of zonal circles are also provided, along with applications to the computation of zonal functions and their variants. The proposed methods are demonstrated through concrete numerical examples and benchmark tests. Theoretical results are verified through specific proofs, drawing from techniques related to spherical harmonics, Gegenbauer polynomials, and Gelfand-Naimark-Segal constructs. The study also establishes connections to recent studies on the approximation of zonal functions. The Python implementation of the proposed methods is made available as an open-source package. The central part of the research is grounded in the context of Euclidean distance and spherical geometry, and an attempt is made to extend the results to the context of a broader metric distance. The study paves the way for further research on the application of zonal functions to the solution of differential and integral equations defined on the surface of a sphere. The IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole has significantly contributed to investigations of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and neutrinos, particularly in the field of multibillion-eV cosmic ray research. This paper summarizes the current status of searches for cosmic ray counterparts of neutrino sources, as well as new analyses looking for correlations between neutrinos and cosmic rays. Findings from the IceCube collaboration on neutrino-cosmic ray correlations remain consistent with random fluctuations, but a recent approach suggesting a possible connection between GZK candidates and neutrino sources requires further data to confirm its statistics-based significance. In addition, there are emerging indications that neutrino sources could be related to cosmic ray sources, with neutrinos potentially representing the low-energy counterpart of cosmic rays. To explore these connections more deeply, new analyses are being implemented to improve detection efficiencies and reduce background interference, including new methods for identifying neutral neutrino channels and suppressing light contamination in photon searches. These studies will significantly impact our understanding of the composition of extremely energetic cosmic neutrinos and, by extension, ultra-high-energy cosmic rays. The current status and future prospects for these investigations, as well as associated scientific implications, are discussed in this review paper. The long-term stability of liquid foams ultimately depends on their surface tension in relation to local geometry. A critical factor known as roughness, which reflects how closely packed soap bubbles are, determines this interaction. It affects viscosity in a nonlinear way and significantly impacts how quickly bubbles coalesce. Although the roughness factor has a substantial impact on these processes, it has not been directly monitored in previous studies, which has made it difficult to establish a clear relationship between roughness and the rate of fusion in liquid foams. This knowledge is essential for a comprehensive understanding of how viscosity influences how quickly liquid foams break down. This research introduces a new method for measuring the roughness factor in a way that is independent of both the 2D and 3D approaches previously used. It involves counting the number of neighboring spheres that influence a given sphere in a three-dimensional context. By utilizing this new definition, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the roughness factor across various stages of foam evolution, including its early development and the effects of sphere packing and friction on its structure. Our research reveals that the roughness factor plays a critical role in the nonlinear relationship between foam viscosity and surface tension. It also explains why foams with high viscosity can persist even when the surface tension is low. Furthermore, our study found that the rate of fusion in liquids is primarily governed by the roughness factor rather than viscosity. This finding challenges the widely accepted idea that forces of repulsion control the rate of fusion, instead suggesting that forces of attraction may play a more significant role. Our research provides a theoretical framework that can be applied to different sizes and types of spheres and also offers computational software that can be used for various numerical analyses. In our research, we successfully applied ensemble learning to convolutional neural networks to resolve the overfitting issue when they're applied to the Anhui University Brain Tumor (AUBT) dataset. We utilized Decoupled Neural Embedding and End-to-End data augmentation to create a diverse set of base CNNs, resulting in a significant improvement in classification accuracy from 54.45% to 61.29%. Additionally, our method achieved a notable gain in robustness, as evidenced by a reduced gap between model performance on labeled and unlabeled data from 11.09% to 3.53%. Our ensemble model demonstrated the highest precision among competing approaches in the MICCAI Braintumor Competition 2017, ranking first in both validation and testing sets. Notably, our study surpasses the current state-of-the-art AUBT dataset methods, with an overall classification accuracy of 65.19%. We have made our code and model publicly available on the MMACII GitHub repository.

We investigate the idea of work done by a system in thermodynamic equilibrium, using the example of a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator to illustrate our points. We consider two primary measures of work: total work and the average of work done on individual microstates, which we call "microwork." By examining the oscillator's equilibrium distribution, we calculate the average total work and microwork done on its microstates. We find that both the total work and microwork have a maximum value and can be negative, indicating that there is a concept of work done by a system in equilibrium. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between work done by the system and its heat capacity, demonstrating that there is a connection between work and the system's thermal energy. Specifically, the work done on the harmonic oscillator is directly proportional to its thermal energy, and this relationship can be expressed through the Boltzmann constant. Finally, we discuss how our findings generalize to more complex systems, using the example of a linear lattice of harmonic oscillators to illustrate the concept of over-damped microwork and how it decay's exponentially with time. Consequently, our study suggests that the concept of work done by a system in thermal equilibrium is worthy of further exploration in both theoretical and experimental research. The CCH and CN spectra were analyzed to determine relative abundance, which showed that cyclopentadiene has a higher CCH to CN ratio than benzene does. Consider a neural machine translation system that uses a look-ahead attention mechanism, allowing the model to focus on parts of the target sentence that are relevant to future words. We've analyzed the attention states and decoding histories of this system and discovered a problem: the introduction of this mechanism causes the model to consistently pay attention to incorrect previous targets during translation. We've investigated the source of this issue by examining additional factors including training methods, attention types, and model architectures. Our findings suggest that heavy use of the look-ahead attention can lead to unstable optimization and increase the risk of erroneous attention on previous targets. We've also found that alternative training methods and other attention designs can mitigate this effect to some degree. We've developed a simple solution to fix the problem by adding a cumulative sum of the look-ahead attention weights as an auxiliary target, leading to significant improvements in translation quality. With this solution, we've achieved significant gains using the look-ahead attention mechanism, resulting in improvements of up to +1.3 BLEU points over the baseline system. We've explored different factors that influence the performance with this attention design and uncovered interesting relationships with factors such as source sentence length, translation direction, and system scalability. We've also conducted evaluations using more stringent metrics including human evaluation and semi-automatic post-editing, yielding comparable results and demonstrating the reliability of our findings. We've made our code and data available for further research and improvement of the look-ahead attention design. We've established a new baseline for neural machine translation with the look-ahead attention mechanism and have set the stage for subsequent studies to build upon our work. We've explored various factors influencing the performance of this attention design, have achieved notable gains using it, and have established a new benchmark for neural machine translation. We've made our code and data available for further research and look forward to seeing improvements to this design in the future. We apply the causal dynamical theory to modify the Einstein field equations, using a linear-rational form for the bulk viscosity coefficient in a viscous fluid model. By solving the modified equations in a flat Friedmann-Robertson-Walker universe with constant positive $k$, we analyze the universe's evolution when the linear-rational viscosity coefficient changes from a negative to a non-negative value at a certain cosmological time. This transition is modeled to occur at the grand unified theory era. Through our calculations, we find that the universe's evolution from this point on can be described by a Big Chill era, followed by a rapid expansion leading to the emergence of structure in the universe. Additionally, we derive a specific quadratic equation that relates the universe's temperature to its age, which implies that the universe experienced a period of accelerated expansion at the GUT era, and that this acceleration cannot be attributed to a constant negative viscosity coefficient. Instead, it may be an indication of the GUT symmetry being related to the symmetry found in the causal dynamical theory. Furthermore, we present a condition for the GUT phase to be connected to the present day phase. We also examine the possibility of the GUT era being followed by an inflationary era, and present a condition for this scenario to occur. Finally, we estimate the relevance of this research to current observational data. Specifically, we find that our model predicts a very low matter-antimatter asymmetry, which is consistent with the observed ratio of matter to antimatter in the universe. We also find that our model predicts a value for the primordial abundance of neutrinos, which is in line with more recent estimates based on cosmic microwave background radiation and large scale structure. Lastly, we note that our model also offers an explanation for the linear-rational form of the viscosity coefficient, which may be an intrinsic property of the gravitational interaction, and that this form may have implications for the behavior of gravity in high-energy regimes. In recent years, research on curiosity has expanded to examine social aspects, particularly how peers influence an individual's curiosity. Our study explores this in a mobile learning setting, where participants' curiosity about mystery objects is triggered and satisfied through interactions with peers who have encountered these objects. Our results from a between-subjects experiment reveal that participants' curiosity about mystery objects is piqued when they learn that peers have also experienced these objects, and that they can learn more from peers who have similar curiosity profiles. Furthermore, our data indicate that learners' motivation to take action and learn from peers is increased when they perceive these peers as similar to themselves. Our approach offers a novel framework for modeling curiosity in social learning situations and can be integrated into existing game engines used for mobile learning. This enables the development of more effective curiosity-driven social learning games for mobile devices. In addition, our system can provide data for analyzing the activation and satisfaction dynamics of curiosity in a socially influenced learning environment. For feasibility, our study was conducted on a small scale using a mobile game developed specifically for the experiment. In future work, our highly dynamic model of curiosity could be applied to complex learning environments, and our social learning approach could be expanded to capture the long-term effects of social influences on curiosity. For now, our model and system are available online at https://github.com/ali8733/curiosity_spring19. In future work, we also plan to investigate the activation and satisfaction dynamics of curiosity in a socially influenced learning environment on a larger scale. For this, we propose a highly dynamic model of curiosity that can handle complex learning situations and incorporate previous experiences and emotions into consideration. In this model, activation and satisfaction of curiosity are intertwined and affected by multiple factors, including learning goals, emotions, previous experiences, and social influences. According to this model, curiosity can be satisfied through both internal and social means, and satisfaction of curiosity can trigger various emotions, which in turn can influence curiosity again in a recursive cycle. We investigate the application of graph Matérn Gaussian processes at larger scales, addressing challenges associated with mini-batch sampling and non-conjugate models. To tackle these issues, we develop a full-conditional distribution for the latent function values and a pseudo-likelihood function suitable for optimization. These innovations enable the use of graph Matérn Gaussian processes within stochastic gradient descent and Bayesian optimization frameworks, and we further explore their connection to deep neural networks by establishing a linear regression model that shares a similar posterior with a neural network. Our methodological developments lead to scalable and efficient algorithms for graph Matérn Gaussian processes, making them feasible for large graphs and models. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approaches through synthetic data analysis and real-world applications, including the prediction of gene expression and multi-task learning in image classification. Our implementation is available in the GraphGANx Python package.

In monitoring the movement of people and objects within an urban environment, a network of mobile sensors attached to ridesourcing vehicles can offer exceptional coverage and high reliability. However, these mobile sensors have limited observation capabilities compared to traditional static sensors with integrated vision systems. Optimizing the movement of these mobile sensors to maximize their coverage area is a complex problem that requires balancing the need to monitor specific areas regularly against the need to explore new areas. In this paper, we develop a discrete-time model that captures the movement of these mobile sensors and their coverage area, and then create a stochastic optimization algorithm to determine the most efficient way to move these sensors and their integrated sensors within the environment. Our solution involves developing a multi-armed bandit model that incorporates time discretization and spatial correlation between the sensors, and our results show that our algorithm outperforms alternative strategies that do not consider the sensors' movement. Furthermore, our model can be applied to various urban surveillance scenarios by adjusting the parameters of the model. We also present computational results showing that our algorithm excels in a simulated scenario compared to static optimization solutions, and that the sensors' movement has a substantial impact on the algorithm's performance. In addition, we present a case study applying our algorithm to an actual city environment with actual ride-hailing data and findings. Our code is openly accessible and can be adapted to suit specific surveillance needs in the community. In the long run, our algorithm contributes to a more effective use of urban sensor networks composed of ridesourcing vehicles, leading to potential reductions in energy consumption, minimization of ride requests, and adjustment of sensor placement to optimize coverage. Ultimately, our model paves the way for a deeper exploration of urban surveillance through mobile sensing, encouraging the development of novel algorithms and the utilization of machine learning techniques. In the future, we intend to extend our model by integrating additional vehicles in the network, factoring time costs for moving these sensors, and incorporating additional sensors with distinct observation capabilities. In the process, we will tackle computational challenges by employing approximate optimization methods, leveraging meta-heuristics, and comparing the performance of these approaches. In the context of the case study, we aim to collaborate with ridesourcing companies and municipal authorities to implement our recommendations in a real-world setting. In the future, we also plan to explore new research avenues in the field of urban mobile sensing, such as modeling the co-existence of human observers within the sensing network and investigating new machine learning approaches to analyze the data collected by these mobile sensors. Researchers have established constraints on the cross-sectional area of nucleon-scattering dark matter using lattice QCD, specifically for the process where a dark matter particle excites a hadron from the vacuum. These studies have focused mainly on visible decay modes, such as the case of the $J/\psi$ meson decaying to muons or electrons. However, for particles like the $\tau$ lepton or the $B$ meson, where hadronic decays are more probable, constraints based on visible decay modes may be less informative. In this work, we utilize lattice QCD to determine the decay rate of the $J/\psi$ meson to invisible particles, specifically dark matter, and demonstrate how this information can be incorporated into existing analyses placing limits on dark matter-nucleon interaction cross-sections. In doing so, we establish a more comprehensive set of limits on the cross-section for this process, taking into account both visible and invisible decay modes, and find that the invisible decay mode places the most stringent lower bound on the cross-section at $5.25 \times 10^{-19}$ GeV$^{-2}$, a more stringent limit than derived from visible decay modes alone. Furthermore, we establish a more precise effective field theory for treating the $J/\psi$-DM system and present a thorough evaluation of theoretical uncertainties associated with this process. In addition, we provide guidelines for implementing these results in existing direct detection experiments and proposed future sensors, and discuss the potential for detecting the dark matter component in experimental data that has already been collected, such as in the SEoul Dark Matter Experiment, the Large Underground Xenon Experiment, and the Dark Matter Experiment at the Los Alamos National Laboratory, assuming no signal detection thresholds are applied. If such experimental data can be analyzed with an appropriate technique for this problem, we estimate that in some cases, such as in the case of 1 GeV dark matter particles and a certain interaction strength, it may be possible to identify the dark matter component in excess recoil event spectra at a 90% confidence level. Finally, we establish the connection between these results and recent findings on the dark matter form factor, presenting the latter in a way that directly relates to the cross-section for this process. In doing so, we clarify the meaning and implications of this quantity in the context of direct detection and outline the path for deriving model-independent constraints on the dark matter form factor using this approach. We develop a new variable stepsize Stochastic Generalized Linear Models (SGLM) estimator for autoregressive and linear mixed models, enabling us to adapt the sampling period based on previous data observations. This variable stepsize approach results in an expanding grid of observations, in contrast to the fixed stepsize method which corresponds to a uniform grid. Theoretical convergence rates for the variable stepsize estimator are derived, showing that an increased rate of convergence results from approximating the finite difference operator on an expanding grid. A correlation structure adaptive algorithm is also proposed and empirically evaluated on simulated and real-world datasets, yielding superior performance compared to traditional fixed stepsize estimators. The results highlight the variable stepsize estimator's ability to balance increased bias due to grid expansion with improved variance reduction resulting from a more targeted sampling approach. The variable stepsize estimator outperforms the fixed stepsize estimator across various datasets and settings, ultimately demonstrating its potential as a superior alternative. The code is freely accessible online.

A fundamental challenge in real-world data analysis, such as temporal temperature curve prediction or scene classification using remote sensing images, is tackling the issue of missing or corrupted data. While recent advances in missing data imputation have primarily focused on individual sequence completion, the task now encompasses not only filling in missing entries but also removing noisy data from the entire input array. To address this comprehensive problem, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Frequency Spectral Summation Autoencoder (MFSSA). This innovative approach includes a customized encoder with frequency-sensitive layers and a multi-frequency decoder that utilizes concatenation and addition modules to successfully handle both missing and noisy data across the frequency spectrum. The impressive performance of our proposed framework is evident when tested on three diverse datasets, showcasing superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art methods during extensive experiments on multiple datasets. Moreover, our innovative approach achieves curtailed performance degradation when confronted with unknown frequency spectra. This groundbreaking work is now available as an open-source repository on GitHub at https://github.com/ghulam-eiman/MFSSA. The code has been successfully executed on NVIDIA GPUs and can be executed on local machines as well.

This paper introduces a novel framework called Multi-Frequency Spectral Summation Autoencoder (MFSSA) that simultaneously handles missing and noisy data across the frequency spectrum for real-world data analysis, such as temporal temperature curve prediction or scene classification using remote sensing images. Unlike conventional missing data imputation that focuses on individual sequence completion, MFSSA encompasses filling in missing entries and removing noisy data from the entire input array. The innovative approach includes a customized encoder with frequency-sensitive layers and a multi-frequency decoder that utilizes concatenation and addition modules, achieving superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art methods when tested on three diverse datasets. Moreover, our innovative approach achieves curtailed performance degradation when confronted with unknown frequency spectra. This groundbreaking work is now available as an open-source repository on GitHub at https://github.com/ghulam-einan/MFSSA. The code has been successfully executed on NVIDIA GPUs and can be executed on local machines as well.

This study investigates how the population dynamics of the target insect, Colorado potato beetle, are influenced by the application of entomopathogenic nematodes. The research aims to identify optimal strategies for using nematodes as a biological control method within a integrated pest management plan for the long-term cultivation of potatoes. The model accounts for the birth rate and death rate of the beetles in relation to their population size, as well as the impact of nematodes on birth and death rates, and considers the possibility of delayed nematode effects. Furthermore, the model incorporates the influence of prey prey on the nematodes and their birth and death rates. To find the optimal control strategy, the study simulates and analyzes different management scenarios at both the local and global levels using numerical methods and multi-nomial search algorithms. The outcomes show that when the population of the prey prey is small, the birth rate of the nematodes remains relatively low, while the death rate of the beetles increases, leading to a decline in the beetle population. However, the model also reveals that the nematodes can provide temporary relief but ultimately fail to control the population in the absence of further chemical treatment. The analysis identifies several optimal control strategies, including the total destruction of the beetle population through comprehensive use of the nematodes, the stable coexistence of the beetle and nematode populations, and the selective control of the beetle population through targeted use of the nematodes. The study also explores the possibility of early warning signs indicating the need for chemical treatment in response to increasing beetle populations despite the presence of the nematodes. The results highlight the potential of the model to inform decision-making within an IPM plan for the sustainable cultivation of potatoes. Nucleus detection is a fundamental image analysis step in cytology. Accurate and efficient detection of multiple nuclei in a single image remains a challenge. Most cytology analysis methods rely on sequential nucleus detection, applying each as an image input, thereby increasing processing time. To address this issue, we present a novel W-shaped network that simultaneously identifies all nuclei within an image. The proposed network achieves enhanced efficiency and accuracy by leveraging a unique composite decoder, which refrains from concatenating feature maps. Instead, it employs an additive strategy for the detection branch, thus reducing redundant information and dimensionality. By testing the W-shaped network on multiple datasets, we demonstrate its superior performance and enhanced efficiency compared to traditional methods and the baseline encoder-decoder architecture. The proposed approach exhibits a notable improvement in average precision and a significant reduction in parameters. To further validate the W-shaped network, we conducted a convergence analysis of the training process. Ultimately, the model's performance exhibits improved generalizability and can be applied to cytological image analysis. For a given graph G, a Hamiltonian path index (HPI) is defined as the minimum number of independent sets required to cover all possible Hamiltonian paths within G. In this study, we explore the concept of HPI in relation to certain graph properties. Specifically, we investigate the Hamiltonian path index of block graphs in relation to their degree properties. Our main contribution involves establishing upper and lower limits for the Hamiltonian path index of block graphs in relation to their maximum degree. Our findings also extend to a broader class of outer-planar graphs known as Halin graphs. For block graphs, our analysis yields an initial estimation of HPI, which is then refined to determine a more precise upper limit in relation to its number of vertices. Our research on Halin graphs leads to the identification of a more complex relationship between its degree properties and HPI. To solve the problem, we developed a new algorithm for identifying hamiltonian paths in linear time complexity. This new approach improves our understanding of the hamiltonian path index and may have implications for research on other covering problems in graph theory. Our research on block graphs provides upper and lower limits for the hamiltonian path index in relation to its maximum degree, and our findings on Halin graphs reveal a more complex degree-dictated hamiltonian path index. By adapting the model to account for travel and using the least squares method for data fitting, we successfully estimate key parameters including the average time individuals spend outside their homes and the effective reproduction number. Lastly, we outline the potential advantages of incorporating pharmacological treatments into the model and present a scenario where this could be applied with the case of Guadeloupe. Identifying external influences that impact an RL system is crucial for its effectiveness. We propose a novel method called Exogenous Discovery via Counterfactual Learning (EDCL) that uses a different perspective to detect the impact of external factors on RL systems. By leveraging counterfactual learning, EDCL identifies actions with significant effects on real-world outcomes by comparing them to outcomes in imaginary scenarios. The algorithm works within a broad framework that includes various reward learning scenarios and utilizes offline data. EDCL's key benefit is its ability to find the few critical actions that have a substantial impact on real-world outcomes, even when confronted with a large number of actions that have little effect. The algorithm's performance is demonstrated through numerical evaluations utilizing real-world datasets, along with a case study of its application in collaborative recommendation systems. The results show that EDCL effectively identifies action variables with a big effect in various scenarios and can be utilized to enhance counterfactual reward learning for offline data. This research presents HELMHOLTZ, a verification tool developed in HOL4 for Michelson code used in Tezos, a popular blockchain platform supporting peer-to-peer transactions through smart contracts. Verifying code correctness in Michelson programmatically is challenging due to its limited reference capabilities and the absence of a static type checker. Consequently, errors often result from mismatched instruction sets or incorrect operation combinations. To address this issue, HELMHOLTZ offers a set of definitions and algorithms to accurately verify code integrity, including a checker for static types and a mechanism for correct execution validation. Furthermore, the implementation includes a tool to automatically generate counterexamples from verification failures, enabling rapid debugging within Tezos' development environment, Nomad. By leveraging HOL4's built-in functions for automatic proof exploration and counterexample generation, HELMHOLTZ can detect potential execution flaws and present them in a usable format for improvement. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the project applies HELMHOLTZ to a set of existing contract vulnerabilities and presents its verification outcomes along with counterexamples generated by the tool. Contrary to existing ad-hoc methods for verifying contract integrity, this research showcases the feasibility of utilizing formal verification for Michelson code through the HELMHOLTZ approach. Furthermore, the project contributes its code to the public domain for the benefit of the Tezos community. To facilitate further research, the project also includes a set of definitions and algorithms that can be adapted for verification of other programming languages and architectures. Ultimately, the success of blockchain-based smart contracts relies heavily on the reliability of their underlying programming languages and verification tools, making the contribution of the project a valuable step towards improving the quality and security of such contracts. Upon further analysis, it becomes apparent that this discrepancy arises from an incorrect identification of conserved charges using the standard procedure of Bardeen, Horowitz, and Myerson. As a result, we've demonstrated that this incorrect identification leads to an inaccurate determination of the entropy. Consequently, it can be shown that the correct formula for entropy does indeed align with that predicted by the general theory of relativity. This specific scenario provides a concrete example of how the usual rules governing the relationship between entropy and other conserved charges can be violated in theories of gravity with the inclusion of higher derivatives, where new terms in the entropy formula can arise without a corresponding increase in the number of other conserved charges. Notably, research on using deep neural networks to estimate tissue displacement from ultrasound images has yielded promising results. However, most elastography applications, including those using deep learning, have focused exclusively on predicting lateral or axial displacement. This paper proposes a novel approach with two distinct estimation models, one each for lateral and axial displacement, leveraging their unique imaging characteristics. Specifically, the axial displacement estimation was found to be more accurate than lateral displacement estimation. Existing studies primarily utilized traditional gradient-based optimization methods. In contrast, this research introduced a elastography formulation that was solved by stochastic gradient descent, enabling the efficient training of non-convex loss functions for uncertainty reduction. The proposed approach was tested using simulated images and real-world data, demonstrating superior performance compared to models estimating a single displacement value and models addressing both displacement components simultaneously. Furthermore, the results showed reduced standard deviation in both displacement estimates and significant improvements in elastography contrast, ultimately enhancing the visual distinction between soft and hard tissues. Traditional program pseudocodes serve as a medium for program descriptions, however, research into the formal analysis of such pseudocodes is scarce due to their frequently inaccurate nature. In contrast, logical pseudocodes are designed with precision and safety in mind, incorporating elements from formal descriptions, specification languages, and traditional programming pseudocodes. These codes balance the need for clarity in description and precision in specification, making them ideal subjects for the formal analysis that program developers intend to ultimately use. In this paper, we outline the capabilities of our automated tool to perform a trio of analyses - format checking, satisfiability checking, and reachability analysis - on logical pseudocodes with no prior knowledge of the program under consideration. Furthermore, we showcase the efficacy of our approach by applying it to a set of real-world examples in the area of configuration management. Specifically, we utilize our tool to conduct a trio of analyses on real-world configuration policies written in a system-specific configuration language, and based on our findings, our approach proves to be an efficient and reliable method for checking the correctness and safety of logical pseudocodes. A one-pass algorithm for creating a smaller representation of data, known as a coreset, can be used to speed up approximate solutions to clustering problems like $k$-means. Previously, constructing a coreset for $k$-means required multiple passes through the data, but in our research, we developed an efficient one-pass method to create a small set of representative points that maintains the same clustering structure as the original data. Our solution works by assigning each data point to the nearest centroid and then creating a coreset consisting of the $k$ most frequent cluster assignments. We showed that with $O(k^2 n^{m-2})$ sample space and computation, our coreset accurately reflects the clustering structure present in the data, where $m$ is the dimensionality of the data. Results from comprehensive evaluations reveal our method achieves remarkable speed and accuracy improvements, surpassing traditional approaches in runtime and accuracy, while matching or outperforming their performance metrics. Furthermore, our innovative technique succeeds in complex scenarios where more basic grid-based algorithms struggle, all while utilizing a remarkably compact policy. An n-tuple of positive integers is considered nonstandard if it meets the following criteria: at least one of its components is greater than 1, and not all of its components are equal. A nonstandard n-tuple is classified as nontransitive if its components do not satisfy the condition required for standard n-tuples. In this paper, we explore the applicability of the Fouvry-Haliassos-Sarzana variety theorem to nontransitive n-tuples, specifically examining the case where one of the components is very large. This investigation enables us to establish an upper limit for the first component of nonstandard 3-tuples that are nontransitive, provided one of the other components exceeds SquaresRoot(n). This finding significantly improves a previous result by Chen and Liu and extends the existing lower limit for SquaresRoot(n) in [1]. Moreover, this research also enables us to prove a higher density for short nontransitive 4-tuples, where one of the components is 2, and provide additional insights into the distribution of nontransitive 3-tuples and 4-tuples. This work is a natural continuation of the research discussed in [2]. This paper is also accompanied by a companion paper titled "Small nonstandard 3-tuples II: Further analysis of large numbers" that delves into the examination of very large nonstandard 3-tuples. This investigation is part of the broader project aimed at investigating the impact of using larger nonstandard 3-tuples on polynomial mod p identities, a topic that was initially explored in [3]. This research is also closely related to the work presented in [4]. In this paper, we focus exclusively on the analysis of nonstandard 3-tuples, in contrast to the companion paper, which will present a comprehensive investigation of nonstandard 4-tuples. This study offers a fresh perspective on using adaptive instance normalization layers within cycleGANs to create photo-sketch conversion models. Our research reveals that AdaIN layers are actually "opposite" learning modules, effectively reversing the mapping they were learned with. By incorporating these "opposite" layers into the generator, the learned source-to-target mapping is cancelled out, while a target-to-source mapping is learned instead. To circumvent the difficulty of directly training these "opposite" layers, we propose an alternative training method that first pre-trains the AdaIN layers with a fixed learned source-to-target mapping, and then fine-tunes the "opposite" layers to obtain a target-to-source mapping. Our research demonstrates that by leveraging these "opposite" layers, cycleGANsachieve accurate photo-sketch conversion performance, outperforming the original cycleGANs on various datasets and evaluation metrics. The proposed method also facilitates semi-supervised sketch synthesis, enabling the generation of more realistic and varied sketches from text labels. Notably, our research demonstrates the generative capability of extending non-base classes (categories not included in the training set), successfully synthesizing sketches for categories that were not directly trained on. The proposed method's code is openly available at https://github.com/zhtsai2/OPA-CycleGAN.

We introduce a new multi-modal dialog representation model that utilizes joint training with multiple views. This model incorporates a diverse set of tasks and score functions, each reflecting a unique aspect of dialog understanding, to produce a unified dialog representation. Unlike existing methods that typically focus on a single task, our model leverages a set of task-score functions with distinct parameters to represent complex dialog dynamics. To facilitate concurrent training of multiple views without interference, we employ a dynamic layer normalization technique, capturing underlying dialog representation patterns while normalizing variables specific to each view. As a result, our model achieves significant improvements over baseline models in multiple settings, showcasing the potential of multi-view dialog representation for understanding human language. The code and data utilized in this research are openly accessible at https://github.com/ghrua/MultiViewDialog.

By analyzing quasi-hole and quasi-particle RHB wave functions within a range of deformations, we identify patterns of high-spin state formation and destroy them using the RHB method. Additionally, our results indicate that multiple rotational states can coexist in deformed halo nuclei, leading to distinct configuration combinations that affect overall shape and density distribution. As such, we propose adjusting traditional definition criteria for deformed halo nuclei. Our study also reveals that volume preservation, a hallmark of traditional halo nuclei, may not apply in their deformed counterparts. Recent video super-resolution models have achieved impressive results due to the effectiveness of convolutional neural networks. However, most of these models fail to optimize memory efficiency, resulting in limited use in real-world applications. To address this challenge, this paper improves the BasicVSR model's performance and computational efficiency. The enhanced model, called BasicVSR++, utilizes a novel frame sampling strategy and adapts the attention mechanism to improve processing efficiency. By refining the encoder and decoder components with additional layers, BasicVSR++ significantly outperforms the original model, achieving a 12.71% improvement in PSNR. Furthermore, the use of a sub-pixel covariance map enhances detail preservation, resulting in a 7.43% improvement in SSIM. In terms of computational efficiency, BasicVSR++ demonstrates a 23.08% reduction in GMACs compared to the original model, allowing for real-time video super-resolution processing. Extensive experiments validate the model's performance and reliability across different scales, frame rates, and video sources. The source code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/BasicVSR++.

This paper provides the parton distribution functions (PDFs) for W and Z bosons, which can be accessed through the MSTW fit website. Additionally, we outline the impact of these distributions on logarithmic corrections in QCD, specifically their universality at any level of precision. Our analysis demonstrates that the previously mentioned corrections increase the PDF uncertainty by at least 100% across the entire $x$ range and become a major contributor to theoretical accuracy at LHC energies. To mitigate this effect, future PDFs must accurately capture logarithmic precision alongside experimental data. To facilitate this goal, we present scale-variant corrections to $f_c$, which exhibit notable $x$ dependence and could serve as a key indicator for assessing the quality of PDFs. These findings emphasize the significance of studying PDF evolution beyond the extraction of central values and determine the relevant uncertainty quantities for PDFs to be useful for logarithmically accurate predictions in QCD. Consequently, our research will contribute positively to more precise theoretical calculations for processes involving vector bosons in future experiments at the LHC.

This issue can be mitigated by training a dynamics model using a variety of task distributions. However, this approach is impractical when working with complex state spaces and requiring a large number of samples. An alternative solution involves using ensembles of simple linear models trained on substantially smaller datasets. These models are inadequate on their own but effective in combination, producing a reliable prediction on complex states via mutual voting. In 1936, Godel demonstrated that any formal mathematical system capable of significant expression has inherently flawed proofs, leading to a variation of his first incompleteness theorem by Rosser in 1936. Building on this, we prove that within such a formal system, there will always exist an unprovable yet true statement within a specific set of arithmetical formulas that not only exists theoretically but can be empirically discovered within a vast range of numbers. Additionally, we demonstrate the practical application of this by creating a formal system in which a specific, empirically verifiable statement is both unprovable and true. Furthermore, we establish that this statement's empirical validity can serve as the foundation for further mathematical derivations within the same formal system. Consequently, this implies the existence of an infinite sequence of statements that are both unprovable and true within the formal system. These statements, in turn, have implications on the fundamental concepts of computability and decidability within the same formal system. Ultimately, this leads to the possibility of constructing a formal system in which a universal arbitrator program, capable of evaluating the validity of statements within the system, will enter an infinite loop when attempting to determine the validity of itself or a similarly constructed program. This has significant ramifications on the concept of computability and the feasibility of self-referential arithmetical theories within formal systems. Our work is based on an enhanced version of the Diagonalization Lemma and incorporates novel applications of the Cantor Space and the Beta function across ordinal numbers. Our proofs are constructed with a focus on clarity, using simple and straightforward arguments across multiple domains, including computability, formal systems, arithmetic, logic, and programming, with additional discussion on further implications and potential future research. Ultimately, our work serves as an exploration of the fundamental capabilities and limitations of formal systems, with a focus on the interplay between empirical discovery and formal proof within these systems. Hadamard's three circles theorem can be extended to a broader class of functions known as monogenic functions, which are fundamental in harmonic analysis for higher dimensions. Initially, this proof is presented for the monogenic case using a method different from Hadamard's original approach. Subsequently, the argument is broadened to cover Arendt's generalised version of Hadamard's three circles theorem. Finally, applications to both the original and Arendt's versions are given, demonstrating how they can be utilized to derive growth estimates for specific functions. Specifically, this results section demonstrates that both the original and Arendt's versions of Hadamard's three circles theorem yield the same estimated rate of growth for these functions. Lastly, an illustration highlights how the proposed approach can be applied to show the boundedness of a particular operator. This operator is subsequently shown to be bounded by a combination of the Riesz operators and volume potentials, both of which are well-studied in the context of monogenic functions. This paper's main contributions are presented in a way that showcases their own significance while also providing a broader understanding of the underlying theories. Consequently, many of the main concepts can be appreciated through this paper's exclusive presentation, without the need for additional background knowledge. Additionally, the paper also presents several novel applications to both the original and Arendt's versions of Hadamard's three circles theorem, as well as an illustration of the proposed approach's applicability to operator theory. Generalized balanced sampling (GBS) is an adaptable version of the randomized response technique, used to protect respondents' confidentiality while gathering data. A novel, non-interactive algorithm is introduced in this paper to select a balanced sample efficiently. Currently, the only available method for choosing a GBS involves interacting with an administrator who randomizes the results. In our proposed solution, the client can independently select a balanced sample. Although the client's selection may not be perfectly balanced due to the randomization process, the probability of an appropriate selection is significantly high. As a result, the security provided by this non-interactive approach is acceptable. Our evaluation indicates that the probability of an appropriate selection exceeds 1 - 10^(-n) when n is the number of items in the sample. In addition, our approach requires minimal modifications to existing data protection protocols. In particular, our solution can be applied to the GBS protocol described in "Protecting Respondents' Confidentiality in Statistical Studies," which was published by Sun and Weng in 2019. Our solution enhances their approach by reducing the communication overhead between the administrator and clients. A common challenge in camera calibration involves estimating a linear function mapping image coordinates to real-world coordinates. This task is often approached using non-linear least squares minimization with explicit position and re-projection constraints. In this study, a direct regression approach is examined as an alternative. Specifically, a linear transformation from two images to 3D points is represented by a matrix with three times the number of degrees freedom than necessary, and the extra variables are eliminated using the method of differentiation. Two approaches are explored to impose the constraints: using regularizers and geometric constraints. An extensive analysis of direct regression versus traditional methods is conducted using various public datasets, and the results show that direct regression yields similar accuracy with significantly reduced alignment iterations. Notably, one of the novel approaches developed in this paper achieves comparable precision to state-of-the-art methods but surpasses them in speed. Consequently, direct regression could provide a more efficient solution for real-time camera calibration applications. Moreover, this paper also explores multi-camera calibration, addressing a notable omission in the existing literature. The authors demonstrate that their proposed method not only applies to single-camera calibration but is equally effective in more complex scenarios, and the associated code is openly available for community use. In the analysis section, various implementation details and comparisons to classic approaches are discussed, followed by evaluations of the proposed methods on publicly accessible datasets, including images with low signal-to-noise ratios, images obtained using fish-eye lenses, and real-world data captured with a mobile device. Ultimately, the findings prove that direct regression yields comparable precision to traditional methods but offers a key advantage in speed, particularly useful for real-time calibration applications. Additionally, a demonstration of the method's applicability to multi-camera calibration is conducted, confirming that the proposed approach can efficiently solve complex calibration problems. This paper introduces a novel application of the conditional Wasserstein gan, which proves beneficial in imaging inverse problems by generating accurate posterior samples. Typically, the posterior distribution is explored using markov chain monte carlo methods or stochastic gradient variational inference. By training a conditional gan with a regularized loss function, we leverage the posterior energy as a discriminator and utilize the optimal transport distance as a generator loss, which results in a cWGAN model. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by reconstructing images in two scenarios: one with a combinatorial matrix multiplication problem and another with a computational magnetic resonance imaging example. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves high-quality images and outperforms traditional methods in certain cases. The cWGAN-based reconstruction process is also efficient, with a significant reduction in sampling computations. Furthermore, we examine the impact of introducing noise to the measurement data and provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed method's performance. Finally, we provide a implementation of the proposed method on mr imaging. The code for the proposed method is publicly available at https://github.com/xuefeng1993/Conditional- Wasserstein-GAN. We investigate a deep neural network model called a cascaded network, which can efficiently capture long-term quasi-periodic signal patterns within speech, and use it to improve speech separation based on a single mixed speech signal. By dividing a complex signal into multiple frequency bands and developing models tailored to each band, we developed a cascaded network that can model ongoing speech patterns within a single pass of the data. Additionally, we incorporated a feedback mechanism into the network to enable the modeling of overlapping speech, which allows for the successful separation of two utterances even when one speaker talks over the other. Our experiments demonstrate significant improvements in speech separation, achieving a mean opinion score (MOS) improvement of 0.15 when compared to the baseline model and 0.07 when compared to the current state-of-the-art technique, and verifying the effectiveness of the cascaded network structure and the use of overlapping speech data. Furthermore, our method proves versatile as it can be applied to various speech separation tasks, including demonstrations on recorded audio from real-world environments. Annotating large sets of text documents for machine learning remains a challenging task due to its labor-intensive and time-consuming nature. A promising approach to streamline annotation involves using active learning methods, which selectively recall specialist annotators for additional documents that are more likely to be informative. Despite its potential, the method's practical application is hindered by the lack of a retrieval module that can efficiently identify such documents. In our work, we present an end-to-end system for active learning annotation, which incorporates a neural document retrieval module based on neural embeddings, and is complemented by a thorough evaluation of various document representation methods. Compared to a straightforward baseline, our system yields significantly improved results, with an increased percentage of informative samples retrieved and a corresponding reduction in annotation costs. Specifically, our approach achieves a relative improvement of 15% in retrieving the top 1000 most informative samples, as measured by expected reduction in annotation cost. Additionally, our study provides insights into the effectiveness of different document representation methods, including neural-based methods that are typically overlooked in active learning research. With improved results across all evaluation metrics, our system provides a viable solution for annotating large text datasets. To address this issue, we've developed RoadAtlas, a mobile application designed to optimize road inspection operations. By leveraging image processing and machine learning techniques, RoadAtlas can automatically identify areas of interest within captured photos and videos and assign relevant labels without requiring human intervention. The application prioritizes label assignment based on inspection criteria and existing data, focusing processing power on low-hanging fruits – images that are easily classified with high accuracy. By streamlining data capture and reduction, RoadAtlas successfully reduced the amount of data collected for each road segment by 3.4-fold and minimized storage needs for each inspection finding. In tandem with its analytical features, RoadAtlas enabled data-driven decisions by mapping road conditions, detecting patterns, and triggering alerts when certain conditions occur. By facilitating efficient data capture and reduction, RoadAtlas has the potential to enhance the effectiveness of other mobile data collection platforms. Sound source separation faces significant challenges due to the complex nature of real-world audio, where information about source and scene is often implicit. Resolving this complexity demands a large, detailed and anatomically precise dataset with clear labels for both source and scene. However, existing sound source separation datasets fall short of this standard, being either small, poorly annotated or limited to specific scenarios. In response, we introduce VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS), the first large detailed dataset with precise labels for source, scene and relevance. Featuring 2000 minutes of audio from 15 sources and 8 scenes, VGG-SS surpasses existing datasets in size and anatomical complexity. To further enhance and standardize the separation task, we develop a score metric called Mean Source Score (MSS), which goes beyond mean squared error to assess separation quality based on explicit scene and source information. To demonstrate the capabilities of VGG-SS, we created SimpleSoundSense, a straightforward source separation model utilizing self-supervised pre-training. SimpleSoundSense achieves remarkable results on VGG-SS, outperforming the state-of-the-art and showcasing the effectiveness of the dataset. With VGG-SS and its scoring metric, we aim to provide a comprehensive foundation for advanced sound source separation models, pushing the field beyond basic feedforward networks. Recently, researchers have focused intensely on constructing graph-agnostic models using hyperbolic space, particularly in the Euclidean plane. However, the underlying assumption that all graphs are similar in structure doesn't reflect reality. In this paper, we develop a new model called Lorentzian Graph Convolutional Network (LGCN) for non-similar graph structures using the Lorentzian space. We represent each graph as a pair of complex manifolds within the Lorentzian space and introduce an innovative projection technique to maintain structural invariance. Additionally, we designed a new hyperbolic graph convolutional neural network cell based on the Schur decomposition, which provides a more accurate node feature representation than existing methods. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed LGCN outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, including Euclidean and hyperbolic graph convolutional networks, on six public datasets. Furthermore, we showcase the effectiveness of the model in graph classification with limited labeled data. The source code for LGCN is available online at https://github.com/huanghaida/LGCN.

A new approach using deep neural networks has been introduced for automatically classifying and grading colorectal adenomas based on video endoscopy images. This technique utilizes a unique dataset containing 1,568 video clips and their corresponding text descriptions, collected from 1,084 patients undergoing regular screening for colorectal cancer. Expert pathologists evaluated the images and provided both video-based and text-based diagnosis/grading, which served as the ground truth for the dataset. Multiple deep neural network models were developed and tested on this dataset, with one model demonstrating exceptional performance. This model achieved: (1) high accuracy (0.83) in distinguishing normal colon tissue from adenomas, (2) effective classification (0.62) among different types of adenomas (tubular, villous, and mixed), and (3) reliable grading (mean absolute error 0.51) of adenomas. Notably, when provided with video clips containing multiple lesions, the model demonstrated the ability to focus on the most clinically significant ones. Additionally, incorporating text-based diagnosis/grading information into the model led to improved classification (0.69) and grading (0.44) performance. Overall, this technique represents a significant advancement in using video endoscopy images and their descriptions for colorectal adenoma classification and grading. However, it is crucial to note that further validation is required through analysis on diverse datasets and in actual clinical settings before it can be adopted for practical use. As a potential clinical tool, it could ultimately contribute to early detection and reduction of colorectal cancer mortality rates. As a technique utilizing video endoscopy and their descriptions, it may also be applied to similar tasks involving other types of cancers. We've assessed the water content in three recent ordinary chondrite falls, namely Benenitra and Chelyabinsk, which contained relatively high levels of water, and compared it with four Antarctic finds that have low levels of water. Using data from CMS at the Brookhaven National Laboratory, we determined water content by measuring the decay of positrons resulting from the measurement of annihilation radiation of both the chondrite and iron samples. The results show that the water content in the three recent falls and the four Antarctic finds range from 0.35 to 0.76 ppm, significantly lower than the estimated 10 ppm water content in the early solar system. This study provides a new measure of the Earth's water depletion and confirms previous findings that the Earth's water loss occurred late in its formation history. Furthermore, this study suggests a possible link between the delivery of water-bearing chondrites and the Earth's active surface, which caused the water to be released into the oceans rather than being incorporated into the planet's interior. In addition, it is observed that the degree of water loss experienced by the delivered chondrites, as reflected in their current water content, does not correlate with their delivery location or final water content, indicating that the water loss in these chondrites occurred prior to their arrival on Earth. The results also indicate that Antarctic finds experienced a longer period of exposure to the solar system's radiation than the falls, and finally, it is found that the degree of metamorphism experienced by these chondrites does not significantly affect their water content. In conclusion, this study provides new insights into the structure and composition of the Earth, the Earth's water depletion, the delivery of water to the Earth, the evolution of the Earth's oceans, the radiation history of the delivered chondrites, the effectiveness of the Earth's magnetic field in protecting the delivery system, and the water loss experienced by the delivered chondrites. Finally, it is noted that a second generation of water-bearing chondrites may have delivered water to the Earth, and it is proposed that a third generation, consisting of chondrites with high levels of water and other volatile elements, may have delivered these elements to the Earth and ultimately became responsible for the planet's current water and atmospheric composition. The study also suggests a possible solution to the Earth's ocean enigma and provides a new perspective on the Earth's accretion history. We introduce an efficient scheme for calculating scattering behaviors of particles using an expansion in terms of vector and tensor multipoles. This method is uniquely adapted to treat inhomogeneous particles with irregular shapes, and demonstrates significant benefits over traditional multipole methods in terms of computational speed and accuracy. By applying this approach, we provide explicit equations that describe the scattering cross-section and the rotational diffusion time in relation to the photophysical properties of the system, and verify its efficacy through computational simulations of the emission characteristics of an irregularly shaped cadmium selenide nanocrystal. The associated code is freely accessible as part of the Jellum package on GitHub. Leveraging this code, we highlight the value of using this multipoles-based approach by comparing it with existing methods that model flat nanoparticles, particularly in the context of treating non-radiative effects and rotational diffusion processes. In addition, we highlight potential applications and future directions for this code, including its potential extension to treat systems composed of multiple particles.

Unlike conventional GANs that generate artificial images from random noise, this model uses a pair of related images to learn representations of diseases and their removal. By manipulating latent codes, the model demonstrates the ability to model complex medical conditions and organ functions, accurately predicting how images would change when patient position or respiratory phase changes. Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of this approach, showcasing superior performance over baseline GANs at generating synthetic images. This research introduces a higher-order two-dimensional monomial approximation using Lagrange polynomials and general divergence terms. The new approach can be viewed as an expansion of the Lagrange polynomial method, enabling the flexible creation of Lagrange polynomials for various degrees and coordinate systems. Theoretical accuracy assessments for function approximation and advection equations were conducted, demonstrating that the proposed method offers similar accuracy to the standard Lagrange polynomial method when using similar degrees of freedom. The study also explores the impact of using a second-order Lagrange polynomial approximation on an irregular triangle mesh, showing that it yields more accurate results than using a first-order Lagrange polynomial approximation on the same mesh. The benefits of the proposed method are further highlighted through a plate bending problem solution, where higher-order Lagrange polynomial approximations yield substantially better results when compared to linear Lagrange polynomial approximations for large deformation scenarios. The study concludes by discussing potential applications and future directions for adapting the proposed approach to other methods, such as the discontinuous Galerkin method.
